arxiv-2510-00173:
Alfredo Gamboa, Juan Limaco, and Luis Yapu wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on steering a heat-like equation to rest. The equation is parabolic and semilinear, and its diffusion fades to zero at one boundary point. The domain itself changes shape over time, which makes control harder. The authors use a game-like Stackelberg-Nash strategy, with one leader control and follower controls chasing Nash balance.

First they handle the linearized system with a Carleman inequality built for degenerate, time-varying cases. That estimate gives local controllability for the linearized problem. A classical inverse function theorem then lifts the result to the full nonlinear equation. The conclusion is local null controllability: nearby starting states can be driven exactly to zero. Results like this extend control theory toward realistic settings where domains move and materials degenerate.
arxiv-2510-00573:
Yen-Ling Tai and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on robots that scoop food without spilling it. Scooping sounds simple, but foods shift, slump, and scatter unpredictably. Demonstration-trained policies often fail on new dishes and portion sizes. Their system, GRITS, wraps a diffusion policy in guidance from a dedicated spillage predictor.

The predictor learns from simulated spills involving spheres, cubes, cones, and cylinders of varied mass and friction. At run time it scores candidate motion rollouts and steers sampling toward safer paths. Training covered six food categories on a real robotic platform. Testing then threw ten unseen categories with different shapes and quantities at the robot. The system succeeded in about eighty-two percent of trials overall. Spillage dropped to about four percent, over forty percent below unguided baselines.
arxiv-2510-00673:
Luciano examines a modified cosmology built on a generalized mass-to-horizon entropy relation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Entropic cosmology explains the universe's faster expansion through forces tied to the cosmic horizon. Earlier work showed that simple versions collapse back to the standard entropy formula and inherit its limits. A generalized relation with two free parameters opens a genuinely different model.

Luciano tests what that model implies for the early universe. Using a spherical top-hat model, he shows the growth of matter clumps changes clearly under the modified expansion history. He also studies primordial gravitational waves, the faint ripples born in the universe's first moments. In parts of the parameter space, the model boosts their expected abundance. Upcoming detectors sensitive below a thousand hertz could therefore test the idea directly.
arxiv-2510-00973:
Constantinou, Shorttle, and Rimmer constrain lightning on Venus through atmospheric chemistry in this 2025 arXiv paper. Whether Venus has lightning at all is still disputed, since flashes, radio signals, and plasma waves have given conflicting answers. The authors take an indirect route through nitric oxide, a gas that only lightning produces in Venus's lower atmosphere. If the reported nitric oxide abundance is real, some lightning rate must sustain it against chemical destruction.

Their photochemical-kinetic modelling asks how much lightning power that balance requires. Matching the reported abundance demands at least three times the total lightning power released on Earth, by their headline calculation. That could mean more frequent strikes, stronger strikes, or both. The rarity of optical flashes hints the strikes may sit deep below the clouds, perhaps from volcanic or wind-driven charging near the surface.
arxiv-2510-01373:
Sakai and a large Thai-led collaboration detect hydroxyl maser emission from a famous returning comet with a national radio telescope. Comet 12P/Pons-Brooks swings by every seventy-one years, and its recent return drew global attention. Water breakdown products produce the hydroxyl signal, a tracer of the comet's activity.

The forty-meter Thai National Radio Telescope made the detection during the apparition. Maser emission signals active outgassing as sunlight warms the nucleus. Such measurements calibrate how much water the comet sheds compared with its dust and gas displays. A regional facility thereby joined the worldwide watch on a historic visitor. Hydroxyl radicals are water's fingerprint after sunlight splits the molecule. Dozens of Thai institutions share the author list. Outburst-prone 12P drew crowds during its bright 2024 approach. Maser amplification makes the faint line detectable at all. Radio eyes complement the optical show.
arxiv-2510-01473:
Halstead and co-authors ask researchers whether they would actually trust language models to find datasets for them. Keyword matching forces searchers to guess the exact words earlier researchers used, and relevant data hides. Semantic search promises relief, but acceptance by working researchers was unmeasured.

Focus groups with twenty-seven researchers fed a conceptual model of adoption. Benefits alone do not persuade researchers to switch tools. Barriers around trust dominate, while transparency features offer the route past them. Developers get a co-design mandate: build with users, or watch the tool sit unused. Natural language questions replace brittle keyword strings in the vision. Missing relevant data is the quiet cost of vocabulary mismatch. Human-centered design frames the whole inquiry methodologically. Reporting limitations openly counts as a transparency feature users wanted. Discovery quietly shapes what science gets done downstream.
arxiv-2510-01573:
Liu, Zhou, and Loureiro show that a common plasma instability can freeze the growth of magnetic fields. In many plasmas, small magnetic tangles merge into larger ones, moving energy upscale. That inverse transfer helps explain how weak seed fields could grow into cosmic magnetism.

Simulations of decaying collisionless plasma reveal the firehose instability spoiling the mergers. By canceling magnetic tension, it stops islands from coalescing and leaves them stretched thin. A strong guide field, or larger starting structures, restores the merging. The result warns that seed fields from early-universe processes may often fail to grow. The structures stall near the particle Larmor scale, far below cosmic sizes. First-principles simulation catches the kinetic effects that fluid models miss. Magnetization level becomes the switch that decides whether growth proceeds. Astrophysical seed theories must now check this kinetic gate. Elongated shapes are the visible scar.
arxiv-2510-01873:
Fabian, Kąkol, and Leiderman clarify a differentiability property for spaces of continuous functions in this 2025 mathematics paper. The Asplund property is well understood for Banach spaces, where it ties to where functions can be differentiated. Extending it to function spaces with the compact-open topology produced clashing definitions in the literature. The authors set out to unify that scattered picture.

Their treatment covers the space of continuous functions on any Tychonoff space, far beyond the Banach setting. They establish a characterization of when that function space holds the Asplund property. Classical results enter along the way, including the Namioka-Phelps theorem and what it implies here. Every proof is presented in self-contained form using standard techniques. The paper thus serves as both a correction and a reference. Functional analysts get one consistent language for Asplund behavior in general function spaces.
arxiv-2510-01973:
Øvereng, Baggaley, and Angheluta simulate collisions between vortices and waves in quantum fluids in this 2025 physics paper. Their system is a two-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate, governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. Vortex collisions drive the decay of quantum turbulence in such fluids. What happens to the energy during each collision type was only partly understood.

When vortex-antivortex dipoles collide, kinetic energy moves from swirling flow into sound-like modes. Below a critical separation, annihilation events release quantum energy that mediates the transfer. Above that threshold, plain vortex acceleration does the job instead. Wave-vortex collisions look different again. An incoming solitary wave splits into two transient phase slips at the vortex. One slip helps annihilate the vortex, while the other grows a stable core and replaces it. Trajectory and spectrum analysis backs each of these mechanisms. The results sharpen the picture of how quantum turbulence spends its energy.
arxiv-2510-02073:
Behrmann and ten co-authors read tissue properties from wearable light signals with a physics-based model in this 2025 paper. Optical sensors in smartwatches use light pulses to yield heart rate and blood oxygen. The waveforms hold richer body information, but deep learning reads it through opaque features. Clinicians cannot interpret those features, and sensor designers cannot use them.

Their model, PPGen, ties the signal to readable physical and optical parameters of the tissue. On top of it, hybrid amortized inference estimates those values quickly and robustly. Simulation-trained inference keeps the speed of deep learning while restoring physical meaning. Validation used synthetic datasets generated by the model itself. The approach promises wearables that report tissue properties, not just pulse statistics. It also gives sensor designers a principled way to test hardware choices in simulation.
arxiv-2510-02473:
Sawczuk and Gnang give two fresh proofs of a classic graph polynomial identity. Their 2025 mathematics paper concerns the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial. That polynomial lists every cycle visiting all vertices once. It also connects to two famous matrix polynomials. The determinant and permanent sit at the heart of algebra. The identity ties the cycle polynomial to both of them. The first proof uses a direct counting argument. It stays accessible to readers with basic combinatorics. The second proof treats monomials as lists of graphs. Algebra and combinatorics meet in that viewpoint.

A matching identity for Hamiltonian paths follows the same route. Hamiltonicity testing is a landmark hard problem in computing. Polynomial identities give theorists new handles on it. Two proofs illuminate different faces of one truth. Students gain an entry point through the simpler proof. Researchers gain a flexible method for related identities.
arxiv-2510-02773:
Al Rahat and co-authors fix security bugs in OpenID Connect programs with a counterexample guided repair engine. Their 2025 software security paper presents a tool called AuthFix. Single sign-on bugs have caused breaches and heavy losses. Hand patching such flaws is slow and error prone. AuthFix chains three stages together. Fault localization finds where the flow breaks. A language model synthesizes candidate patches. A Petri net model checker verifies each patch. Counterexamples steer the next repair attempt when checks fail.

A dataset of known OpenID bugs graded the tool. It produced correct patches for seventeen of twenty three bugs. Many patches matched developer fixes in meaning. The verifier keeps plausible but wrong patches out. Authentication code guards nearly every online account. Automated, verified repair scales where audits cannot. The model checker is the trust anchor of the design.
arxiv-2510-04273:
Strang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on learning better branching decisions while a mixed-integer programming solver works through a stream of problems. Branch-and-bound solvers depend heavily on which variable they branch on, yet expert heuristics are tuned for broad average performance. Industrial users often solve many similar instances whose matrices, right-hand sides, bounds, or objectives change slightly. The authors exploit that repetition with an online learning method built around a graph-based heuristic called influence branching.

The heuristic uses graph representations of an instance's structure during the early branch-and-bound iterations. Thompson sampling ranks representations by the speedup they deliver over SCIP, updating choices as more instances arrive. Competition experiments achieved performance comparable to leading online learning approaches. The authors report evidence that the method transfers to online settings with changes in several parts of an instance and more samples for learning.
arxiv-2510-04373:
Hadi Nekoei and coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on helping AI agents learn new tasks. Agents do well on familiar work but often fail in new settings. Fixing them with training runs is costly, and it can make them forget older skills. Past work sessions hold useful lessons, but the records are long and noisy. The team built a system that turns those old records into short hints.

The system is called JEF Hinter, and it zooms in on key steps inside long work records. It learns from failed runs as well as good ones, which most older methods cannot do. At run time, it picks the hints that fit the current task and shows them to the agent. Tests on three task suites beat strong baselines, including hints written by people. The gains held on new goals and new tasks, at only a small added cost.
arxiv-2510-04573:
Haoqiang Kang and six coauthors at the University of California, San Diego wrote this 2025 paper on better reasoning in language models. Models reason by writing a chain of thought, one token after the next. That order locks early words in place, so the model cannot go back and revise them. The team moved reasoning into a latent space where whole blocks can be reworked.

An autoencoder first compresses text reasoning steps into blocks of latent thought tokens. A diffusion model in that space then denoises a block at once, with attention running both ways inside the block. Longer horizons and repeated refinement become cheap in that setup. Many diverse reasoning paths can grow in parallel for one question. On math and planning tests, the system beat rival methods. It won on accuracy, on diversity of solutions, and on how readable the reasoning stayed. The authors call the system LaDiR.
arxiv-2510-04673:
Chan Hee Song and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on teaching computer agents from videos of people. Agents that use software need demonstrations of real tasks, but labeled demonstrations are scarce and costly. The web, meanwhile, overflows with screen recordings of people doing tasks in real programs. Their framework, Watch and Learn, mines those videos for training material. It turns footage into action traces an agent can replay.

The key move is an inverse dynamics task: guess the action that links two screen states in a row. That puzzle is easier to learn than generation and needs little hand engineering. A retrieval step first gathers videos that match a task family. The pipeline produced more than fifty three thousand high quality traces from videos. Those traces helped agents both as examples inside the prompt and as training data. Gains showed up on an operating system benchmark, for leading frameworks alike.
arxiv-2510-04973:
Arjan Cornelissen extends a young framework for building quantum algorithms in this 2025 arXiv paper. In the framework, an algorithm is drawn as a hypergraph. The edges act like switches that route inputs to the output the algorithm computes. Until now, the framework handled only yes-or-no style problems.

Cornelissen generalizes it to problems with many possible answers. The wider framework turns out to contain three older approaches as special cases. They are quantum divide and conquer, decision trees, and unified quantum walk search. For walk search, his methods let subroutine costs be shared across runs. That change simplifies the algorithm and removes log factors from its query cost.
arxiv-2510-05073:
Watwood and twenty-three colleagues probe the inner structure of a silicon isotope in this 2025 arXiv paper. They study silicon-32, whose protons and neutrons occupy a shell called 1s-0d. Knowing which orbitals sit empty reveals how the nucleus arranges itself. The team fired helium-3 at silicon-32 in inverse kinematics to add a proton.

The reaction produced phosphorus-33 states up to about 4.5 MeV of excitation. From the measured rates, the authors extracted spectroscopic factors for each orbital. Combined with neutron data, these gave the proton vacancies in the silicon-32 ground state. The 1s orbital proved consistent with being completely empty, in both silicon-32 and silicon-34. Shell-model calculations matched the measured distributions well.
arxiv-2510-05373:
Utkarsh Saxena and Kaushik Roy squeeze the memory cache of large language models to two bits in this 2025 arXiv paper. The key-value cache grows with every token and dominates GPU memory at long contexts. Quantizing it aggressively introduces errors that corrupt attention. Generation quality then degrades noticeably.

Their framework, KVLinC, attacks the two error sources separately. A Hadamard rotation reduces quantization error in the stored values. Lightweight linear correction adapters then compensate for errors in the quantized keys. Across LLaMA, Qwen2.5, and Qwen3 models, KVLinC matched or beat strong baselines at higher compression. A custom attention kernel ran up to about 2.55 times faster than FlashAttention.
arxiv-2510-05473:
Yánez-Parreño and colleagues grew aluminum films in deep cold and watched the metal change. Aluminum is the workhorse material of superconducting quantum circuits. The team deposited thin films on sapphire in vacuum at six kelvin, far below room temperature. Their 2025 paper compares those cold-grown films with normal ones across structure, optics, and electrical behavior.

Cold growth made the films grainy and more disordered than usual. Thicker cold films even turned yellow instead of mirror bright. The smaller grains strengthened superconductivity, raising the temperature and field the films could withstand. The method offers a clean way to tune disorder without adding chemical impurities. The team then built microwave resonators from both kinds of film. Both kinds showed similar quality, limited by the same surface loss process. Cold films also carried higher kinetic inductance, a trait prized in sensitive detectors.
arxiv-2510-05773:
Haisch settles a dispute over tiny hadronic effects in a flagship Higgs decay. The Higgs decay into two photons runs through W boson and top quark loops. Recent studies reported puzzling, contradictory sizes for non-perturbative hadronic contributions. His 2025 dispersive analysis computes them systematically at last.

Dispersion relations respecting low-energy QCD symmetries organize the calculation. Hadronic effects enter through form factors of intermediate hadronic states. The result shifts the decay width by only about zero point zero zero four percent. That is negligible even for future high-precision collider measurements. The finding matches the naive expectation that perturbative loops dominate completely. The channel thus stays among the cleanest for precision Higgs studies. The Standard Model prediction's accuracy now rests on perturbative corrections alone. Percent-level branching ratios at the high-luminosity LHC motivated the check. Haisch also estimates hadronic effects in gluon-fusion Higgs production.
arxiv-2510-05973:
Smagin and colleagues extend the Fourier modal method to bi-anisotropic gratings. The method is a fast, exact workhorse for layered optical stacks. Standard versions cannot treat matter that couples electric and magnetic fields. Their 2025 version admits any magneto-electric tensor for such chiral matter.

Fourier tensors of the matter values are derived for two schemes. One scheme applies Lifeng Li's factor rules, and the other omits them. Without magneto-electric coupling, both fall back to the standard forms. With coupling, the factor-rule scheme gains speed much faster. The gain holds even when the chirality strength is large. Circular dichroism and optical activity are the effects behind the advance. Chiral molecules, lacking mirror symmetry, cause both effects at root. The scope is layered stacks periodic in two directions. Non-reciprocal and chiral stacks can now be modeled exactly with the standard toolkit.
arxiv-2510-06273:
Srivastava and Niedzielski classify transient noise in LIGO data with a vision transformer in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Short glitches contaminate the detector stream and hinder gravitational wave detection. Gravity Spy sorts these noise events into classes, and the O3 run added two classes older models never saw.

They fine-tuned a pretrained Vision Transformer, ViT-B/32, on a combined dataset. Training merged the original classes with two additional O3a classes, twenty-four in total. The model reached classification efficiency near ninety-two percent. Sorting glitches reliably helps analysts veto noise and protect real signals. It feeds detector characterization, since glitch families guide hardware fixes. Image transformers transfer well to spectrogram-like detector data. Vision transformers join the toolkit for keeping gravitational wave searches clean as new noise types appear.
arxiv-2510-06573:
Xinyun Cao and four colleagues build tools that help blind and low-vision people use virtual 3D worlds. Their 2025 paper presents RAVEN, a system for real-time access to virtual scenes. Blind users often struggle with spatial awareness, navigation, and interaction in these spaces. Older aids add sound or touch cues, but those aids are fixed in advance.

RAVEN lets users ask questions and request changes in plain language while a scene runs. The system understands the scene and generates code to modify it on the spot. Eight blind or low-vision participants tested the system in a study. They found it intuitive, flexible, and empowering to use. The team also reports real limits around reliability and clear error reporting. Their work moves accessibility from a static feature toward a conversation that users control themselves.
arxiv-2510-06973:
Zhantao Yang leads a team tackling a failure in captions for long videos. Their 2025 paper studies the ID-Matching problem, where a caption must recognize the same person across different frames. Getting identities wrong makes captions confusing and hurts text-to-video generation. Prior fixes relied on point-wise matching and generalized poorly.

The team built a benchmark to measure identity matching in captions. Probing GPT-4o with it revealed two levers that help. Captions improve when the model uses image information more fully, and when each person's description carries more detail. Their method, RICE, builds on those insights inside vision-language models. It tracks individuals through a long video. On GPT-4o, identity precision jumped from fifty percent to ninety percent. Recall leapt from fifteen percent to eighty percent. RICE beat the previous best system, ShareGPT4Video, on every benchmark tried. Consistent identities make long captions more trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-07173:
Khondaker, Harrington, and Shehata introduce NurseLLM, which they call the first language model built just for nursing. Their 2025 paper notes that medical models mostly serve doctors' tasks. Nursing has its own knowledge, exams, and daily decisions. The team set out to build both training data and tests for that field. Their model targets multiple-choice questions across a wide range of nursing topics.

A multi-stage pipeline generated a large set of nursing questions for training. New benchmarks were built to grade models fairly on nursing knowledge. In tests, NurseLLM beat general and medical models of similar size. The authors also probed step-by-step reasoning and teams of cooperating models. Both showed promise for harder nursing tasks. Specialized models like this could support nurse training and exam practice. The work argues that each health profession may need its own tailored model.
arxiv-2510-07373:
Lesser and co-authors teach a machine to predict which materials will superconduct, and at what heat limit. Their 2025 paper mixes chemistry-aware inputs with learning whose logic can be inspected. Their inputs sum up local bonding patterns through graphlet histograms and symmetry counts drawn from crystal structures. A custom kernel feeds those inputs into Gaussian-process models. The models both estimate the limit and sort likely superconductors, reporting doubt alongside each call. Training data came from a checked database of three-dimensional superconductors.

The heat predictor explained most of the spread in measured values. A test of which inputs mattered then found that just four local bonding inputs nearly matched the full model's power. One overlooked input stood out: the gap in electron affinity between neighboring atoms. Bonding-related values proved surprisingly strong across compounds. Readable predictors like this guide lab synthesis toward promising candidates.
arxiv-2510-07573:
Willcox and a large team argue that black hole masses come in two families, and the gravitational wave data now show it. Their 2025 paper uses the latest LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA catalog, which nearly doubles the known merging binary black holes. Below thirty solar masses, the distribution of chirp masses, the combination detectors measure best, shows three peaks. Recent stellar evolution models independently predict two families of newborn black hole masses, stamped by structure in the collapsing star's core. Folded through binary pairing, two black hole families naturally produce three chirp-mass peaks.

The trimodality survives every variation, emerging as a robust fingerprint of the new remnant-mass prescription. Traditional formation models without the bimodal spectrum cannot reproduce it. The updated models also predict merger rates a few times lower, closer to what the detectors observe.
arxiv-2510-07673:
Nguyen and a large collaboration wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on supernovae and cosmic structure. Type Ia supernovae explode with nearly standard brightness, so small brightness changes carry information. Their host galaxies drift with the growth of large-scale structure. Those drifts should leave matching patterns in galaxy maps and supernova brightness. The team searched for that cross-pattern using survey data. Their sample covered only the nearby universe, within redshift one tenth.

They combined the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey release with the Pantheon+ supernova collection at low redshift. The cross-correlation signal was detected between galaxy positions and supernova brightness. Fitting the signal gave a growth rate of structure that matches the standard cosmological model's prediction. Mock catalogs from large simulations confirmed the method recovers the true value. The authors argue that supernova brightness patterns can become a new tool for measuring how cosmic structure grows.
arxiv-2510-08473:
Lynn Engelberts and co-authors speed up a quantum attack on lattice cryptography in a 2025 arXiv paper. Finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, the problem called SVP, underpins post-quantum cryptosystems. The fastest heuristic attacks use sieving, which repeatedly combines lattice vectors into shorter ones. Taking triples instead of pairs in each step saves memory but was slower in quantum time.

Their improved 3-tuple sieving cuts the quantum time exponent from 0.3098 to 0.2846 in the dimension, a meaningful drop for exponential algorithms. A preprocessing step links each vector to nearby center points, focusing the search on promising neighborhoods. Two-level amplitude amplification, a quantum search booster, does the rest of the work. Memory use matches the improved time budget in their accounting. They call it the fastest known quantum algorithm for this problem under that memory limit.
arxiv-2510-08873:
Jin and co-authors design custom AI chips by snapping together a small set of reusable blocks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Modern accelerators are usually built as one uniform design, yet each operation inside a neural network has its own pattern of work and memory needs. Custom chips fit those patterns better but cost a fortune to design from scratch. Chiplets, small prefabricated pieces of silicon, promise reuse, if designers can tell which pieces are truly needed.

Their framework, Mozart, breaks networks down operation by operation and explores mixes of chiplets and memory types. Eight well-chosen chiplets sufficed to build composite chips that cut energy use by more than forty percent against uniform rivals. Performance stayed within a few percent of designs with no reuse limits. For data center language model serving, energy fell by roughly a sixth, and speculative decoding ran much faster while using far less power.
arxiv-2510-08973:
Patra, Kolte, and Bandyopadhyay solve a geometry problem with practical uses in simulation and robotics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Given a point in space and a quadric surface, a bowl- or saddle-shaped surface with a central axis of symmetry, how close is the point to the surface? The answer feeds collision checks, where a physics engine must know the gap to a curved wall.

The team first classifies general quadrics to recognize the axisymmetric ones. Symmetry then lets them flatten the three-dimensional problem into a two-dimensional one about conics, the classic curves of plane geometry. Their method works directly with conic properties such as eccentricity and the sub-normal. Cases split by where the point sits: two sub-cases for parabolas and three for ellipses and hyperbolas. Implemented in the C language, the solver ran faster than the widely used Bullet physics library.
arxiv-2510-09573:
Siphiwe Shandu, Thabiso Moropa, and Alain Ndjiongue explore a new way to connect underground mines in a 2025 arXiv letter. Mines need wireless links deep below ground, and laying new infrastructure is costly. Their idea, contactless power line communication, sends signals through the radiation of existing power cables, treating the wires as long-wire antennas rather than plugging into them directly.

The authors build a system-level model that cascades a radio channel with the power line channel. It accounts for multipath propagation, frequency-dependent weakening, and Rician fading, a standard model of signal fluctuation. Simulations between one and twenty gigahertz show the wire's length strongly shapes its radiation pattern, directivity, and input impedance. The findings suggest the approach transmits waves without direct electrical contact. The team presents it as a robust, low-cost option that fits existing mining power infrastructure and reduces maintenance.
arxiv-2510-09673:
Simone Fischer-Hübner, Leonardo Martucci, Lejla Islami, Ala Sarah Alaqra, and Farzaneh Karegar survey cybersecurity readiness in Swedish organisations in a 2025 arXiv paper. Threats and incidents keep growing, and organisations in Värmland, a region of Inner Scandinavia, must raise their defences. The authors ask what competence those organisations have and what education they still need.

The study combines interviews with key leaders from firms and public sector bodies and an earlier survey of the same population. It examines current readiness and the demand for training and skills growth. The authors then discuss how far the findings generalise beyond Värmland and Sweden, and which parts may be specific to the local context. They conclude by proposing concrete efforts to strengthen cybersecurity competence across Inner Scandinavia, aimed at both firms and public bodies.
arxiv-2510-09873:
Chan, Pantangi, Razafimahatratra, and Peter Sin study state transfer in oriented Cayley graphs in this 2025 arXiv paper in quantum information. Perfect state transfer means a quantum state placed at one vertex arrives intact at another after a fixed time. Oriented Cayley graphs are directed networks built from a group's structure.

The authors construct examples of perfect and multiple state transfer across a wide range of groups. Their examples span abelian groups, where operations commute, up to nonsolvable groups with far richer structure. They also prove general restrictions and nonexistence results, marking where transfer cannot happen. The results map the border between groups that support faithful quantum communication and those that do not.
arxiv-2510-10073:
Ying and co-authors present SecureWebArena in this 2025 arXiv paper on the security of web agents. Agents built on large vision-language models can automate complex online tasks. In real deployments they face serious security risks, from malicious pages to deceptive prompts.

SecureWebArena is a holistic benchmark for those risks. It evaluates how agents behave when the web environment itself turns hostile, rather than only whether they finish a benign task. A shared security benchmark lets developers compare defenses on equal footing. The authors motivate the work by the gap between agent capability and agent safety: automation that books, buys, and clicks must also resist manipulation while doing so.
arxiv-2510-10173:
Haimes introduces Chord Colourizer in this 2025 arXiv paper on music visualization. The system finds the musical key of an audio signal in near real time and shows it visually. Notes are assigned colors from Isaac Newton's original color wheel, keeping the historic link between pitch and hue.

A graphical interface displays the key as the music plays. The system also drives an Arduino-controlled LED display with 3D-printed star-shaped diffusers, giving a physical ambient representation in the room. The design joins music analysis with synesthetic display, where one sense is rendered as another. Such tools can support teaching, performance, and accessible music experiences for listeners who benefit from visual cues.
arxiv-2510-10373:
Salas studies boundary behavior of analytic functions on Banach spaces in this 2025 arXiv paper in functional analysis. The spaces considered hold analytic functions on the unit disc, with polynomials dense inside them and point evaluations continuous. The question is how wildly a typical function's values can grow near the boundary circle.

Salas proves that if such a space contains one function whose modulus has limit superior infinity almost everywhere on the circle, then the same holds for a residual set of functions. Residual means topologically generic: wild boundary behavior is the rule, not the exception. The result extends classical facts about Hardy-type spaces to a broad abstract setting.
arxiv-2510-10673:
Filippo Calderoni and Adam Clay measure how hard it is to classify a class of ordered groups, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The groups are finitely generated and bi-orderable, meaning their elements can be lined up in an order respected by multiplication from both sides. The question is the isomorphism problem: how complex is it to tell whether two such groups are really the same? The authors approach the problem through descriptive set theory, which grades classification problems by difficulty.

They analyze the standard Borel space of left orderable groups that are finitely generated, and its subspace of bi-orderable ones, using spaces of relative cones to encode the orders. With this setup, they show the isomorphism relation on these groups is weakly universal. That is a strong complexity statement, ruling out any simple complete invariant for them.
arxiv-2510-10973:
Sanchit Sinha and four co-authors train vision language models to reason about charts reliably and explainably, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These models ace many visual tasks but falter on unfamiliar chart data, and asking them to show their reasoning often makes answers worse. Their Chart-RVR framework fine tunes models with reinforcement learning driven by automatically verifiable rewards. Three rewards are combined: correct chart type classification, faithful reconstruction of the chart's data table, and conformity to a sound reasoning process.

Applied to models with three billion parameters, Chart-RVR consistently beat standard supervised fine tuning on both familiar and out of distribution chart datasets. It closed much of the out of distribution gap while improving the fidelity of the reasoning traces. The resulting models set state of the art results on six chart reasoning benchmarks among models of comparable size.
arxiv-2510-11673:
Nihar Gargava, Vlad Serban, Maryna Viazovska, and Ilaria Viglino count special matrices in this 2025 arXiv paper. The matrices have entries drawn from the integers of a number field, which is a finite extension of the rational numbers. Each matrix has a fixed rank, and its entries stay below a chosen size bound. Earlier work by Katznelson settled the counting problem over the ordinary integers.

The team proves an asymptotic formula for the count over any number field, giving the main growth term as the bound grows. They then apply the formula to lattices built from algebraic codes, deriving an approximate Rogers integral formula for these module lattices. As a payoff, earlier moment estimates about short vectors in random lattices carry over to these code-based lattices when the sets are large enough. Short vectors govern how secure and efficient such lattices are.
arxiv-2510-11773:
Matteo Robbiati and fourteen colleagues present Qiboml, a free software library for hybrid quantum-classical machine learning. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes a toolkit for building models that mix ordinary neural networks with quantum circuits. It builds on the Qibo quantum computing framework and plugs into TensorFlow and PyTorch, the two most popular machine learning libraries. The aim is to let researchers build hybrid models without rewriting plumbing for each machine.

Qiboml models can run almost anywhere. Simulations execute on multi-threaded processors, graphics cards, or multi-GPU systems, using either statevector or tensor network methods. The same models can also run on real quantum processors, whether installed locally or reached through cloud providers. The library supports noise-aware simulation, which imitates the errors of real hardware. It also performs error mitigation and calibration in real time. The authors showcase these features as steps toward practical quantum learning workflows.
arxiv-2510-11973:
Emilia Del Bono, Angus Holford, and Tommaso Sartori ask whether a child's rank in class echoes forty years later. Grades alone might not capture it: being near the top of one's class could build confidence independent of raw scores. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses records for every child in Aberdeen's primary schools in 1962. Quasi-random differences in classmate composition let them separate rank itself from ability.

A higher rank improved performance on the high-stakes eleven-plus exam. It also strengthened internalizing skills, traits tied to self-concept and confidence, which the authors identify as the main channel. A follow-up survey forty years on finds lasting effects. Rank raised educational attainment, especially for girls. Long-run income gains, however, appeared only among boys. The authors read that gap as a fingerprint of the era. In the nineteen sixties, women's access to higher education and skilled jobs was sharply constrained.
arxiv-2511-00073:
Harald Kristen, Daniel Kulmer, and Manuela Hirschmugl compare AI architectures for detecting habitat and land cover change in Gesaeuse National Park, an Austrian alpine protected area. Climate change demands frequent monitoring, but manual mapping is too expensive at the needed rate. Long-term alpine habitat data, with fuzzy class boundaries and highly imbalanced classes, tests geospatial foundation models.

Two paradigms are compared: detecting change after classifying each date, versus detecting change directly. A Prithvi Earth observation model is among the systems evaluated for post-classification change. Environmental monitoring readers get guidance on applying foundation models to complex natural terrain rather than tidy urban scenes.
arxiv-2511-00273:
Sander de Jong and five co-authors study what the public gets wrong about gig work, jobs arranged through apps and platforms. Behind myths of freedom and fair pay sit hidden risks: unclear pay, health and safety dangers, and privacy breaches. In the first phase of their study, more than two hundred crowd workers rated five common myths, and nearly all believed at least one.

In phase two, each person had to defend their view against a counterargument written by an expert or a language model. The exercise exposed how little workers know about shared risks in gig jobs. The authors discuss which persuasion styles worked best and how better public understanding could support fairer rules for platform work.
arxiv-2511-00573:
Wei Feng and Zongyuan Ge tackle category discovery when the data itself shifts domains. Generalized category discovery uses labeled examples of known classes to cluster unlabeled data that may hide new classes. Under distribution shift, performance usually crumbles, and unlabeled samples may also come from unknown domains. Their framework, FREE, reads the problem in the frequency domain, where domain signatures show clearly.

Those amplitude gaps first separate known from unknown domains. Two perturbation strategies follow: swapping amplitude parts across domains to teach adaptation, and perturbing within the unknown domain for robustness. Extended contrastive and clustering losses guide training, and a resampling step focuses effort on groups that are hard to cluster. Across benchmarks, the method finds known and new categories more steadily under shift.
arxiv-2511-00673:
Dominik Drexler speeds up automated planning for tasks with numbers. Most planners translate a task written in a first-order-like language into ground facts before searching, and that grounding step can explode exponentially on hard tasks. Drexler extends a leading lifted successor generator, which works with the compact lifted form, to handle numeric preconditions on actions for the first time.

The method enumerates maximum cliques in a substitution consistency graph, where each clique yields one ground action, now augmented with numeric checks. The generator is proved exact under stated conditions. When conditions fail it may over-list actions, but a final applicability filter restores completeness, and in practice the failure is rare across benchmark domains. Rich numeric planning fragments become searchable without the grounding blowup.
arxiv-2511-00873: A. Puhalskii proves tightness and exponential tightness for the stationary queue lengths of generalised Jackson networks, a standard model of linked service stations where jobs move between queues. The abstract states the scope only: uniform proofs covering several setups concerned with large, normal, and moderate deviations of the queue length sequences.
arxiv-2511-01073:
Marco Buratti and colleagues construct additive Steiner 2-designs, highly symmetric arrangements of points and blocks used in combinatorics. A design is additive over a group when its points are group elements and every block sums to zero. Nearly all known manageable examples live over elementary abelian groups.

The authors give general constructions that unify the known ones and produce new designs. Among them are a resolvable design on fifty two points over the group of order two hundred fifty six. Three pairwise non-isomorphic designs on one hundred twenty one points, none equal to the classical point line design of the projective space. They also prove a negative result: a sought design on five hundred eleven points cannot be cyclic, ruling out one natural construction route.
arxiv-2511-20073:
Zhao, Huang, and Lu teach video models to understand procedures through visible states. Their 2025 paper addresses how machines learn from instructional videos. Agents must grasp tasks as sequences of concrete steps. Prior methods aligned video with task and step descriptions. Those descriptions stay too abstract to match pixels well.

The team adds states: text snapshots of how objects look. States anchor steps to things a model can see. Their Task-Step-State framework links tasks, steps, and states hierarchically. Steps drive transitions between one state and the next. A progressive pretraining strategy unfolds that hierarchy gradually. Training cycles from task to step to state and back. Tests ran on the COIN and CrossTask video datasets. Recognizing tasks, recognizing steps, and forecasting the next step all improved. Ablations credit state supervision as the key driver. Progressive training beat plain joint training clearly. Grounding procedures in visible states is their central claim.
arxiv-2511-20273:
Ahmad, Joshi, and Modi peer inside transformer heads along their singular directions. Their 2025 paper reframes model reading at finer grain. Researchers usually treat each attention head as one unit. That view assumes heads do single jobs. The authors suspect richer substructure hides inside.

Any weight matrix splits into orthogonal singular directions. Circuits may live along a few such directions. The team tested classic interpretability tasks. Indirect object identification was the primary benchmark. Gender pronoun and greater-than tasks checked generality. Famous heads like the name mover were reexamined. One head encoded several overlapping subfunctions at once. Each subfunction aligned with a distinct direction. Circuit nodes lit up along compact low-rank subspaces. Meaningful computation seems concentrated in small direction sets. Some directions resist reading still, they admit. Model behavior looks more compositional than assumed. Future explanations may stitch together a few directions.
arxiv-2511-20373:
Belkova, Ignatyeva, Kalish, and colleagues find light twisted by film surfaces, not just the bulk. Their 2025 paper reports a sign-changing Faraday effect in very thin magnetic films. The Faraday effect rotates light's polarization inside magnetic matter. Textbooks tie its sign to one bulk property. That picture fails once films shrink to nanometers.

Films of five, ten, and sixty-five nanometers were measured. At one fixed wavelength their rotations differed in sign. Thickness alone flipped the direction of rotation. An interface contribution grows important at these scales. Absorption bands make the effect most visible. A model mixes bulk and surface terms. It reproduces the measured spectra nicely. Rotation purely from interfaces was demonstrated too. No bulk contribution was needed for that signal. The sign thus stops reporting magnetization faithfully. Designers must model their exact film stack. Data encryption hardware could exploit the trick. Nanoscale polarization control gains a new lever.
arxiv-2511-20573:
Gou and a large team teach open models to answer picture questions with pictures. Their 2025 paper studies visual question-visual answering, or VQ-VA. Given an image-based question, the model must reply with an image, not text. Closed systems like GPT-Image show this skill already. Open models lag far behind them.

The team built VQ-VA World, a data pipeline run by agents. It crawled and curated about 1.8 million training samples. Image and text interleave in those samples for targeted teaching. A human-curated benchmark, IntelligentBench, grades world and design knowledge plus reasoning. Fine-tuning LightFusion on the new data transformed its score. It jumped from 7.78 to 53.06 on the benchmark used. The best prior open baseline managed only 1.94 points. Closed leaders score near eighty-two, so a gap remains. All weights, data, and pipelines are released openly.
arxiv-2511-20673:
Zheng Hui and co-authors address in 2025 a quiet inefficiency inside generative recommender systems, which suggest products by generating item codes token by token. Each item is stored as tokens from a single codebook, a dictionary of codes, used for every item. Popular items carry rich behaviour records, while obscure long-tail items depend mostly on what they are, so one codebook serves both badly.

Their system, FlexCode, splits a fixed token budget across two codebooks. One captures collaborative signals, patterns in shared user choices; the other captures semantic content. A small mixture-of-experts gate shifts the balance per item, favouring behaviour tokens for hits and meaning tokens for rare items. On public and industrial-scale datasets FlexCode beat strong baselines on every ranking metric used, and even a fixed half-and-half version outperformed most rivals, with the clearest gains on hard-to-recommend tail items.
arxiv-2511-21073:
Runqi Kang and Xing Rong propose in 2025 a way to stretch the reach of possible forces far beyond their natural range. New bosons beyond the Standard Model would mediate exotic interactions between fermions. Those forces fade exponentially over the boson's Compton wavelength, so tabletop searches are confined to tiny scales. Kang and Rong show that as the interaction's oscillation frequency approaches the boson mass, the bosons go nearly on-shell and the effective force range tends to infinity. They call this near-threshold enhancement.

With range no longer the limit, apparatus size sets sensitivity. Their search design targets boson masses from 80 to 800 micro-electronvolts. For one electron coupling, the expected upper bounds improve by 10 orders of magnitude at 800 micro-electronvolts over earlier ones. The trick generalises to other interaction types among the 16 exotic forms. If the bosons exist in that window, this method could find them, or rule them out.
arxiv-2511-21273:
Ana Cordón-Avila, Mostafa Selim, and Momen Abayazid address a moving-target problem in medical robotics in 2025: the liver shifts with every breath while a doctor tries to insert a needle precisely. Their system compensates robotically, predicting the organ's motion with estimation models, while the physician steers remotely through teleoperation. Proximity-based haptic feedback, forces felt through the controls, guides the insertion, and the remote setup keeps the doctor away from X-ray exposure.

Cordón-Avila and her coauthors validated the approach on a robotic liver phantom across five insertions. Motion estimation errors stayed below 3 millimeters in every direction. Final 3D placement errors measured about 2.6 millimeters up-down, about 7.8 millimeters sideways, and about 2.9 millimeters front-back, with the sideways figure reflecting the phantom's larger lateral motion. The team expects fewer mistargeted biopsies and less radiation for staff.
arxiv-2511-21573:
Gabriela Conde-Saavedra, Odylio Denys Aguiar, H. P. de Oliveira, and Maximiliano Ujevic forecast how precisely future gravitational-wave detectors can weigh the heaviest possible neutron star, in 2025. That ceiling, the TOV mass, encodes matter's behavior at extreme densities. It can be read from the post-merger ringdown of two colliding neutron stars, a high-frequency signal future observatories are built to catch.

The team simulated binary neutron star coalescences, using two datasets varying the equation of state and the component masses. They asked what the Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer, and NEMO could each extract. Cosmic Explorer did best, reaching roughly 8 percent precision on that mass under the most optimistic merger rate, 250 events per cubic gigaparsec per year. Even so, the authors conclude that high-frequency sensitivity must improve further, especially to tell whether the remnant collapsed into a black hole. The measurement is coming, but not yet sharp.
arxiv-2511-21673:
Pandiyaraju V, Sreya Mynampati, Abishek Karthik, Poovarasan L, and Saraswathi build a two-stage deep learning system for brain tumor care, in 2025. Gliomas are deadly, and reading their MRI scans manually is slow and error-prone. The team's hybrid pipeline first segments the tumor in three-dimensional MRI volumes, then grades it, aiming to cut diagnostic errors and inspection time for clinicians.

A 3D U-Net performs the segmentation, while a hybrid DenseNet–VGG classifier with multi-head and spatial-channel attention grades the demarcated tumor, focusing on clinically relevant features. Preprocessing normalizes, resamples, and augments the volume data. In testing, the framework reached a Dice coefficient of 98 percent on segmentation and about 99 percent accuracy on grading, beating the older models and attention-free variants cited in the study. The authors frame the system as decision support toward faster clinical outcomes, not a replacement for radiologists.
arxiv-2511-22073:
Arai, a knot theorist, constructs infinitely many pairs of Seifert surfaces. The surfaces that span a given knot or link the way a soap film spans a wire loop, with a surprising combination of properties. Each pair shares the same ambient neighborhood up to deformation and has Seifert matrices that are congruent in the unimodular sense. So the standard algebraic invariants see the two surfaces as identical, yet the surfaces themselves cannot be deformed into one another through space.

The construction works for every link, producing infinitely many such indistinguishable-yet-different pairs. To prove the two surfaces in each pair really differ, Arai uses invariants built from multiple group racks, an algebraic system for distinguishing spatial surfaces. The result sharpens a basic classification problem: even fixing the neighborhood and the Seifert matrix leaves infinitely many genuinely distinct Seifert surfaces for the same link.
arxiv-2511-22373:
Hong works in several complex variables, on numbers measuring how bad a singularity of a plurisubharmonic function is. Such a function can spike downward at a point, and its weighted log canonical threshold records how strong an exponential weight it can carry before an integral blows up near that point. A related measure, the Lelong number, captures the local density of the spike.

Hong proves four theorems giving inequalities between these thresholds. The first generalises a classical inequality of Skoda, which sandwiches the ordinary threshold between two multiples of the reciprocal of the Lelong number, to the weighted case. Examples show the bounds are sharp. Later results add assumptions, such as the Cegrell class of well-behaved functions, for stronger estimates. One further theorem bounds how much the threshold can grow as its parameter increases, in terms of the Lelong number and the dimension.
arxiv-2511-22473:
Al Khansa teaches a neural network to count radar targets in future wireless systems that sense and communicate at once. In OFDM integrated sensing and communication, targets appear on a range-Doppler map. Counting them faces a trade-off: windows sharpening the map leave sidelobes, ghost echoes hiding weak or closely spaced targets, while windows suppressing sidelobes blur the map. A system normally commits to one window.

Instead, the method feeds a convolutional neural network two maps of the same scene, one windowed for resolution and one for sidelobe suppression, and lets it learn to fuse the complementary views. In numerical experiments the dual-window counter beat single-window baselines consistently, scaled more gracefully as scenes grew denser, and stayed more robust as noise changed. Because training happens offline, counting stays lightweight enough for real-time operation.
arxiv-2511-22573:
Rudakovskyi, Vazza, and Tsizh turn the cosmic web into a graph and read cosmology off its shape. In their MAKITRA suite of magneto-hydrodynamical simulations, 300 megaparsecs across with 21 physical model variations, matter haloes become network nodes. The team measures correlation functions, counts of haloes in random spheres, and network centrality statistics. They ask how sensitively each responds to the clustering parameter sigma-8 and to primordial magnetic fields from the early universe.

Centrality statistics prove a novel, sensitive probe: differences of 0.1 in sigma-8 are detectable in their distributions, though cubic-gigaparsec volumes are needed to beat cosmic variance at that precision. The approach also distinguishes primordial magnetic fields of about 4 nanogauss initial strength from much weaker scenarios, even where halo mass functions look identical. Strong fields mimic a lower sigma-8 in network statistics. Ultraviolet reheating, though, erases weaker fields' effects.
arxiv-2511-23173:
Phan and colleagues describe team 3KA's entry to the 2nd WEAR Dataset Challenge. The entry recognizes workout exercises from a single wearable sensor despite messy real-world conditions in the wild, where sensor placement varies and movements are unconstrained. From raw acceleration they derive angle and signal-magnitude features, then extract statistical, fractal and spectral, and higher-order differential descriptors of each movement window.

To fight placement variability they fuse left- and right-limb data into one training set and augment it with sensor rotations and axis inversions. They then classify with a soft-voting pair of gradient boosting models. Under group five-fold evaluation, a genuinely hard split, the system reached a macro F1 score of 58.83 percent overall, scoring 61.72 percent on arm exercises against 55.95 percent on leg exercises, and their feature analysis found fractal and spectral features mattered most for arms yet least for legs.
arxiv-2511-23273:
Andreetto and colleagues present MUSIC, a proof-of-concept detector designed for a proposed muon collider running at 10 tera-electronvolts. It is an energy no lepton collider has ever reached. Muon beams decay as they circulate, flooding the detector with machine-induced background. The concept combines a full central tracking system, electromagnetic and hadronic calorimeters, and dedicated muon detectors, all shaped around surviving that hostile environment while measuring extremely energetic particles.

The paper details each subdetector and the reconstruction strategies for the key physics objects, reporting performance for electrons, photons, muons, and jets. Studies of jet flavour identification under the background conditions are included. Because Higgs decay products at this energy spray increasingly into the forward region, coverage there gets special attention. Forward muon tagging is flagged as essential for separating W-boson fusion from Z-boson fusion in future electroweak studies at the collider.
arxiv-2511-23473:
Yiping Wang and colleagues open-source the AlphaEvolve idea. Letting a language model evolve programs against open mathematical problems while actually learning from the experience at test time. Their ThetaEvolve simplifies the closed original to a single model with a large program database, batch sampling, lazy penalties against stagnant outputs. And optional reward shaping, and it adds reinforcement learning so strategies get internalized rather than discarded for everyone.

Running a small open 8 billion parameter model, ThetaEvolve reaches overall new best-known bounds on two problems AlphaEvolve publicized, circle packing at 2.63598308 and the first autocorrelation inequality at 1.503133 in the reported values, and its circle-packing program finds its best solution in 3 seconds against a rival's roughly 75 in the comparison. Across two models and four open tasks, test-time reinforcement learning consistently beats inference-only baselines and transfers to unseen tasks.
arxiv-2512-00073:
Detecting vehicles at night is hard, and rain makes camera images even noisier. Aswinkumar Varathakumaran and Nirmala Paramanandham present ProvRain in a 2025 study, a system built to clean rainy images and spot vehicles. Their approach looks beyond headlamps, using other features to catch oncoming vehicles earlier.

ProvRain pairs a MobileNet-UNet model for denoising with Faster R-CNN for detection. The cleaning step helps the detector work when rain streaks and low light hide parts of a vehicle. Better night detection supports safer roads, since drivers and driver-assistance systems both need early warning of traffic ahead. The authors frame the system as a step toward dependable perception in bad weather.
arxiv-2512-00373:
Earth and its sibling planets formed from the same disk, yet their bulk compositions differ markedly from simple condensation predictions. Paolo Sossi and co-authors review physicochemical controls on planet compositions in 2025. Metallic cores fix each planet's oxygen fugacity, a measure of its internal oxidation state.

Those values sit far above the oxidation level of the original nebular gas. The review explains which physical and chemical processes drove the planets away from their starting material. Understanding that divergence helps scientists read exoplanet compositions and reconstruct how rocky planets, including Earth, acquired their ingredients. Oxygen fugacity records how oxidized a planet's interior is, a basic chemical fingerprint. For a reader who likes deep time, the tale is a good one. Worlds born from one cloud of dust took on such unlike forms, and the clues lie in their cores.
arxiv-2512-00473:
Text-to-image models follow prompts well, yet their people often look fake, with overly smooth skin and oily sheens. Junyan Ye and co-authors present RealGen in 2025, a method for photorealistic image generation guided by detector-based rewards. Advanced models still show distinct AI artifacts even on simple tasks.

RealGen uses detectors to spot those artifacts and turns their judgments into reward signals for training. Rewarding realism directly attacks the plastic look that prompt engineering cannot fix. More believable generated faces matter for media, advertising, and any setting where synthetic images stand in for photographs. Detector-guided rewards give the generator feedback that pure text matching cannot. Photorealism is the specific gap the authors target, not image quality in general.
arxiv-2512-00573:
Higher spin fields extend the usual cast of particles and forces, and supersymmetry doubles the stage again. A 2025 study develops higher spin theory with extended supersymmetry using harmonic superspace methods. Harmonic superspace was introduced in 1984 for describing supersymmetric field theories geometrically.

The harmonic approach gives an off-shell description of supersymmetric theories, covering Yang-Mills theory, supergravity, and matter with spins up to two. Extending it to higher spins tests whether those exotic fields can interact consistently. The work sits at the foundations of supersymmetry and quantum field theory. Off-shell descriptions keep all symmetries visible, which higher spin theories badly need. The maximal spins of the classic theories are one, two, and one half. The work is deep theory, and its worth is in the base it lays. If such fields can play well with the known ones, new doors in physics may open.
arxiv-2512-00773:
Toshiki Katsube and five coauthors present DEJIMA, a large Japanese dataset for vision and language, in a 2025 paper. Models that caption images or answer questions about them need lots of good training data. For Japanese, such large, high-quality resources have been scarce.

The team built a pipeline that collects web images at scale, then filters and deduplicates them with care. It pulls evidence from object detection and uses large language models to refine the text, under rules that keep text tied to the image. DEJIMA gives Japanese vision-language research a firmer base to train and test on.
arxiv-2512-00973:
John Douglas Moore generalizes a classic geometry theorem in a 2025 math paper. Hilbert's theorem says the hyperbolic plane, a surface of constant negative curvature, cannot be placed inside ordinary three-dimensional space without distortion. Moore works with submanifolds of constant negative curvature in higher dimensions.

He uses the generalized Gauss-Bonnet formula for Riemannian polyhedra, discovered by Allendoerfer, Weil, and Chern. With it, he shows hyperbolic space of dimension n has no isometric immersion into Euclidean space of dimension twice n minus one. Such no-go results draw a firm line between what curved spaces can and cannot do inside flat space. The result shows how much room curved spaces need when they sit in flat ones.
arxiv-2512-01173:
Shiho Oi and Kaito Sato study special maps between function spaces in a 2025 math paper. The Wiener algebra collects functions whose Fourier series converge absolutely, a well-behaved class used in analysis. Its positive cone holds the functions in it that take nonnegative values, in the sense used there.

The authors study surjective maps between such cones that preserve the spectrum of the sum of any two elements. They show these maps extend to isometric real-linear isomorphisms of the whole algebra. In plain terms, preserving a small amount of spectral data forces the map to be rigid and fully structured.
arxiv-2512-01573:
Meiqing Zhong, Cui Meng, and Yinong Liu test how combined pulses harm a common transistor. A vertical NPN bipolar transistor faced X-ray bursts and electromagnetic pulses at once. Each stress alone is known. Together they may do more harm than the sum.

Lab tests under pulsed X-rays measured the damage. Computer-aided design simulations traced the physics inside. A positive pulse case showed clear combined effects. Knowing how the two stresses add helps harden circuits for space, defense, and nuclear settings where both can strike. Pulse shape and timing both matter, so the tests vary each in turn to see which one drives the transistor toward failure first.
arxiv-2512-01773:
Chenghao Gu and co-authors generate robot training data from open-world images. Generalist robot policies need vast training data. Collecting data on real robots is slow and tied to one setting. Open images hold huge scene variety that matches manipulation tasks well.

Their IGen frame turns such images into robot learning data at scale. Scenes from the wild supply objects, layouts, and contexts. Generated data can pretrain policies before costly robot time. That path could widen robot skills to homes and shops that no lab can rebuild. Image-derived data also spans rare scenes, like disaster zones, where robot trials cannot be staged but photos exist in bulk.
arxiv-2512-01873:
Fractional Chern insulators are exotic quantum materials that host unusual states of matter, but predicting which settings will support them is hard. A 2025 paper by Oriol Mayné i Comas and co-authors builds a data-driven way to judge their stability from the geometry of a material's energy bands.

Using large-scale exact calculations, the team scores stability across a wide range of settings, producing a smooth measure rather than a yes-or-no label. Machine learning then refines simpler rule-of-thumb predictors against that measure, while staying readable enough for physicists to interpret. The result is a clearer map of where these fragile quantum states can survive.
arxiv-2512-01973:
Checking whether a multi-threaded recursive program can reach a bad state is, in general, impossible to decide. C. Aiswarya and four co-authors study this reachability problem for multi-pushdown automata in 2025, a model equivalent to interleaved Dyck reachability, widely used in program analysis.

Because the full problem is undecidable, researchers build decidable under-approximations that still catch real errors. The authors bring in bounded treewidth and multiple context-free grammars, two structural tools for taming such systems, along with downward closures. Their results help draw the line between program properties that verification tools can settle and those they provably cannot.
arxiv-2512-02073:
Graph contrastive learning teaches a model what makes a graph itself by comparing altered views of it that should still match. Qirui Ji and seven co-authors present HTG-GCL in 2025, a method that reads a graph's topology at several levels of detail, from fine to coarse.

Existing methods that alter graph structure often miss the topological patterns a task actually needs, and different tasks need different levels of detail. The authors extract hierarchical topological granularity from cellular complexes, richer structures built on top of graphs, and feed it into the contrast. Respecting topology at the right scale should yield graph representations that transfer better across chemistry, biology, and network tasks.
arxiv-2512-02273:
Text-to-video models have learned to generate smooth, plausible motion, and that talent may double as a repair kit for damaged images. Peng Kang, Xijun Wang, and Yu Yuan repurpose the video model CogVideo in 2025 for progressive image restoration, fine-tuning it to produce restoration trajectories instead of natural motion.

The damaged image is treated as the first frame of a short film whose final frame is the restored picture. Generating the in-between steps gradually may recover detail more gracefully than a single leap. The study opens a new use for video generation's temporal strength, suggesting that restoration is really motion through quality space.
arxiv-2512-02473:
Yuta Oshima and colleagues at the University of Tokyo study video models that predict what a scene will look like next. Given past views and a move, such as turning left, a world model paints the next frames. Keeping those frames steady over space and time has stayed hard for years.

Long scenes need long input, and long input costs too much computing power to use directly. The team's WorldPack method squeezes memory into a compact form the model can carry along. That compressed memory helps the video stay consistent as the view moves through space. Steadier video helps robots and games that must act on what they see.
arxiv-2512-02773:
S. O. Kara builds a precision ready framework for new forces that talk only to leptons. In this extension, leptons carry family dependent charges under a new symmetry, while quarks stay neutral. Keeping the theory consistent requires a minimal set of vectorlike leptons.

Kara connects those high energy interactions to their low energy fingerprints in standard effective theories. The translation lets precision data, from meson decays to collider runs, test the idea fairly. Model independent bridges like this help experiments squeeze meaning from null results and guide where to look next. Clean links from high scale law to low scale data let null finds bite, which is how most new laws fall in the end.
arxiv-2512-02873:
Luca Di Stefano extends automata that read endless streams over huge alphabets. Extensions of omega automata handle infinite inputs, using symbolic guards to keep transitions finite. Registers can carry past values forward, but their formal semantics grow intricate and tractability suffers.

Symbolic transitions alone, though, cannot act well on stored information. Di Stefano's obligations offer another way to track duties across a run. Cleaner machinery for infinite streams supports verification of reactive systems, like controllers and protocols that must run forever without a final state. Clean rules for streams that run on and on are the base on which proofs for live rigs will rest in years to come.
arxiv-2512-03073:
Open AI models have grown fast since 2019. Shayne Longpre and seven co-authors trace that growth in this 2025 study. They focus on Hugging Face, the main global site where open models are shared.

The authors share a full record of weekly model downloads from mid 2020 to late summer 2025, plus model details. With that record they test how much power sits with a few makers. They also track how the open model world has changed over time. The data help readers judge who shapes open AI and who takes part. Its download record also lets readers see which firms and labs release models most often, and how that lead shifts over time.
arxiv-2512-03173:
What an object is for depends on culture. Joan Nwatu, Longju Bai, Oana Ignat, and Rada Mihalcea study that fact in this 2025 work. Image and language data sets tend to favor rich, Western settings, which skews what AI models learn.

That skew can hurt people in lower-income and non-Western places. The authors build a culture affordance atlas that maps objects to their uses across cultures. The atlas aims to reconcile diverse uses of the same object. Fairer data could help vision and language tools serve all users better. An atlas format lets model builders audit training data for gaps across regions and incomes.
arxiv-2512-03273:
A simple game of balance leads to deep math questions. Imre Bárány and Jeck Lim study balancing games on unbounded sets in this 2025 work. They define a set as closed under a step rule tied to a finite set of moves.

Given a point in the set and a move, at least one of adding or subtracting the move stays in the set. The authors explore what structures satisfy that rule. Such games connect geometry, number theory, and combinatorics. Their results may inform tiling and discrepancy problems. Closed sets under such rules form rich structures from a very simple demand.
arxiv-2512-03373:
AI-written ads may persuade as well as human ones, or better. Elyas Meguellati and co-authors test that claim in this 2025 work. As language models grow better at persuasive text, firms need to know how their ads perform.

The study looks at ads through two lenses. One is personality-based targeting, the other is psychological persuasion principles. Comparing the two shows where model ads match or beat personalization. The results matter for marketing practice and for rules on AI use in advertising. Personality and persuasion tests together show whether gains come from targeting or from craft.
arxiv-2512-03473:
Supersymmetric theories break in subtle ways worth mapping. Digvijay Roy Varier, Zijian Gu, Bea Noether, and Hitoshi Murayama study one such theory in this 2025 work. They examine symplectic QCD with several flavors, perturbed by anomaly mediated supersymmetry breaking.

The team studies minima where chiral symmetry breaks, plus other potential minima. Knowing which minimum wins decides the theory's low-energy behavior. Careful study avoids false conclusions from shallow minima. The results add to the map of how supersymmetric gauge theories behave when softly broken. Other minima can trap naive analyses, so mapping them all is essential groundwork.
arxiv-2512-04373:
Hann Woei Ho and Ye Zhou borrow a landing trick from bees to help small spacecraft touch down on sloped ground. Light craft have weak computers and little room for heavy sensors, so deep learning gear and lidar rigs do not fit. Bees land smoothly with tiny brains by watching optical flow, the drift of the ground image. One cue, flow divergence, compares fall speed with height. Their 2025 arXiv paper adapts that cue for planetary landers.

Two snags block a straight copy. A single global flow reading hides the tilt of the slope. Raw divergence control can also go unstable under standard controllers. The authors answer with a nonlinear control design that uses two distinct flow readings to sense tilt and keep the descent steady. The method suits rotorcraft and small landers headed for rough, tilted terrain on other worlds.
arxiv-2512-04473:
Pan-Pan Wang, Hao-Kang Chen, Wei-Liang Qian, and co-authors examine how a space gravity detector's sensitivity swings with the direction of incoming waves. Planned space detectors will listen for millihertz waves from merging massive bodies. Their laser links span millions of kilometers, and laser noise must be canceled by time-delay interferometry, which recombines signals with tuned delays. Each recipe has its own directional response. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies that response in detail.

Studies usually average sensitivity over all sky directions, since a source's spot is unknown before detection. The authors argue the average hides useful structure. Once a first signal pins down the source's location, a recipe tuned to that spot can sharpen later readings. They map how response varies with angle for known recipes. The work guides how missions like LISA can squeeze more from a detected source after the first catch.
arxiv-2512-04673:
Gunjan Das, Paheli Bhattacharya, Rishabh Gupta, and co-authors run a head-to-head evaluation of general-purpose and code-specific language models across many task kinds. Past studies usually grade one skill at a time. A unified comparison across language, reasoning, and code was missing. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests five general models and three code-specialized models on six benchmarks.

The benchmarks span language skill, math reasoning, and trustworthiness. The team also probes the CoNaLa dataset, where models must explain code snippets in plain words. Code-tuned models, such as the CodeLLaMA family, showed strong reasoning and sharp syntax control. General models held edges elsewhere. The findings sketch a practical map: which model class fits which job. For teams picking a model for mixed work, that map can save costly trial and error.
arxiv-2512-04773:
Giorgos Polychronis, Foivos Pournaropoulos, and Christos Antonopoulos study a small decision with big time costs in drone missions: after sensing a spot, should the drone wait for analysis or move on? Data-driven missions process readings on board to judge whether the spot needs action. Waiting wastes flight time when nothing is found. Leaving wastes a return trip when action was needed after all. Their 2025 arXiv paper turns that stay-or-go call into a learning problem.

The authors borrow branch prediction, the trick chips use to guess which way code will jump, and pair it with reinforcement learning variants. Tests span many scenarios where the chance of an event drifts over time. Their methods beat fixed rules across the board in the reported runs. Smarter waiting can stretch a battery across more inspection points, which matters for drones checking crops, roofs, and disaster zones.
arxiv-2512-05073:
Shashwat Shankar and six co-authors ask whether small language models, wrapped in the right workflow, can rival big ones at designing computer hardware. Running large models is costly in computing and energy, and chip design — writing and fixing Verilog code — is exactly the kind of specialized work where bills pile up. The team tests small models on a benchmark of real design problems assembled by NVIDIA.

Instead of asking a small model for one-shot answers, the authors embed it in an agentic workflow that breaks tasks down, tests the results, and feeds errors back for correction. With that scaffolding, the small models reach close to large-model performance at a fraction of the cost. The loop also teaches the agents as they go, the authors argue, pointing toward design tools that are cheaper, adaptive, and easier to run at scale.
arxiv-2512-05473:
Yeongjun Jang, Kaoru Teranishi, Jihoon Suh, and Takashi Tanaka let a team of agents learn one model together without any of them revealing their data. Gaussian process regression is a flexible way to learn an unknown function from examples, and distributing it lets multiple agents pool knowledge — but pooling is exactly what privacy forbids. Their protocol wraps the distributed computation in secure multi-party computation, so each agent's contribution stays hidden from coalitions of curious peers, beyond what the combined result itself implies.

Built on secure distributed averaging, the method provably converges to the same global model ordinary distributed regression would reach, with privacy formalized in the standard simulation-based paradigm.
