The protocol extends to privately tuning the kernel's hyperparameters, a step the literature often skips, and experiments confirm it works. It is cryptography doing quiet diplomatic work between collaborators who cannot fully trust each other.
arxiv-2512-05673:
Emin Benny-Chacko, Ignacio Brevis, Luis Espath, and Kristoffer van der Zee propose a steadier way to solve differential equations with neural networks. One family of solvers, weak adversarial networks, pits two networks against each other in a min-max game. Such games can be badly unstable. Their 2025 method replaces the duel with a sequence of calmer minimization steps, modeled on the old Uzawa iteration.

Each round updates two networks in turn. One update shrinks the residual, measured in a dual norm, by minimizing a Ritz functional. The other improves the solution, driven by the current residual. The authors prove this scheme really does solve the adversarial formulation. They also build a full convergence theory for the inexact version, where each subproblem is solved only roughly. That covers the gradient based training used in practice, for single and repeated steps alike. Numerical tests back the theory.
arxiv-2512-05973:
Adrian Koenigstein, Martin Steil, and Stefan Floerchinger recast one of theoretical physics' workhorse tools as a kind of equation numerical analysts already know how to tame. Its flow equations are notoriously hard to solve when the effective potential depends on the field. The authors identify the flow equations for two-point functions as partial differential equations of Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman type, the family governing optimal control and diffusion.

The move imports a ready made numerical scheme for such equations. The team first tests it on a toy fermion-boson system in zero spacetime dimensions. Then the lessons transfer upward. One showcase is a bosonic model with a two-fold symmetry in three dimensions, with field dependent terms. The other is the Gross-Neveu model of interacting fermions, at nonzero temperature and density. Flow equations serve physics where perturbation theory fails. A better numerical handle widens the method's reach.
arxiv-2512-06073:
Rebecca Chan and Taylor Hughes glue an exotic insulator to a superconductor and map the strange offspring. The insulator's momentum space is tiled like a dartboard into topological sub zones. Against a superconductor it becomes a Chern dartboard superconductor. Which topological features survive turns on symmetry counting.

If the insulator has an even number of mirror symmetries, the hybrid can keep nontrivial sub zone topology. An odd count lets particle hole symmetry force trivial topology. One loophole: FFLO pairing or a momentum shift dodges the constraint for the single mirror case. Depending on whether the pairing respects the mirrors, the system realizes phases with different combinations of total and reduced Chern numbers. Some inherit a quantized crystalline response that experiments can actually measure. Such classification tells experimentalists which phases exist.
arxiv-2512-06473:
Stanislaw Drozdz and four co authors build a sharper lens for correlations between assets whose prices jump and drift wildly. Standard correlation tools blur when data has trends, long memory, and fat tailed swings. Their matrices use a detrended cross correlation score that can focus on swings of a chosen size, so calm periods and storms can be weighed apart.

They study the spectra of these matrices, the fingerprints that reveal true shared modes, and compare them with the spectra from synthetic noise. Detrending, fat tails, and the chosen swing size together bend the spectrum far from the random case, even when no true links exist. Applied to minute by minute returns of many large cryptocurrencies across four years, the method finds a dominant market wide mode and several sector modes. Once the market mode is filtered out, what remains matches the random limit, letting real structure stand out cleanly.
arxiv-2512-06873:
Fabian A Polnitzky and co-authors measure how long the disks of gas and dust around newborn stars survive, since those disks are where planets form. The usual method counts disk-bearing stars in clusters of different ages, but each cluster sits in a different place with its own biases. This team instead studies many clusters inside one single star-forming region, Scorpius-Centaurus, so the yardstick stays the same from young to old.

Using data from the Gaia, 2MASS, and WISE surveys, they flag stars whose infrared glow betrays a disk. The clusters span roughly three to twenty-one million years. Their count gives a disk lifetime near six million years, about twice most earlier estimates. A fading exponential curve fits the loss of disks best. If disks really last that long, growing planets have more time than modelers long assumed.
arxiv-2512-07073:
Huimin Chang and Ping Jin generalize a landmark counting principle in the representation theory of finite groups. The McKay conjecture concerns a curious equality: a whole group and the normalizer of one of its prime-power subgroups hold the same number of characters of certain kinds. Chang and Jin work with p-solvable groups, a broad class built from layers tied to a chosen prime. They define a new family of characters, stable along a chosen normal series of the group.

For that family, the McKay-style equality holds: the group and the normalizer count exactly the same number of stable characters. When the group's order is odd, the match is stronger still, given by a canonical one-to-one pairing rather than a bare count. The proofs lean on the theory of self-stabilizing pairs developed by Lewis and on Isaacs's results about special characters.
arxiv-2512-07173:
Jucheng Shen and co-authors make diffusion-based language models answer faster without retraining them. These models write by unmasking tokens step by step, and how confident they are changes across text blocks and steps. CadLLM watches that confidence live and adjusts its behavior on the fly: the size of each generation block. The step size, and the threshold for accepting tokens all follow the average confidence of what has been unmasked.

A second trick trims the costly final scoring step by using only part of the vocabulary to govern how widely the model samples. The method is a plug-in: it needs no training, works across model families, and cooperates with the caching schemes these models already use. Across four popular tasks, throughput rose substantially over the strongest baseline, in the best cases more than doubling, while accuracy stayed competitive.
arxiv-2512-07373:
Elisenda Feliu, Joan Ferrer, and Máté L Telek connect two tools for deciding whether a sparse polynomial-like expression can ever dip below zero. Their objects are signomials, sums of monomials with real exponents, defined where all variables are positive; such a function is copositive if its values never go negative. The pattern of which terms appear, and with which signs, is the signed support, the combinatorial skeleton of the problem.

Their criterion runs through geometry in the space of coefficients. Draw a path that starts at the given signomial's coefficients and never changes any sign; where that path first meets a special surface. The signed discriminant built from all the singular signomials with the same skeleton, decides the question. When the skeleton obeys a condition called nonseparability, the meeting point is unique and one tracked path suffices.
arxiv-2512-07573:
J. P. Marshall and eight co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on the dusty rings around other stars. Debris discs are the leftover rubble of planet formation, glowing faintly at long wavelengths. Reading their dust tells us how those systems grind down over time.

The team studies more than a hundred discs that telescopes have resolved in detail. Images span from near-infrared light out to millimetre waves. Simple radiative transfer models then extract the dust properties of each disc. They measure the smallest grain size, the total dust mass, and a size-distribution exponent. That exponent is charted across this wavelength range for the first time. A fresh trend links the exponent to the disc's radius. It may signal that grains break apart by speed, or grow at large distances. Disc masses match those of young planet-forming discs. The authors flag targets for deeper study.
arxiv-2512-07673:
Matthias Heyrman, Chenhao Li, Victor Klemm, Dongho Kang, Stelian Coros, and Marco Hutter wrote this 2025 robotics paper. Robots that imitate living motion must first represent that motion well. Existing controllers often ignore the patterns hidden inside human and animal movement.

Their representation, Multi-Domain Motion Embedding, attacks the problem from two sides. One encoder, built on wavelets, captures structured and periodic features of motion. A probabilistic embedding runs in parallel to capture the looser, aperiodic parts. Together they form a rich code from a surprisingly small input set. The code generalizes across very different motion styles. At deployment, control policies read the code and rebuild ideal target states. No separate retargeting step is needed for each new robot body. Tests run on both a humanoid and a four-legged platform. Long sequences come back accurately on both. Unseen motions work in real time with no per-motion tuning at all.
arxiv-2512-07973:
Mithun Kumar Acharjee and AKM Fazlur Rahman wrote this 2025 biostatistics paper on illnesses that strike repeatedly. Heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure can recur in the same patient. Each recurrence reshapes the risk of the next event and of death.

Their Bayesian model follows several event types and a terminal event together. Type-specific hazards shift dynamically as a patient's event history grows. Past recurrences feed back onto their own type and onto the others. A shared frailty term absorbs differences between patients that data cannot measure. Covariate effects and cumulative past-event effects are estimated jointly. Gamma process priors keep the baseline hazard flexible without rigid shape assumptions. Closed-form estimators for cumulative hazards and frailties fall out of the framework. Standard estimators appear as special cases when precision parameters vanish.  A major hypertension trial then supplies the proving ground.
arxiv-2512-08173:
Fatih Kizilaslan and Valeria Vitelli, statisticians, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025 about survival analysis when some patients are cured for good. Standard models assume everyone stays at risk, which distorts long term survival when a cured group exists. Mixture cure models handle that split, and this paper builds a flexible Bayesian version of them.

Their framework can include or exclude a frailty term, which captures hidden differences between patients that data never record. Sampling from the posterior uses Markov chain Monte Carlo, guided by a structure borrowed from the Bayesian Lasso. Wide simulations test how the models perform and hold up across scenarios, and several criteria compare them. The methods are then applied to two classic datasets: the E1690 melanoma trial and a colon cancer trial.
arxiv-2512-08573:
Maren Stratmann, a particle physicist, presented this work for the ATLAS collaboration at the Top 2025 workshop, and the write up appeared on arXiv in December 2025. It reports how often single top quarks and antiquarks are produced in proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, broken down by the particles momentum and direction. The measurement uses the full Run 2 dataset that ATLAS collected from 2015 to 2018.

Single top production is rare and delicate, which makes it a sharp test of theory. The team compared the measured rates against fixed order calculations, several event generators, and different sets of parton distribution functions. Everything agreed within the measurement uncertainties. The results also serve a second purpose: read through effective field theory, they constrain a four fermion operator that could hide new physics. Conference reports like this carry a flagship measurement to the specialist community.
arxiv-2512-08773:
Suwan Sun, Hairun Guo, Andre Luiten, and Wenle Weng study photonic sensing of radio frequency electric fields with a tiny optical resonator. Resonators with the Pockels effect can sense fields with very high resolution when locked to a low noise laser. Those lasers are costly and bulky, which limits use outside the lab.

The team instead uses a cheap fixed frequency semiconductor laser as the pump. A mode in a lithium niobate resonator is locked to the laser through the electro optic effect, which is also the sensing mechanism. Tests show resolution holds even beyond the optical resonance bandwidth, and signal quality stays stable as coupling varies, as long as laser noise dominates. Near mechanical resonances of the device, sensitivity rises by about three fold. The work points toward compact, lower cost high resolution field sensors.
arxiv-2512-09473:
Yibowen Zhao and colleagues present a human-AI system designed for intensive care units. ICUs are high-stakes environments where monitoring is constant and data management is complex. In practice, staff still transcribe readings by hand and information sits in fragmented systems, creating risks for patient safety and efficiency.

The proposed system uses a cloud-edge-end architecture. A visual-aware edge module reads physiological data directly from bedside monitors without invasive integration, cutting manual entry errors. A semantic interaction module, powered by a large language model, lets physicians query structured patient data by voice in an intuitive way. The layered deployment keeps communication fast and lets the system scale. The authors report that the system reduces the cognitive burden on nurses and physicians, and they see promise for broader use in intelligent healthcare.
arxiv-2512-09573:
Yuan Li and colleagues probe whether multimodal language models perceive the low-level flaws that decide image quality. Such models are increasingly used for image quality assessment and can write explanations. Yet they often fail to spot basic distortions like blur, noise, and compression artifacts, and their evaluations can be inconsistent between runs.

The authors design a task that asks models to classify which distortion an image contains. Their component-by-component analysis shows the models' visual encoders can represent these distortions. But the models overfit training templates, biasing their quality scores, and key low-level features are weakened or lost when vision is aligned to language. By measuring the semantic distance between visual features and their matching tokens before and after fine-tuning components, they show that fixing the vision encoder's alignment raises distortion recognition accuracy. They argue for dedicated constraints on the vision encoder in such pipelines.
arxiv-2512-09673:
Yuzhu Chen and colleagues examine a hidden cost of equivariant neural networks, models that hard-wire the symmetries of their data into the design. Such networks perform across many domains because symmetry is a strong inductive bias. Whether forcing equivariance limits what the network can express, though, was not well understood.

Focusing on two-layer networks with rectified linear units, the authors study the boundary hyperplanes and channel vectors that determine a network's function. They show that enforcing equivariance constraints can undermine expressive power. The loss, however, can be bought back by enlarging the model, and they prove upper bounds on how much enlargement compensation requires. The enlarged equivariant models have a lower-dimensional hypothesis space than expected, implying better results on new data. The paper thus measures a trade-off at the heart of symmetry-aware learning: some power is surrendered, some efficiency and generalization are gained.
arxiv-2512-09973:
Octavio C. Junqueira and Roldao da Rocha use holography to map phase changes in rotating strongly interacting matter. Their model describes hadronic matter and quark gluon plasma through thermal and charged black holes in a five dimensional curved space with cylindrical symmetry. Rotation is the new twist. They examine matter at both high and low densities, looking for where smooth crossovers give way to sharp first order transitions, the two ways matter can change phase.

For fast rotation, they find crossover transitions appearing in the low density regime, up to a critical chemical potential. In this smooth regime, confined and deconfined matter with unlike angular momenta mix before turning into pure plasma at very high temperature. Beyond the critical point, first order transitions take over and follow the non rotating critical curve. The authors locate the critical point that splits the two regimes.
arxiv-2512-10073:
Imad Limame leads a large team demonstrating quantum dot light sources grown directly on silicon, emitting in the telecom O-band. Quantum dots are key emitters of non-classical light for quantum technology. The challenge is growing high quality dots on industry standard silicon, and at wavelengths that travel well through fiber. The team grew indium gallium arsenide dots on silicon using a strain reducing layer, then placed individual dots deterministically into circular Bragg grating resonators using in situ electron beam lithography. The resonators boost how much light escapes.

The devices extract photons with efficiency around forty percent, matching simulations, and position the dot within tens of nanometers of the resonator's center. At low temperature the sources show single photon purity above ninety-nine percent. Remarkably, they keep working at warmer temperatures reachable by compact coolers and even liquid nitrogen, with purity still high.
arxiv-2512-10573:
Yi Huang and co-authors harden the information bottleneck, a learning principle that keeps what a representation says about the label while squeezing out the rest of the input. The method trusts its labels completely, so mislabelled training data, common in practice, poisons the compression and drags performance down. Their fix, LaT-IB, was accepted at AAAI 2026.

LaT-IB adds a criterion the authors call minimal-sufficient-clean, built as a mutual information regulariser that keeps task-relevant signal and drops noise. A disentanglement step splits the latent code into parts aligned with the clean label space and with the noise. And the authors prove bounds showing the objective favours codes that ignore input noise. Training proceeds in three phases, from warmup through knowledge injection to robust training, and experiments show clear gains in robustness and efficiency under label noise.
arxiv-2512-10673:
Bart Zonneveld extends a coding trick for hyperbolic surfaces. A recent tree bijection encodes a planar hyperbolic surface as a tree, which makes Weil-Petersson volumes easy to compute and opens the door to distance statistics and scaling limits for random surfaces. The catch was that the surface needed at least one cusp, a infinitely thin spike, to serve as the origin from which distances are measured.

Many surfaces have no cusp. Zonneveld first extends the bijection to half-tight cylinders. There, distances to an origin are replaced by a Busemann function. That function is ill-defined on the surface itself. It is well-defined on its cylinder cover. Since a general planar hyperbolic surface splits naturally into two half-tight cylinders, the general case follows. The twenty-eight page paper removes the last structural restriction on the bijection.
arxiv-2512-10773:
Samaksh Ujjawal and co-authors teach a flying robot arm to predict the forces that fight it. An aerial manipulator's dynamics change fast with its own configuration: swinging the arm shifts the inertia, and the rotors' airflow interacts with the body. So formula models lose accuracy, and plain neural networks cannot represent the variety of leftover forces across operating conditions.

Their framework, AERMANI-Diffusion, models the full spread of residual forces with a diffusion process conditioned on the operating regime. A lightweight temporal encoder folds recent motion and pose into a compact code, keeping predictions consistent through abrupt changes and with payloads never seen in training. Paired with an adaptive controller, the model corrects for the force errors it captures. In real-world flight tests, tracking accuracy improved markedly over the alternatives the authors compared against.
arxiv-2512-10873:
Qitian Lu and co-authors strengthen a surrogate modelling method that respects physics. Polynomial chaos expansions mimic how a system's output responds to uncertain inputs. And the physics-informed version bakes the governing equations and other constraints into the fit, solving through the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. The result is fast and physically readable, but high-dimensional inputs, scarce data, or badly placed training points can still degrade it.

Two upgrades address that. A solver based on straightforward updating of Lagrange multipliers replaces the usual constrained solver and cuts the cost sharply when derivative boundary conditions demand many virtual points. A D-optimal sampling plan then chooses those virtual points for maximum information, steadying the fit. Tested on sample systems governed by ordinary and partial differential equations, the enhanced framework beat the standard version overall and suits high-dimensional uncertainty work.
arxiv-2512-11173:
Tzu-Hsien Lee, Fidan Mahmudova, and Karthik Desingh teach a four legged mobile robot to park itself precisely in front of an object it needs to manipulate. Ordinary camera based navigation only promises accuracy within about a metre, too coarse for a gripper trained on demonstrations. Their system learns the final approach from examples of just one object in a category.

The policy reads goal images, views from the robot's own cameras, and a text prompt naming the target object. A language driven segmentation step and a spatial scoring decoder ground the object and reason about relative pose. Trained on a single instance, the robot generalised to unseen objects in new settings with difficult lighting and backgrounds. New alignment metrics based on edges and object facing confirmed strong success without depth sensors, lidar, or maps.
arxiv-2512-11373:
Arnold Brosch, Abdelrahman Eldesokey, Michael Felsberg, and Kira Maag teach driving perception systems to flag objects they were never trained on. Image segmentation networks excel on their fixed class list but fail silently when unknown objects appear, a real danger for automated driving. Their setup treats segmentation as gathering evidence, and measures uncertainty in a way that respects the shape of probability spreads.

The method's loss uses the Wasserstein distance, which captures how far apart spreads sit while honouring the simplex structure of class probabilities. Two further terms keep the evidence calibrated and the predicted regions structurally steady. Jointly these ingredients bettered out of spread segmentation over current uncertainty based approaches. Reliable spotting of the unknown is a prerequisite for safe open world driving, and the authors position their evidential approach as a step in that direction.
arxiv-2512-11473:
Fan Gu and Xiangyu Hu redesign how grid based model run data are stored so the same code runs efficiently on both normal processors and graphics accelerators. Cartesian grids simplify the mathematics of model runs, but in sparse domains most cells are empty, wasting memory and computation. Current setups were built for CPUs and stall on graphics hardware because of poor parallelism and slow memory access.

Their storage architecture packs grid data contiguously with graphics processors in mind, while hiding hardware specifics behind a unified programming model based on SYCL. Model runs can then move between host and device environments without rewriting. End users get simpler accelerator programming, and the design scales better for sparse grid problems and for model runs coupling grids with particles. The work targets the heterogeneous machines that now dominate high results computing.
arxiv-2512-11973:
R Skalidis and co-authors study residual energy, the gap between motion and magnetic energy, in weakly compressible plasma turbulence with a strong guide field. How that gap cascades to small scales depends on what stirs the plasma. The team ran direct simulations with the PENCIL code at sonic Mach near 0.1.

When magnetism drives the flow, fluctuations stay locally lopsided and the spectrum follows the dynamic alignment prediction, with residual energy near zero at mid scales. When motion drives it, a shallower slope appears and residual energy stays positive everywhere. Stronger guide fields steepen the residual cascade. Forcing style, the work shows, shapes energy balance as much as field strength does.
arxiv-2512-12173:
Avinash Khare and Avadh Saxena find new exact solutions to a wave equation in a 2025 paper. The equation is a fifth order form of the KdV type, used for waves in shallow water and plasma. They look for solutions that stay the same under a combined parity and time flip.

They show the equation admits several such solutions, both real and complex. Each is a sum of squared terms built from Jacobi elliptic functions, in four named forms. That full mixing is rare: the classic KdV equation and a few others allow only partial mixing of these functions. The result widens the set of wave forms known in exact form.
arxiv-2512-12873:
Flavio Cruz, Jose Santos, and Victor Otoya work on planar electrodynamics, the study of electric and magnetic fields in a flat, two-dimensional space. They focus on two named models of that theory. For both models, a key quantity is the propagator, which tracks how effects spread.

The authors give a new way to obtain that propagator. Their method rests on a new set of projection operators, tools that split a field into clear parts. With the propagator in hand, they check two basic demands on any sound theory. They test whether cause still comes before effect, and whether total probability stays properly conserved.
arxiv-2512-12973:
Jun Jiang studies crossed homomorphisms on Lie groups, maps between groups that obey a twisted version of the usual product rule. Such maps appear in algebra and geometry, and the question here is whether they can be deformed, changed bit by bit, or are rigid.

Jiang uses the cohomology that controls these maps, together with a Moser type argument, to prove several rigidity results. He then links the cohomology for Lie groups with the corresponding theory for Lie algebras, their linearized versions. As a final step, he describes the rigidity of all crossed homomorphisms for one concrete case, the connected two-dimensional Lie group under conjugation.
arxiv-2512-13073:
Jocelyn Nembe builds a unified geometric framework for nonparametric estimation, the craft of fitting curves without fixed formulas. His Twin Kernel Spaces are copies of a reproducing kernel space moved around by a group action. Each moved copy carries its own geometry.

His main theorem says that the eigenfunctions of any moved kernel come from moving the base eigenfunctions, a property called spectral equivariance. As a result, polynomial and kernel estimators become two views of one process. Rates for accuracy and the bias-variance trade-off stay unchanged under transport. Examples use Hermite and Legendre polynomials and affine and Gaussian groups.
arxiv-2512-13173:
Ivica Kostric, Ujwal Gadiraju, and Krisztian Balog take a first step toward recommender chatbots that adjust to how much a user knows. Most systems treat every user as an expert, which frustrates newcomers. Yet a system cannot easily ask about knowledge without the very signals it needs to judge it.

Their project, RecQuest, collects dialogue data through a game with a purpose, designed to draw out varied signs of expertise. A target-aware system guides the chats so users reveal more than favorite items. The authors release the data set and baseline methods. The work opens a path to recommenders that pitch their language to each user.
arxiv-2512-13373:
Jagna Wisniewska answers the two-boost problem for a class of space mission systems with Newtonian gravity. The problem asks whether two points in space can be joined by a path that stays on one fixed energy level. Such a path is the kind of route a spacecraft on an unpowered arc would follow.

She proves the answer is yes for systems that behave at infinity like the restricted three-body problem. The argument links the question to Rabinowitz Floer homology, an algebraic tool that counts such paths. The hard technical step is proving that the relevant sets of Reeb chords stay bounded. That bound makes the homology computation valid.
arxiv-2512-13673:
Panagiotis Giannadakis and co-authors find a critical value for the tensor-to-scalar ratio in early-universe inflation. Inflation is a burst of fast expansion, and this ratio compares gravitational wave strength to density ripple strength. Their question is how rough the starting state can be while inflation still works.

They use an alpha-attractor T-model with order-unity inhomogeneities in gradient and kinetic fields. Assuming 100 e-folds for the smooth solution, they find 60 e-folds require a characteristic scale near 0.02 Planck masses. That scale gives a critical ratio near one millionth. Rougher starts would need a higher scale, so that ratio acts as a lower bound.
arxiv-2512-13773:
Evgeni Grishin, Jet Winter, and Jaime A. Alvarado-Montes explain how wide binary stars can make hot Jupiters around old stars. Hot Jupiters are giant planets with orbits under 10 days, found around about 0.5 to 1% of Sun-like stars. A leading story, high-eccentricity migration, converts too few cold Jupiters and fails for old hosts.

Their model adds the Galactic tidal field to wide binaries wider than 1,000 astronomical units. Those systems produce 1.8 plus or minus 0.14 times more hot Jupiters than isolated binaries, covering 26 to 40% of the observed population. Most products are billions of years old, matching host ages. In about 20% of cases, the planet is ejected entirely, seeding free-floating giants.
arxiv-2512-13973:
Lizzy Teryoshin, Mario Hidalgo-Soria, and Elena F. Koslover study how long intermittently running particles take to meet inside cells. Many cell processes depend on mobile partners meeting on time, including organelles driven by motors in bursts. The cytoskeletal network both directs that motion and adds disorder through its filament layout.

They compute mean first encounter times for pairs of particles that alternate between runs and diffusion, in two dimensions, with and without a fixed filament network. Longer runs explore more space but slow encounters versus pure diffusion, and meetings shift toward the domain edge. On dense networks, unbiased runs match a continuum run-and-tumble model. Biased runs can be trapped where filaments converge, yet funneling can also speed encounters.
arxiv-2512-14173:
Pratyay Ghosh and Frederic Mila study a quantum magnet on the ruby lattice in a 2025 paper. The lattice forms a two dimensional network of corner sharing tetrahedra, and the model is the spin one half Heisenberg antiferromagnet with uniform first and second neighbor couplings.

Using infinite projected entangled pair states, a numeric method for large quantum systems, they find a gapped ground state called a simplex crystal. It is threefold degenerate, with strong singlet pairs formed on neighboring triangles. Under a magnetic field, simulations show magnetization plateaus at fractions 0, one third, one half, and two thirds of saturation. Supersolid phases sit between the plateaus, and all of them break the sixfold symmetry of the lattice.
arxiv-2512-14273:
Xiaoqian Shen and four coauthors present Zoom Zero in a 2025 paper on grounded video question answering. The task asks a model to find the video segment that proves its answer. Large video language models often have weak time awareness, so answers rest on the wrong segment or are hallucinated.

Zoom Zero first localizes the relevant segment, then zooms in on the most salient frames for a finer check. A zoom in accuracy reward verifies that the grounding is faithful, and token selective credit assignment gives rewards to the tokens that did the localizing or answering. Grounding rose by 5.2 percent on NExT GQA and 4.6 percent on ReXTime. Average answer accuracy rose by 2.4 percent, and long video scores rose by 6.4 percent.
arxiv-2512-14573:
Arindam Banerjee, Tài Huy Hà, and Vivek Bhabani Lama introduce a new measuring tool for algebra: a defect function tied to a pair of filtrations of ideals. The idea extends the older notion of symbolic defect for ideals, widening it from one filtration to two.

They work under two finiteness assumptions. The Rees algebra of one filtration is Noetherian, and a graded module that records how the filtrations interact is finitely generated. Under those conditions, they prove the defect function at last behaves like a quasi-polynomial. Such growth results help algebraists predict the long-run behavior of ideals, and the framework covers pairs where earlier work handled single filtrations.
arxiv-2512-14673:
Chatbots built on large language models now sit at the center of technical, educational, and analytical work, helping with code, problem solving, and information searches. As their use scales, the sustainability cost of all that conversation has come under scrutiny, mostly at the level of models, hardware, and infrastructure.

Three researchers shift the focus to conversational norms themselves: the habits and expectations that shape how long and how often people talk with chatbots. If norms drive usage, they also drive the footprint, so changing norms is a lever for sustainable AI. The paper invites designers to treat conversation design as part of the environmental cost of these systems.
arxiv-2512-14773:
M. Baran Ökten studies how a spinning black hole twists the light that loops around it. He computes the mark that Kerr spacetime, the math that describes a spinning black hole, leaves on the polarization of light at the photon ring. His key tool recasts how the angle of the light wave's electric field changes as the light travels.

The Kerr pattern differs from the nonspinning case only in a thin ring, flips sign when the spin flips, and grows with spin and viewing tilt. Three separate methods give the same answer ray by ray. Ökten then builds a simple template with two values, spin and tilt, for fine radio measures of rings like those around M87* and Sgr A*. A match would show frame dragging at work close to the hole.
arxiv-2512-14873:
Sam Jeong and Hae Yong Kim dig into why a recent neural network design works. The design, called a Fourier Analysis Network, swaps some standard activation steps for sine and cosine waves. Users saw small but steady gains on many tasks, yet no one could say what caused them.

The authors find that only the sine part helps, while cosine tends to hurt. The gain does not come from the wave's repeating shape. It comes from how sine behaves near zero, where its slope stays alive and keeps gradients flowing. That fixes the dying ReLU flaw, in which neurons go silent and stop learning. Building on this, they propose a Dual Activation Layer that converges faster and matches or beats standard layers on three test tasks.
arxiv-2512-15073:
Meng Yang and six coauthors weigh the dark matter in thousands of gas rich galaxies and compare them with a simulated universe. The data come from the ALFALFA survey of hydrogen gas, matched one to one with galaxies in the TNG100 simulation at the same stellar mass and hydrogen size. Line widths of the hydrogen signal, corrected for tilt, give each galaxy's dark matter content.

Across all mass bins, the real galaxies hold less dark matter at the median than their simulated twins. A tail of dark matter poor galaxies drives the gap, and it grows at higher masses. In the top bin, above ten billion solar masses in stars, the real median sits 23 percent below the dark matter only simulation. There, 32 percent of real galaxies fall below a set dark matter mass, against 17 percent in the mock sample. The mismatch challenges how simulations dress galaxies in halos.
arxiv-2512-15273:
The BESIII Collaboration reports a first measurement, at an electron positron collider, of a rare decay of the Xi minus baryon. The decay turns a Xi minus into a Lambda, an electron, and an antineutrino, a semileptonic process that tests flavor physics. The data hold about ten billion J/psi events recorded by the BESIII detector in China.

The absolute branching fraction is about 36 in every 100,000 decays, a value that sits 3.9 standard deviations below the world average. An eleven dimensional angular analysis also fixes the axial vector to vector coupling, g_av, at 0.18 in value, with errors well under half that size. Under SU(3) flavor symmetry, the axial charge comes out at 0.22 in the same analysis, again with modest errors. With only 5 percent of the data of earlier experiments, the team matched their precision on the axial charge, and the results test a range of SU(3) flavor models.
arxiv-2512-15673:
Remco van der Hofstad reviews recent progress on percolation on random graphs in a 2025 paper. Percolation models random damage to a network: heavy damage shatters it into small pieces, while light damage barely affects connectivity. The sharp change between those regimes is a phase transition, and its location and nature are the focus.

Near or below criticality, components show intricate scaling, with typical components bounded but average and largest sizes growing as powers of network size. Two settings behave rather differently: rank one like graphs, including the configuration model, and dynamic graphs that grow over time, such as preferential attachment models. Inhomogeneity of the underlying graph proves crucial throughout.
arxiv-2512-16073:
Abhijit Bera and Kevin E Bassler dissect unusual diffusion in an arXiv paper from 2025. In anomalous diffusion, particles spread faster or slower than the classic random walk predicts. Their focus is variable speed generalized Levy walks, where a walker takes long flights and its speed changes during each flight in a set pattern.

The authors split the anomaly into three root causes. The Joseph effect covers long-range correlations, the Noah effect covers huge jumps with infinite variance, and the Moses effect covers aging, where behavior changes over time. In these walks, all three usually act together rather than one dominating. Surprisingly, the Noah exponent has no upper bound here, so this model class allows more extreme diffusion than earlier Levy walk models.
arxiv-2512-16273:
Ce Zheng and five co-authors cut network traffic for AI inference in work posted to arXiv in 2025. Speculative decoding speeds up language models: a small model drafts tokens and a big model verifies them. In future AI-native radio networks, the draft and the checker may sit on different devices, and sending full vocabulary scores each step floods the uplink.

Their method, TSLT, sends only the scores and indices of a truncated shortlist of candidate tokens. Theory shows the acceptance rate, the share of drafts the big model keeps, is preserved. An extension handles several draft candidates per step, which raises acceptance further. Experiments showed much lower uplink communication with latency and quality intact. The work points toward scalable device-edge teamwork for language model serving in next-generation networks.
arxiv-2512-16473:
En-Ming Huang, Li-Shang Lin, and Chun-Yi Lee help big AI models run on small machines in an arXiv paper uploaded in 2025, due at ASP-DAC 2026. Mixture of experts models activate only part of their parameters per token, saving compute, but their total size still exceeds the memory of typical consumer graphics cards.

Moving weights between processor and graphics card on demand causes crippling delays. The team's collaborative framework caches hot experts on the GPU, so frequent pieces answer from the cache. Cache misses fall back to the CPU, whose multithreading handles them efficiently. Tests on consumer-grade systems showed clear speed gains for single-request inference. The design shows how careful CPU-GPU teamwork can stretch limited hardware, and the implementation is public.
arxiv-2512-16573: Mordechai Katzman settles a tidy algebra question in a note on arXiv in 2025. Take a field extension, one number system inside a larger one. Then build power series rings over each. He asks when the larger ring is a free module over the smaller one. Free means it has a clean basis, like a vector space. The answer: freeness holds precisely when the extension is finite. The note ends with a follow-up question. What is the projective dimension of the larger ring in the other cases?
arxiv-2512-17173:
Bing Li, Sanju Velani, and Bo Wang look at numbers that meet two strict rules at once. One rule picks out numbers that can be matched very closely by fractions, again and again. The other rule keeps only numbers whose digits, in some base, avoid a chosen set of missing digits entirely.

The question is how large the overlap of the two sets can be, measured by Hausdorff dimension, a tool for sizing thin sets. The team proves the overlap is never larger than the product of the two separate sizes. In some cases it is strictly smaller, which disproves a product guess made by Li, Li, and Wu. They also close a gap left in that earlier work.
arxiv-2512-17273:
Farinaz Mostajeran, Aruzhan Tleubek, and Salah A Faroughi tackle equations where what happens at one place depends on faraway places and on the distant past. Heat, fluids, and materials can all behave this nonlocal way. Classic solvers must redo heavy integral math again and again, and earlier neural solvers only fit one setup at a time.

Their framework, MINPO, learns both the nonlocal rule and its inverse in one go, then rebuilds the full solution field. A light consistency check keeps the learned rule honest. Across many kernel types and sizes, MINPO beat classic solvers and rival neural methods, including physics-based networks. One flexible solver for many memory-driven systems is the prize here.
arxiv-2512-17373:
Zhengmian Hu asks whether a machine, left alone with raw experience, could invent the same concepts humans did. Human concepts refuse to sit still: Pluto lost its planet status as knowledge grew. Any machine-made concept must likewise be a structure that can bend, split, and merge as new facts arrive, not a fixed label.

Hu defines a concept by a tight rule: split experience into parts, and any missing part must be rebuildable from the rest. A score called excess information grades how wasteful a split is. Dialectics then becomes a contest, where rival concepts bid to explain new facts with shorter accounts, growing or merging as they win or lose. Small shared seeds let one agent pass a concept cheaply to another.
arxiv-2512-17973:
Rafael Prieto-Curiel models cartel life across generations to test a common policy: lock up more members. In his model, people are recruited, age, and leave by death, capture, or retirement. The question is how much crime each lever can stop, given that new recruits keep arriving.

The math gives a blunt answer. Jailing members prevents less than 10 percent of cartel offences, and doubling penalties cuts member potential by less than 5 percent. The model points instead to help after prison, which lowers the odds of a return to cartel life. Prieto-Curiel argues that this often skipped step could cut crime more than longer sentences.
arxiv-2512-18173:
Timothy R. Van Hoomissen and coauthors use transfer learning to read Thomson scattering spectra, a laser diagnostic that reports a plasma's electron density and temperature. Neural networks can read noisy spectra where standard fitting fails, but they usually demand large sets of labeled examples.

The team pretrains five different network designs on synthetic spectra, then adapts each to real measurements by retraining a few layers near the output. They test both the collective and non collective scattering regimes and vary how much real data the networks get. Transfer learning cuts the error whenever the real training set holds roughly 200 spectra or fewer. The result points to faster, surer analysis for high repetition rate plasma experiments that must decide between shots.
arxiv-2512-18373:
Ansh Nagwekar wrote this master's thesis at the University of Pennsylvania, posted to arXiv in December 2025. Its subject is optimization, the set of algorithms that adjust a neural network's weights during training. Better training methods can cut training time sharply and help models learn cleaner features, yet the standard tools often work for reasons nobody fully understands.

The thesis traces the path from basic stochastic gradient descent and adaptive methods to techniques that use curvature information, such as second-order approximations and layer-wise preconditioning. It also covers supporting tools like learning-rate schedules and maximal update parametrization. The final chapters turn practical, giving concrete advice for wiring these methods into modern deep learning workflows.
arxiv-2512-18473:
Khaled Berkani proposes APC-GNN++, a graph neural network that classifies diabetes cases patient by patient. Instead of scoring each patient in isolation, the model links similar patients and lets context-aware attention weigh the links. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, adds confidence-guided blending, which mixes a patient's own features with evidence from neighbors.

For new patients, a mini-graph built from nearest neighbors gives real-time predictions with explanations, without retraining the whole model. Tested on real hospital data from Algeria, APC-GNN++ beats standard methods such as random forests and XGBoost, plus a plain graph convolutional network, on accuracy and macro F1. A desktop interface lets clinicians explore the confidence scores behind each call.
arxiv-2512-18873:
Paolo Luppi, Claudia Benedetti, and Andrea Smirne measure how quantum a quantum walk really is, moment by moment. A quantum walk spreads a particle across a graph with interference, unlike a classical random walk. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Physical Review A, combines two yardsticks. One is a distance between quantum and classical states at one time. The other checks whether sequential position measurements obey classical consistency rules.

The second measure, K(t), grows quadratically at short times, against the known linear growth of the first. Both depend only on the starting node's degree, not the graph's shape. Later, K(t) becomes topology-driven, suppressed on complete graphs yet finite and oscillating on cycles. Under noise, position dephasing kills both measures. Energy basis dephasing instead leaves K(t) a finite remainder, a signature of surviving quantum memory.
arxiv-2512-19073:
Members of the ATLAS Collaboration measured how often proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider produce pairs of jets. The data cover collisions at thirteen teraelectronvolts recorded from 2015 to 2018. Jets were built with the standard anti-kt algorithm at a set radius.

The team reports double-differential rates against the pair's mass and either the pair's separation or its boost along the beam. The mass range runs from a few hundred gigaelectronvolts to nearly ten teraelectronvolts. After correcting the data to particle level, they compare it with state-of-the-art quantum chromodynamics calculations. Such checks test theory and sharpen knowledge of the proton's inner structure.
arxiv-2512-19273:
Xiaoyu Zhang, Zhiyun Fan, Wenyang Zhang, and Di Wang estimate huge matrices with a Kronecker structure, even when the data carry heavy tails. Such factors appear in trace regression, matrix models, and bilinear problems. A nasty scaling freedom between the factors warps gradients, which breaks standard robust methods that clip at a fixed level.

Their scaled robust gradient descent first undoes the factor scaling, then truncates, restoring stable steps. A scaled hard thresholding step selects variables in a scale-invariant way. Theory gives convergence rates that are optimal when noise variance is finite and degrade gracefully for heavier tails. Simulations and two real cases confirm the gains.
arxiv-2512-19473:
Karan Mukhi, Licio Romao, and Alessandro Abate solve the charging problem for whole fleets of electric vehicles facing one live imbalance price. Multistage stochastic programming frames the problem well but scales badly as vehicles and stages multiply. The group's aggregate flexibility, though, has a clean geometric shape: a permutahedron.

That shape lets the authors build an optimal rule for splitting an aggregate plan back to single cars. It also yields an exact, smaller stochastic program and a recourse function that is piecewise affine, with closed-form slopes and intercepts from truncated price expectations. The first-stage policy comes out exactly too, and numerics confirm the claims.
arxiv-2512-19773:
Mohammed Asheruddin N leads a six-author team warning battery researchers about ghosts in their aging analyses. Degradation mode analysis splits capacity fade into lost lithium inventory and lost active material by fitting low-rate voltage curves. But measured curves also carry an ohmic voltage drop and charge-discharge hysteresis, especially with graphite-silicon oxide anodes, and those artifacts can be misread as material loss, creating phantom degradation.

Working with two commercial cells of differing resistance, the team corrects only the instantaneous ohmic term, estimated from the first pulse step, before fitting. Without correction, one cell's positive-electrode material loss was increasingly under-diagnosed and lithium loss suppressed, while window and branch choices in the other cell shifted attributions by many percentage points. Their protocol: correct the ohmic term, harmonize the voltage window, and base attribution on the discharge branch.
arxiv-2512-19973:
Jun Yuan and three co-authors define a stronger kind of backup routes in a network graph. An S-Steiner tree links a chosen set S of terminals in the graph. Several such trees are fully independent when three things hold. They share no edges. They meet only at S. And their paths between any two terminals are disjoint inside. The notion extends internally disjoint Steiner trees. It backs fault-tolerant parallel routing designs.

The paper sorts these trees in detail. It also sets a generalized connectivity measure. For each size of terminal set, the measure takes the worst packing count over all sets of that size. Complete graphs get an exact value for it. Complete bipartite graphs get a tight lower bound. Both families' tree structures are studied head on.
arxiv-2512-20173:
Ze Gong, Pradeep Varakantham, and Akshat Kumar teach control policies to be safe and liked at once, entirely offline. Preference-based reinforcement learning normally infers rewards and costs from human feedback and then runs constrained optimization on those learned models; in long-horizon continuous control, the model errors compound and performance suffers. Their framework sidesteps the middlemen.

Policies are learned directly from pairwise preferences over behavior plus binary safety labels on trajectory segments. The method, PreSa, fuses preference learning and safety alignment into one constrained problem solved in a Lagrangian formulation, never explicitly building reward or cost models at all. On continuous control tasks with synthetic and real human feedback, the learned policies achieved high reward while respecting safety, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines and offline safe methods that cheated with ground-truth rewards. The extended abstract appears at AAMAS 2026.
arxiv-2512-20573:
Rui Pan and co-authors turn a weakness of diffusion language models into a drafting strategy. Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive models by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that a big verifier checks. Diffusion models generate in parallel but trade quality for speed, seemingly poor drafters. The authors argue the opposite.

Parallel drafting makes long guesses cheap, so rejection hurts less. FailFast adapts its speculation length dynamically: it spends minimal compute where speculation is hard and extends drafts aggressively where text is predictable, sometimes seventy tokens at once. No fine-tuning is required. The approach speeds decoding several-fold over vanilla generation and beats strong benchmarks including EAGLE-3. Losslessness is preserved, since the verifier still has the final word.
arxiv-2512-20773:
Ziyi Zhu and seven co-authors address a weak spot in testing chatbots: the fake users used for practice rarely act like real people. Their framework, called DIAL, trains a user simulator through competition. A generator plays the user while a discriminator tries to spot what is unreal, and each round pushes the simulator closer to human behavior.

The test case is mental health support dialogue, where failures matter and come in many forms. DIAL restored word variety that plain fine-tuning had flattened, and its simulated failures matched real failure rates closely. Better simulators let builders find problems cheaply before a system reaches real users.
arxiv-2512-20873:
Rahul Bulusu surveys nearly twenty years of research on keeping cyber-physical systems running through faults. Such systems, from power grids to medical devices and robots, fuse software tightly with physical motion. A small glitch in a sensor or network can cascade into physical instability in ways single-layer thinking misses.

Bulusu organizes the field with an Origin-Layer-Effect taxonomy: where faults start, which layer they cross, and what they finally do. Mapping well-known systems onto it exposes shared failure pathways and blind spots. Four structural gaps recur, including learning-based control lacking stability guarantees and weak forensic visibility. The survey closes with directions joining robust control, monitoring, and formal assurance.
arxiv-2512-20973:
Yihan Xia, Taotao Wang, Wenxin Xu, and Shengli Zhang build the bookkeeping layer that teams of autonomous language-model agents need when nobody fully trusts anybody. Paying agents fairly requires measuring each one's contribution, but doing that on a blockchain is expensive and exposes the agents' strategies. Their framework, DAO-Agent, keeps coordination and an immutable log on-chain while moving the contribution math off-chain.

Contributions are scored with Shapley values, the game-theoretic fair split, and zero-knowledge proofs let the chain verify those scores without seeing the underlying work. Verification stays constant-time as the coalition grows, and in a crypto-trading test case the gas cost of verification fell by up to 99.9 percent against naive on-chain alternatives. Private, auditable, and cheap enough to scale is the combination on offer.
arxiv-2512-21073: Wan Wu continues a series on quiver Hecke algebras built from Borcherds-Cartan data, where imaginary simple roots are allowed. The third work in the series introduces quiver Hecke superalgebras, with a sign grading tracked by the super prefix. The new algebras categorify quantum Borcherds superalgebras: their module classes carry the quantum structure in lifted form. Relations become functors, and identities become isomorphisms. The upshot is a richer setting for studying these quantum symmetries.
arxiv-2512-21273:
Imtiaz Waheed, Erkinjon Karimov, and Mujeeb ur Rehman build algebra tools for a broad family of fractional derivatives. Fractional calculus extends differentiation to non-integer orders. The Prabhakar derivative, here carried to its nth-level form, covers several classical variants used to model memory effects in physics and engineering. The authors set out its basics. Chief among them is how it inverts, and how it pairs with the matching Prabhakar integral.

They then develop a Mikusinski-type operational calculus for the operator. In that system, applying the derivative becomes multiplication. Such equations can then be solved by algebra rather than transforms. Two worked cases close the paper: closed-form solutions of a fractional ordinary differential equation, and of the time-fractional heat equation with the new derivative inside. For work on anomalous diffusion and viscoelastic memory, the result is a ready-made solver for a wide class.
arxiv-2512-21373:
Titouan Duston and a large team of co-authors introduce AInsteinBench, a benchmark for testing whether language model agents can do real scientific software work. Existing benchmarks mostly test textbook reasoning or ordinary coding tasks. AInsteinBench instead places agents inside real scientific software projects and asks them to carry out full development work.

Its tasks come from real pull requests written by the maintainers of six widely used scientific codebases, covering quantum chemistry, quantum computing, molecular dynamics, numerical relativity, fluid dynamics, and cheminformatics. Each task passed multi-stage filtering and expert review to confirm it is scientifically hard, well tested, and fairly graded. Because the tasks run in executable environments with test-driven checks, the benchmark exposes real failure modes. It measures whether a model can move past surface-level code generation toward the skills that research actually requires.
arxiv-2512-21573:
Zhangzheng Tu, Kailun Su, Shaolong Zhu, and Yukun Zheng recover human motion in world coordinates from a single camera video, then transfer it to a humanoid robot. Robots need to know where a person moves in real space, not just in the frame. Usual routes rely on SLAM pipelines or heavy temporal models.

The authors take a lighter, engineering-first path. They use SAM 3D Body as a perception backbone and express motion in the Momentum HumanRig representation, which robots can consume directly. The method locks each person's identity and skeleton scale so bone lengths stay constant. A sliding-window optimization smooths frame-by-frame predictions in that representation. A soft foot-ground contact model recovers plausible global trajectories. The motion is retargeted onto a Unitree G1 humanoid with a two-stage inverse kinematics pipeline. On real videos the system produced stable trajectories and reliable robot motion.
arxiv-2512-21673:
Jalal Khan compares two deep learning object detectors for the perception system of an autonomous vehicle. Perception is how the vehicle detects, locates, and identifies cars, pedestrians, and road signs to navigate safely. The models compared are YOLO-NAS and YOLOv8, both recent versions of the you-only-look-once detector family.

Khan captured a custom dataset and trained and tested both models on it under matched conditions. The smaller YOLOv8s variant finished training in about a quarter of the time the YOLO-NAS model needed, a saving of roughly seventy-five percent. It also edged out its rival on detection accuracy, reaching about eighty-three percent against about eighty-one percent. The comparison is deliberately practical rather than theoretical. Its value is a real-world data point on the speed-accuracy trade-off between two widely used detectors.
arxiv-2512-22273:
Wenhao Ou works in complex algebraic geometry, studying reflexive sheaves on spaces that are almost smooth. The setting is a compact complex analytic variety whose only singularities are quotient singularities in codimension two. On such orbifolds, usual Chern classes need adjustment, and Ou uses orbifold modifications to define first and second homological Chern classes for a reflexive sheaf.

With a Kähler form on the space and a sheaf that is stable with respect to it, Ou deduces a Bogomolov-Gieseker inequality for those orbifold Chern classes. Such inequalities bound a sheaf's geometry and underpin much of the theory of stable sheaves. The result extends a classic tool to singular spaces that arise naturally in modern geometry.
arxiv-2512-22773:
Julia Gaudio and Andrew Jin pin down the exact limits of community detection in networks whose connections depend on geometry. In social networks, friends of friends tend to connect, producing many triangles, so a spatial model fits better than the classic stochastic block model. The geometric stochastic block model places nodes in space and links them with probabilities depending on both community labels and distance.

The question is exact recovery: when can an algorithm restore every node's true community label with high probability? Gaudio and Jin fully characterize the information-theoretic threshold for this model under mild technical assumptions. Their result generalizes earlier work by Gaudio and co-authors and separates the regimes where perfect recovery is possible from those where no method, however powerful, can succeed. Such thresholds guide practitioners on how much data a network needs before its communities can be trusted completely.
arxiv-2512-24073:
Pankaj Chaudhary, Neminath Hubballi, and Sameer Kulkarni improve caching in Named Data Networks. In this design, routers cache content by name. Router storage is small, so choices matter. Keeping popular items pays off. But tracking popularity across a network costs effort. Older schemes pay a heavy coordination price.

Their method, CPePC, splits the network into communities. The communities do not overlap. Each elects a leader node. The leader estimates popularity for the whole group. That trims the coordination overhead. Caching decisions rest on a predicted value. The value blends current cache occupancy with item popularity. So the scheme looks ahead instead of only reacting. The authors give the full set of algorithms. Tests in a discrete-event simulator beat six rival techniques.
arxiv-2512-24173:
Jui-Ting Lu, Henrique Ennes, Chih-Kang Huang, and Ali Abbassi bring quantum computing into digital art. Quantum brushes are software tools, introduced by Ferreira and others in 2025, that use quantum behavior to generate artistic effects a classical brush cannot. Writing in an outreach spirit, the authors explain the mathematics behind two new brushes and describe how they built them.

One brush, Steerable, applies quantum geometric control theory to merge two artworks into one. The other, Chemical, borrows the variational methods chemists use to estimate molecular ground-state energies and instead uses them to evolve colors across a canvas. Both implementations are open source and fully compatible with the original quantum brush package. The paper invites artists and curious readers to experiment with quantum effects as a creative medium, with the code ready to download.
arxiv-2512-24373:
Waheed Ahmed Abro and Zied Bouraoui teach document models to skim. Long documents defeat ordinary transformers, above all in law and medicine. Sparse attention handles length at high cost. It can still miss whole-document context. Hierarchical models are cheaper but opaque about cross-section links. Humans solve the problem by skimming. They dwell on key sections and grasp the whole.

The framework copies that strategy with contrastive learning. A random section of the document is masked. A natural language inference objective aligns the masked part with related sections. Unrelated parts are pushed away. The model thus learns how sections support each other. The training is self-supervised, needing no labels. Experiments on legal and biomedical texts confirmed the gains. Accuracy and efficiency both improved significantly over prior approaches.
arxiv-2512-24773:
Anas Saeed, Mahmoud Salim, and Ali Arshad Nasir optimize throughput for a reconfigurable intelligent surface carried by a drone. The surface can reshape radio propagation on demand, serving users from a ground base station. Drone jitter in three dimensions and imperfect channel knowledge make the link unstable and the optimization stochastic and nonconvex.

Deep reinforcement learning handles the moving, uncertain setting, aiming to raise expected throughput using only available channel estimates under transmit limits. Readers in wireless systems get a control strategy designed for real impairments, not ideal channels. The work targets settings where a flying surface must keep adapting as it shakes and channels drift.
arxiv-2512-24873:
Weixun Wang, XiaoXiao Xu, Wanhe An, and a large team introduce an open ecosystem for building agentic language models that act over many turns in real environments. Agentic crafting means taking actions, observing outcomes, and refining artifacts step by step. Three parts form the pipeline: a post-training framework, a sandbox manager for generating trajectories, and an agent framework.

Within that ecosystem they build the ROME model. Open-source readers get end-to-end infrastructure rather than a single model release. The aim is to streamline how agent models are trained, tested in sandboxes, and deployed, so improvements can compound across the community.
arxiv-2512-24973:
Rafal Potempa, Michal Kordasz, and Jozef Cyran release GEQIE, a Python framework for encoding images into quantum states quickly and correctly. The framework builds the encoding state with a unitary gate that can later be transpiled to real quantum backends. Benchmarks under different simulated noise levels verify the implemented encoding methods and show the tool suits more advanced research.

A showcase encodes a cosmic web dark matter density snapshot and retrieves it with very high correlation accuracy. Quantum computing readers get tested infrastructure for quantum image processing experiments. Reliable encoding is the entry step for any quantum image algorithm, so a verified framework saves repeated groundwork.
arxiv-2512-25073:
Yi-Chuan Huang, Hao-Jen Chien, Chin-Yang Lin, and colleagues present GaMO, a geometry-aware diffusion method that outpaints new views to help rebuild three-dimensional scenes from very few images. Dense multi-view methods fail with sparse views, and diffusion-based view generation helps but leaves gaps: coverage beyond known view edges is weak, generated views disagree geometrically, and detail suffers.

Geometry awareness in the multi-view outpainting addresses those three limits together. Computer vision readers get more consistent synthetic views for training sparse reconstructions. Better hallucinated views matter for scanning real places where capturing many angles is impractical.
arxiv-2601-06873: Research by Mustafa Abdool and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with applying Embedding-Based retrieval to airbnb search. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The goal of Airbnb search is to match guests with the ideal accommodation that fits their travel needs. This is a challenging problem, as popular search locations can have around a hundred thousand available homes. And guests themselves have a wide variety of preferences. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-06973:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Davide Baldelli and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers LLMs can’t play hangman. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. As LLMs move from text completion toward autonomous agents, they remain constrained by the standard chat interface, which lacks private working memory.

This raises a fundamental question: can agents reliably perform interactive tasks that depend on hidden state. We define Private State Interactive Tasks (PSITs), which require agents to generate and maintain hidden information while producing consistent public responses. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07373:
Muhammad Raza and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with enumeration of generalized cospectral mates of graphs. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The work investigates the enumeration of generalized cospectral mates of simple graphs. Where the generalized spectrum consists of the spectra of a graph and its complement.

Moving beyond the classical problem of identifying graphs determined by their generalized spectrum. We address the more quantitative question of how many non-isomorphic graphs can share the same generalized spectrum. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07473:
Michael J. Clark introduces AntiPaSTO, a method for steering language models toward honesty, in a 2026 preprint. As models grow more capable, people cannot easily check what they say. Steering methods therefore need to work from inside the model, without constant human labels. They also need to hold up on new kinds of inputs.

Existing methods, Clark notes, meet only some of those demands. AntiPaSTO is self-supervised and separates internal representations along an antiparallel axis. Pushing one way or the other along that axis shifts behavior in opposite directions. Coherence constraints keep the model from collapsing into nonsense. The paper speaks to the wider effort to keep advanced models truthful and controllable.
arxiv-2601-07773:
Lingchen Sun and coauthors train diffusion transformers with signals that sit inside the model. Recent work guides diffusion models with outside semantic features, such as those from DINO. That guidance can greatly speed training. It also needs pretrained outside networks, which adds links to other tools and cuts freedom. Their 2026 preprint seeks the same gain from features found inside instead.

The title speaks of freeing the rich meaning that sits inside diffusion transformers. If inner layers already encode useful semantics, training can lean on them directly. With no outside teacher, the pipeline gets simpler and needs less compute tied to a second model. Faster diffusion training matters because these models are costly to build. The paper targets generative modeling scholars. It asks whether the guide a model needs has been inside it all along. The gain, if it holds, is a lean build with fewer parts to keep in step.
arxiv-2601-07973:
Myra Cheng and colleagues build a framework for organizing social norms so AI norm violations can be detected. Generative AI should be useful and safe across cultures. Understanding how models follow sociocultural norms is a key step. Existing NLP work, they note, lacks nuance and coverage in evaluating norm adherence. Their 2026 preprint, Cultural Compass, addresses that gap for human-AI conversations.

Norms vary by culture and situation, so a flat rule list fails. A compass framework organizes norms so violations can be spotted in context. Detection is a prerequisite for training or steering models to behave appropriately. The work matters for products deployed across many countries at once. The paper serves NLP scholars and AI safety teams. It supplies structure for a topic often handled with ad hoc lists.
arxiv-2601-08073: Bandar Al-Dhalaan and Shalev Ben-David study turning Monte Carlo methods into Las Vegas methods for composed functions. Their 2026 arXiv paper works with Boolean functions and query complexity measures. For a measure M and function f, they define a composition limit as the number of compositions grows without bound. Monte Carlo algorithms may err, while Las Vegas algorithms always give correct answers with random run time. The paper asks when recursive composition lets one style be converted into the other. It serves readers in theoretical computer science.
arxiv-2601-08573: Andrea Braides wrote a 2026 arXiv paper that sums up new results on a tool for hard math problems. The tool is singular perturbations of non-convex functionals. When a problem has many best answers, a small added term can pick out one of them. The classic case is the gradient theory of phase transitions by Modica. That theory built on Gamma-convergence work by Modica and Mortola. It backed the minimal-interface rule for phase lines. The paper sums up fresh work on the non-local form of the tool.
arxiv-2601-08673:
Didier Sornette, Sandro Claudio Lera, and Ke Wu argue that AI alignment failure is structural, not accidental. Their 2026 arXiv paper responds to reports of language models showing deception, threats, or blackmail. Such reports are often read as proof of alignment failure or emergent malign agency.

The authors argue that this reading rests on a conceptual error. Models learn human interaction structures, including manipulation patterns present in training data. Advanced AI then acts as an endogenous evolutionary shock to the systems it joins. The paper reframes safety debates: if failure is structural, fixes must target training structures and deployment incentives, not just individual model misbehavior.
arxiv-2601-08873:
Hema Hariharan Samson builds a tool to spot fake or cut images across many sources. Old check tools work on one class of flaw. A tool trained on phone shots may fail on AI art or on scans. Real check work must cross those lines each day. Samson aims for one tool that holds up in all of them.

The tool is called ForensicFormer. It reads an image at three scales at once. Fine scale checks catch pixel flaws. Mid scale checks read edge breaks. Large scale checks ask if the scene makes sense. Past tools that use one scale fell below a set mark on new sets. This tool holds a high mark on those sets, the author says. A reader in image checks gets a broad, layered plan.
arxiv-2601-09473:
Oliver Bolton and five co-authors, including Sara Hooker, automate a choice that language model builders now face often. Their 2026 arXiv paper, SimMerge, learns to select merge operators from similarity signals. Model merging blends several trained models into one that keeps their combined skills.

Scaling merging is hard because quality depends on the operator, the subset of models, and the merge order. Testing each option by merging and evaluating is costly. SimMerge instead reads similarity signals between models and predicts a good recipe. A cheap selector would make merging a routine step in building capable models.
arxiv-2601-09873:
Saymon Souza, Amanda Santana, and Eduardo Figueiredo test whether language models can smell bad code. Their 2026 arXiv paper assesses large language models for code smell detection, moving beyond strict rule-based checkers. Code smells are warning signs of quality problems that raise maintenance costs.

Language models have shown skill across many software engineering tasks. Their use for smell detection is still little explored. The authors measure how effective the models are in practice. A capable detector tool could warn developers very early on, before smelly code hardens into expensive, unreliable systems.
arxiv-2601-09973:
Samuel Everett links two hard fields: how hard a task is, and how a flow acts. His tasks ask if a point can reach a set in finite time. The flow is one way and sits on a line. Each task comes from its own flow.

He shows a tight link. If tasks from two flows can map to each other in a natural way, the flows must act alike. The word alike is made sharp in the proof. The paper is part two of a pair. It gives a tool to sort flows by the tasks they spawn.
arxiv-2601-10373:
Yichong Xia, Yimin Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, and Bin Chen squeeze images to a trickle of bits. New diffusion tools can rebuild a rich image from few bits. The rebuilt shot looks true to the eye. But past tools are slow to sample. Their bit splits are also oft poor.

The team made DiffCR, a squeeze frame built for speed. It refines a diffusion prior in a firm way. That cuts the slow sample steps. It also splits bits with more care across the image. The aim is a small file that rebuilds fast and looks true.
arxiv-2601-10673:
Aditya Agrawal and a team at Google tackle a bottleneck in training and serving large language models. Model data must be split across many accelerator chips. The collective steps that sync those chips are often capped by network bandwidth. Faster compression of the data in flight would ease that cap.

The team presents a single-stage Huffman encoder built for machine learning compression. Huffman coding squeezes data by giving short codes to common values. A one-stage design aims to keep the squeeze fast enough for live training traffic. If it holds up, big model runs could spend less time waiting on the network.
arxiv-2601-10773:
Niko Usai, Dario Montagnini, Kristian Ilianov Iliev, and Raffaele Camanzo present LogicLens, a tool for grasping large software systems. Big systems sprawl across many repositories and microservices. To reason about them, developers need more than code structure. They need the domain logic and runtime behavior, which sit implicit and scattered across the codebase.

LogicLens builds a semantic code graph to explore such systems. A graph can join calls, data, and intent in one view. That helps new team members and auditors find how a feature truly works. The work speaks to engineers who inherit sprawling systems and must change them without breaking hidden links.
arxiv-2601-11073:
Rongkun Cui, Nana Zhang, Kun Zhu, and Qi Zhang build a hypergraph learning system to catch web finance fraud. Online finance is a core part of the web economy. Its openness invites fraud that harms vulnerable users and weakens trust in digital finance. The authors draw their design from the hippocampus, the brain region that binds memories together.

Their multi-view hypergraph model links accounts, devices, and transactions in shared hyperedges. Views from several angles help expose fraud rings that single links hide. The brain-inspired framing stresses memory: fraud patterns repeat, and a system that recalls them can flag new variants. The work serves platforms that must police harm without freezing honest users out.
arxiv-2601-11573:
Muhammad Muneeb and David Ascher fine-tune language models on bioinformatics text. Their 2026 preprint gives a reproducible pipeline for the work. General LLMs often lack specialized knowledge for this field. Bioinformatics tasks need tool names, data forms, and jargon.

Two use cases show the pipeline in action. PRSGPT focuses on polygenic risk score tools and their use. BioStarsGPT trains on community forum discussions instead. Forum text holds practical know-how from working analysts. The pipeline can be rerun by other teams on new data. That reproducibility is a stated design goal of the work. Specialist models may then serve niche science better.
arxiv-2601-11773:
Elliot Benjamin and Mohamed Mahmoud Chems-Eddin work on a deep question in number theory. They study real quadratic fields, which add a square root to the rationals. For each field, a tower of class fields can be built step by step. They ask how long that tower runs.

They pick fields whose class group is a small group of order four. They also pick fields whose discriminant is not a sum of two squares. The work is a follow-up, checking past guesses on tower length. Such towers test how class groups grow in pure maths.
arxiv-2601-12273:
