europmc-pmc2361173:
Karakas, Bachman, and Park reviewed mutations in the PIK3CA gene in 2006. PIK3CA makes a working part of PI3K, an enzyme in a signal path that tells cells to grow and survive. That path had already been tied to cancer, and new reports kept finding PIK3CA faults in tumors.

The authors gathered reports from the previous year covering many cancer types. They found the gene mutated again and again across human malignancies, marking it as a true cancer driver rather than a bystander. Because the enzyme can be blocked by drugs, they discussed what the mutations could mean for diagnosis and for targeted therapy. Testing a tumor for PIK3CA faults, they argued, might one day guide which patients get PI3K-blocking drugs.
europmc-pmc2375073:
Giatromanolaki and colleagues measured oxygen-sensing proteins in lung cancer in 2001. The proteins, HIF1 alpha and HIF2 alpha, rise when cells run short of oxygen and switch on genes for blood vessel growth and energy use. The cancer was operable non-small-cell lung cancer, the common form.

They stained 108 tumor samples. HIF1 alpha appeared in 62% of cases and HIF2 alpha in 50%, while healthy lung stained weakly or not at all. Both proteins tracked high levels of vessel growth factors such as VEGF. Patients whose tumors showed HIF2 alpha died sooner, and this held even in tumors with few blood vessels. In the combined analysis HIF2 alpha stayed an independent warning sign of poor outcome. HIF1 alpha showed only a weak trend the same way. The authors suggested drugs aimed at the HIF pathway.
europmc-pmc2387073:
Dugan and a large team mapped bird flu diversity in wild birds in 2008. Wild birds are the natural home of type A influenza viruses, the family behind human flu pandemics. The team read the full genomes of 167 viruses gathered from 14 bird species at four US sites.

The viruses spanned 29 combinations of the two surface proteins used to name flu subtypes. Up to 26% of samples showed signs of mixed infection with more than one subtype at once. Family tree analysis, the largest of its kind then, revealed constant genome reshuffling. Flu viruses swap their eight genome segments when two infect one bird, and here segments mixed with no fixed pattern. Some segments had even crossed between hemispheres. The authors called these short-lived genome constellations, unlike the stable sets seen in mammal flu.
europmc-pmc2429973:
McIntosh, Kovacevic, and Itier measured brain signal variability during development in 2008. Adults answer more steadily than children on mental tasks, so the natural guess was that mature brains also fluctuate less. The team recorded scalp electrical signals, called EEG, while children aged 8 to 15 and adults aged 20 to 33 did a face memory task.

Children were indeed slower, less accurate, and more variable in response times. Yet their brain signals varied less from trial to trial than adults' signals did. Brain variability rose with age and tracked performance: more variability meant steadier responses and better accuracy. The authors read this as growing neural complexity. A more variable brain holds a wider stock of states and switches between them more fluidly, they argued, making variability an index of mental capacity.
europmc-pmc2435273:
Supekar, Menon, Rubin, Musen, and Greicius mapped resting brain networks in Alzheimer's disease in 2008. Even at rest, brain areas pulse in coordinated networks with a small-world layout: tight local clusters joined by short paths. The team asked whether that layout breaks down in Alzheimer's, the commonest dementia.

They scanned 21 patients and 18 matched healthy adults with fMRI, a brain imaging method, while they rested. In healthy adults the networks showed the expected small-world pattern at low frequencies. Patient networks had lost it: the clustering measure was significantly lower, signalling weakened local links. The drop centred on the hippocampus, a memory structure, on both sides of the brain. Clustering alone separated patients from controls with 72% sensitivity and 78% specificity. The authors proposed network measures as imaging markers of the disease.
europmc-pmc2447873:
Gao and colleagues catalogued the bacteria living on psoriatic skin without growing them in dishes in this study. Psoriasis is an inflamed, scaly skin disease of unknown cause. Earlier work relied on cultures, which miss most skin microbes, so the team read bacterial DNA directly from skin samples.

They took 19 samples from six patients, 13 from lesions and six from healthy-looking skin, and sequenced 1,925 gene clones. About 95.6% matched known bacteria, spanning 189 species-level groups. Lesions were dominated by the Firmicutes group at 46.2% of clones, far above its 24.4% share on healthy volunteers' skin. The usual skin leaders, Actinobacteria, fell from 47.6% on healthy skin to 37.3% in lesions in this data. One common skin genus, Propionibacterium, dropped from 21.1% on healthy skin to 2.9% in lesions.
europmc-pmc2559873:
Dunker and colleagues reviewed in 2008 a decade of work on intrinsically disordered proteins, proteins that never fold into a fixed shape. The classic view held that a protein's function flows from its folded structure, like a key fitting a lock. Yet experimenters had long reported proteins that work while unfolded, and a predictor from the authors' group had opened the field ten years earlier.

Genome-wide predictions now show disordered proteins are everywhere, across all three domains of life, and number far beyond the few early examples. Many key functions depend directly on the unfolded state, including signalling and binding that folding would prevent. The authors argue textbooks still ignore this evidence. Disorder prediction, they say, has forced a rewrite of how structure relates to function.
europmc-pmc2667673:
Danaei and colleagues counted in 2009 how many American deaths could be blamed on fixable risks, from smoking to poor diet. Death certificates name the final disease but not the habits and body measures that led there. Earlier counts had used patchy methods and left out diet almost entirely, so the authors rebuilt the tally on one shared footing.

They combined national survey data on exposure with known risk sizes for each disease. Smoking and high blood pressure came out as the two largest killers, ahead of excess weight, inactivity, and high blood sugar. Both leaders already have proven treatments and public programs, which makes their toll a policy choice as much as a medical fact. The study gives officials a ranked list of where prevention would save the most lives.
europmc-pmc2700273:
Kalmar and colleagues showed in 2009 that embryonic stem cells are not a uniform pool. Each cell's level of Nanog, a core stemness factor, flickers up and down over time. The flicker steers its fate. Stem cells keep the ability to become any tissue, held by a small gene network. The textbook picture treated that state as stable and identical in every cell.

Tracking single living cells, the team watched Nanog levels rise and fall on their own. Cells caught in a low phase were primed to specialize, quick to answer a differentiation signal. Cells in a high phase resisted and stayed flexible. Crucially, low cells could climb back: the fluctuation is reversible, not a one-way exit. Fate decisions in the dish, the authors argue, are partly a matter of timing, of which phase a cell happens to occupy when the signal arrives.
europmc-pmc2729073:
Patrick and co-authors ran a randomized trial in 2009. They tested a weight-loss program built mainly on daily text and picture messages to mobile phones. No prior study had tested whether weight control could be driven this way in overweight adults. Seventy-five adults were assigned to monthly print materials alone, or to the message program plus print and brief monthly counselor calls.

After four months, the message group lost more weight than the print-only group, an adjusted difference of about two kilograms. Average loss in the message group was close to three percent of body weight. Nearly all message-group participants who finished said they would recommend the program to friends and family, which suggests phone messaging is a practical channel for weight support.
europmc-pmc2750773:
Osborne, Wakeling, and Nicholson reviewed in 2004 fulvestrant, a new breast cancer drug. It blocks the estrogen receptor and lowers the receptor itself. It has no estrogen-like effects. Hormone therapies are favored for hormone-sensitive metastatic breast cancer because they are well tolerated. Older drugs such as tamoxifen partly mimic estrogen, and cross-resistance limits how long similar drugs can be sequenced.

Their review explains estrogen signaling and how fulvestrant differs. It binds the receptor, blocks it fully, and drives its loss, so receptor levels fall in the cell. Lab and clinical data support that novel mechanism. A drug that is not cross-resistant lets doctors extend tolerated hormone treatment before turning to harsher chemotherapy. Women who still respond to hormone drugs gain more time on gentler care first.
europmc-pmc2791173:
Lorincz and colleagues recorded single nerve cells in awake cats to learn how the brain's alpha rhythm shapes visual signals. Alpha waves are slow rhythms tied to sight and attention. The team watched relay cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay station that passes visual news from the eye toward the cortex.

Relay cells fell into two groups whose firing was briefly hushed at opposite peaks of the alpha wave. That timed hushing came from bursts of inhibition, meaning calming signals, sent by nearby interneurons between relay cells. The pattern chops the stream of visual signals into timed frames, which may match how seeing itself comes in brief snapshots.
europmc-pmc2825373:
Stephan, Penny, Moran, den Ouden, Daunizeau, and Friston wrote ten simple rules in 2010 for dynamic causal modeling, a math approach that infers hidden brain activity from scans. The method estimates how strongly brain regions drive each other and how tasks change those links. It has spread fast across brain imaging since its debut in 2003, but its complexity traps new users.

The rules walk through good practice, from setting up the model to reading its outputs with care. Each model states how unseen neuron groups evolve over time, then links that hidden activity to the measured signal through a body-based forward model. Judgments stay Bayesian, meaning prior knowledge shapes every estimate and models are compared by evidence. The authors aim the tutorial at the growing user community.
europmc-pmc2831073:
Boyko and colleagues showed in 2010 that stressed Arabidopsis plants pass a tougher state to their offspring, and that the handoff needs chemical tags on DNA. Offspring of plants hit by salt, cold, heat, flood, or ultraviolet light rearranged their DNA more often. They also carried more genome-wide methylation tags and withstood stress better than offspring of sheltered plants.

The boost lasted one generation, not more. A drug that strips methylation tags changed both tag levels and tolerance in the offspring. Plants missing either of two enzymes that make small silencing RNAs, called DCL2 and DCL3, lost most of the inherited response. The authors tie the effect to altered methylation plus the small RNA silencing pathway working together.
europmc-pmc2836773:
Webb, Joseph, Yardley, and Michie pooled results in 2010 from eighty-five trials of internet programs meant to change health behavior, covering over forty-three thousand people. Websites can coach smoking quits, exercise, or diet at scale, yet earlier reviews never coded what the programs actually contained, so nobody knew which ingredients worked.

On average the programs nudged behavior by a small but real amount. Effects grew when a program leaned harder on theory, and programs built on the theory of planned behavior, which weighs intentions and social pressure, did notably better. Programs using more behavior change techniques also did better. Extra contact channels helped most of all, above all text messages to phones.
europmc-pmc2857873:
Pancreatic cancer is rarely curable once it spreads, so Gillen and colleagues asked in 2010 whether treatment before surgery could help more patients reach an operation. Their systematic review and combined analysis covered studies of pre-surgery drug or radiation therapy. The therapy is called neoadjuvant, meaning it is given first to shrink the tumor.

Pooling the published studies, Gillen found that tumors judged removable shrank or stayed stable in most treated patients, and surgery rates stayed high in that group. Among patients whose tumors first looked unremovable, about one in three could still have surgery after treatment, a rate close to that group overall. The authors argue such patients belong in pre-surgery treatment programs rather than being ruled out at once.
europmc-pmc2887173:
Schöchl and colleagues reported in 2010 an Austrian trauma program that treats bleeding by replacing specific clotting factors, guided by a bedside clot test. The test, thromboelastometry, watches a blood sample clot in minutes and shows which ingredient is missing. The analysis covered one hundred thirty-one major trauma patients who each needed at least five units of red cells within a day.

Nearly all received fibrinogen concentrate, the protein that forms the clot mesh, as their first treatment. Most also received a concentrate of several other clotting factors, and a few needed platelets when the mesh stayed weak. Deaths in the group ran lower than two standard injury scores predicted for such severe cases. Test-guided concentrates may cut blood product use, the authors argue, though only a randomized trial can prove it.
europmc-pmc2955973:
Merrall and co-authors pooled studies on drug deaths shortly after release from prison in a 2010 meta-analysis. Time inside lowers tolerance to drugs such as heroin, making the first weeks outside especially dangerous.

Six prison systems contributed follow-up covering tens of thousands of person-years and over a thousand early deaths, most drug-related. Risk in the first two weeks ran several times higher than in later weeks, though the multiple varied by country, from about threefold to more than eightfold. Weeks three and four stayed moderately risky. The authors urge release planning focused on that window.
europmc-pmc3028573:
de Boer and colleagues tested in 2011 whether a blood protein called galectin-3 can forecast outcomes for people with heart failure. The protein had looked promising in smaller studies, mostly in patients whose hearts pumped weakly. The team measured it in nearly six hundred patients admitted to hospital with heart failure, then followed them for a year and a half.

Higher starting levels meant a higher risk of dying or returning to hospital, even after accounting for age, kidney function, and other markers. The signal was strongest in patients whose pumping strength was still preserved, a group that is hard to assess. Combining galectin-3 with another common marker improved prediction beyond either one alone. Repeat levels months later added little beyond the first reading.
europmc-pmc3031573:
Flutre, Duprat, Feuillet, and Quesneville tackled in 2011 a practical problem in genome science: how to label jumping genes in a fresh DNA sequence automatically. These mobile pieces, called transposable elements, copy themselves around genomes and shape their size and function. New sequencing projects need fast, accurate ways to find and group them.

The team benchmarked grouping methods against two well finished genomes, from a fly and a small plant, where expert labels already exist. Only one pairing of methods recovered the known families well. They then added a step that merges rival groupings and classifies the pieces in a single pipeline. The combined approach also reveals how copies within a family have diverged over time. That view helps track how jumping genes spread and change across species.
europmc-pmc3072373:
Lafos and colleagues showed in 2011 that a gene silencing mark in plants is busily added and removed as cells take on their final identities. The mark, a triple methyl tag on a DNA packaging protein, is placed by the Polycomb system and was thought to lock genes off in a lasting way. The team mapped the mark genome wide in stem cells of the growing tip and in mature leaf cells of Arabidopsis.

Hundreds of genes gained or lost the mark during the shift, and losing it generally let genes switch on in the matching tissue. The mark directly silences only certain regulator families, yet it frees others indirectly by silencing the tiny RNA genes that restrain them. A whole plant hormone pathway, from making to sensing the growth hormone auxin, sits under its control. The authors propose the mark as a main sculptor of tissue specific patterns.
europmc-pmc3072973:
Burridge and coauthors built in 2011 a single recipe that turns any human pluripotent stem cell line into beating heart muscle cells, solving a notorious reliability problem. Heart cells grown from patient stem cells promise safer drug testing and disease models, but older recipes worked well on some lines and barely at all on others. The team tuned more than forty five variables to find one universal method.

Their recipe clusters the cells into balls, feeds them a defined broth, lowers oxygen to body like levels, and times two growth signals carefully. The recipe was tested across eleven stem cell lines of several origins. Nearly all cell balls started beating within nine days. Most of their cells were genuine heart muscle by protein and electrical tests. The cells answered heart drugs as expected. The authors offer the method as a cheap, scalable source of human heart cells.
europmc-pmc3103473:
Luca Cucullo and colleagues published a laboratory study in BMC Neuroscience in 2011 on how blood flow shapes the barrier between blood and brain. They worked with a human cell model grown under flow, asking whether the push of moving fluid helps vessel cells take on barrier traits.

Flow raised levels of proteins that seal gaps between cells and made the layer tighter and harder for test substances to cross. It also lifted drug pumps, ion channels, and carrier systems for sugars, while shifting energy use away from simple sugar breakdown toward fuller respiration. Flow further slowed cell division. The work shows that fluid force alone helps build and keep a selective brain barrier.
europmc-pmc3123173:
Katrin Loeschner and colleagues fed rats silver in two forms for a month and tracked where it went, in a 2011 paper in Particle and Fibre Toxicology. Tiny silver particles are added to food-related products for their germ-killing power, so swallowing them is a realistic exposure. The team compared the particle form with a dissolved silver salt.

Both forms spread through the body in the same pattern, settling most in liver and kidneys, with some reaching lungs and brain. Total tissue levels were lower for the particle form, matching greater loss in faeces. Under the microscope, small granules containing silver sat in gut wall tissue in both groups, at sizes much like the fed particles. The overlap suggests the two forms may act alike once swallowed.
europmc-pmc3163573:
Nabil-Fareed Alikhan and colleagues built a desktop program that draws circular comparison maps of bacterial genomes in a 2011 paper in BMC Genomics. Ring diagrams, with one reference genome in the centre and matches from others as coloured rings, reveal differences between close relatives at a glance. Existing tools capped the number of comparisons, handled draft genomes poorly, or demanded scripting skill.

Their program removes the comparison cap and runs the underlying matching itself through a point-and-click interface. Rings shade by match strength, and extra tracks can show assembly gaps, repeat collapses, or raw read coverage. Unassembled reads can also be mapped onto references. The cross-platform tool is free, putting large multi-genome comparisons within reach of any lab.
europmc-pmc3167373:
Pedro Valdes-Sosa, Alard Roebroeck, Jean Daunizeau, and Karl Friston closed a journal debate series on mapping directed influence between brain areas in a 2011 paper in NeuroImage. Simple correlations show areas active together, but claims about which area drives which need models of cause. The authors argue such claims stand or fall on models grounded in brain biophysics.

They compare the main approaches, including their own dynamic causal modelling and a rival based on prediction timing, and connect both to older statistical ideas about influence and dependency networks. Models, they insist, must include realistic observation and state equations, prior knowledge about parameters, and checks that parameters can actually be identified from data. The paper maps promising fixes for the field's known challenges.
europmc-pmc3242773:
Gretchen Hofmann and a large team compared natural swings in ocean acidity across ecosystems, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Predicting how ocean acidification will affect sea life suffers from a basic gap: few measurements describe the acidity conditions organisms actually live in. The team deployed autonomous sensors that recorded pH continuously in places from polar waters to coral reefs.

Month-long records varied enormously by site. Some places were nearly steady, while others swung through more than a full pH unit, with daily, tidal, and irregular rhythms of different strengths. Many resident organisms already endure acidity extremes not expected on average until the next century. The authors say knowing each habitat's exposure history should sharpen laboratory experiments and help identify refuges and vulnerable areas as the ocean changes.
europmc-pmc3260173:
Ronny Herzog and colleagues introduced LipidXplorer, open-source software for lipidomics, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Lipidomics aims to inventory the fats in a sample, and shotgun mass spectrometry produces huge datasets toward that end. LipidXplorer reads those spectra to describe complex lipid mixtures and measure their amounts.

The software works with spectra from any brand of tandem mass spectrometer. It identifies and measures molecular species from any ionizable lipid class by reasoning from known or assumed fragmentation pathways, without depending on libraries of reference spectra. It supports routines from high-throughput screening for diagnostic markers to precise absolute measurement of scarce species. The paper points users to a wiki carrying full documentation, a tutorial, interpretation scripts, a question archive, and a forum.
europmc-pmc3285573:
Purvesh Khatri, Marina Sirota, and Atul Butte reviewed the first decade of pathway analysis in this 2012 paper in PLoS Computational Biology. Faced with long lists of changed genes, researchers turned to pathway analysis, which interprets results through known biological routes, reducing complexity and adding explanatory power. It became the method of first resort, and the authors trace how it evolved.

They divide knowledge-base-driven methods into three generations, each fixing limitations of the one before, and explain which limits remain specific to each. Annotation problems, gaps and errors in the pathway knowledge bases themselves, now look like the binding constraint, alongside methodological challenges the next generation must meet. Their agenda aims at methods that exploit modern genomics and proteomics for sharper, more relevant results.
europmc-pmc3323073:
Van den Hoogen and colleagues sorted out the varieties of a newly recognized respiratory virus, in a 2004 study. Human metapneumovirus, found only a few years earlier, causes cold like illness and more serious lung infections, especially in young children. Early gene readings hinted it came in several lineages, as its close relatives do, but whether those lineages behaved as distinct types for the immune system was unknown.

The team compared gene sequences from many virus samples and tested how well antibodies against one lineage neutralized another. Two clear serotypes emerged, meaning immunity to one does not fully cover the other. Each serotype split further into two genetic lineages, though those inner splits mattered little for antibody recognition. The sorting helps explain repeat infections and guides vaccine thinking.
europmc-pmc3346773:
Halldorsson and colleagues followed Danish children from before birth to age twenty to test whether a persistent chemical affects weight, reporting in 2012. The chemical, PFOA, is used in many products and shows up in people worldwide. In mice, low doses before birth made female offspring heavier after puberty. The team checked humans next, using blood samples from six hundred sixty five pregnant women recruited in the late nineteen eighties.

Daughters of mothers with the highest chemical levels were about three times as likely to be overweight at twenty as daughters of the lowest group, with larger waists to match. Their blood also showed higher insulin and appetite hormone levels and lower levels of a protective hormone. Sons showed weaker, less certain hints of the same pattern. Related chemicals showed no independent link. The authors say the human results line up with the animal warning.
europmc-pmc3348673:
Booth and colleagues described the building of an international register where systematic reviews are logged before they are done, in a 2012 article. Systematic reviews pool evidence on treatments, but teams often unknowingly duplicate each other, and finished reviews can quietly shift methods to suit results. Registering the plan in advance, as clinical trials already do, promises to cut both problems.

The register, called PROSPERO, was developed at the University of York with an international advisory group and public consultation. Registration is free, records are public and searchable, and changes to the plan are kept in an audit trail. Reviews qualify if they address health outcomes and have not yet finished gathering data. By late 2011 the register held two hundred reviews from twenty six countries. The authors lay out the required information and the checks each submission passes through.
europmc-pmc3353173:
Bennette and Vickers argued against a habit deeply embedded in epidemiology: chopping continuous measurements into groups such as thirds, quarters, or fifths before analysis. The practice feels intuitive, letting researchers contrast low against high, but the authors contend it distorts the evidence it is meant to clarify.

Categorising throws away information, hides the true shape of dose–response relationships, and can manufacture apparent thresholds that vanish under better analysis. The authors describe alternatives, including keeping variables continuous and modelling non-linear relationships directly, and they examine why the field has been slow to adopt them. Their summary verdict is that quantile groups are usually inadequate for the job.
europmc-pmc3381573:
Amarasinghe and co-authors reviewed dengue in Africa in 2011, where the disease's true scale was unknown. Reported cases had climbed worldwide, yet Africa reported few. The team gathered five decades of reports, from 1960 to 2010, plus antibody surveys and traveler cases.

Twenty-two African countries had reported local cases or outbreaks, and twelve more appeared only through infected travelers. Antibody findings suggested the virus circulates widely, so low case counts likely reflect missed diagnosis, weak testing, and other fevers crowding it out. Rival explanations include cross-protection from related viruses and less efficient local mosquitoes. Population studies of fever, they urge, are needed to size the problem.
europmc-pmc3413573:
Tandon and co-authors studied over seven hundred children in 2012 to see how home surroundings shape activity, sitting time, and screen time, and whether family income changes the picture. Children in poorer homes are more likely to be overweight. Parents reported on the home, while motion sensors measured the children's activity directly.

Lower-income children had far more media gear in their bedrooms but less portable play equipment such as bikes and jump ropes. Their parents also set tighter rules on active play, yet watched screens together with them more often. Total active time did not differ by income, but daily screen time did, running higher in poorer homes. Bedroom media fed that gap, marking a clear target for change.
europmc-pmc3419673:
Pinto and Raskin tested in 2012 how the copying step behind DNA-based community surveys distorts the picture of bacterial and archaeal life. Sequencing a marker gene has become the standard way to census microbes, and labs had polished away sequencing errors. The bias introduced when many templates are copied together had drawn far less attention.

Building fake communities with known members in known proportions, the team separated the effects of sequencing depth, copying artifacts, and copying bias. Deeper sequencing sharpened comparisons between samples despite extra artifacts. Junk types from sequencing errors warped simple headcounts but barely touched structure-aware measures. The largest error source was the copying bias itself, which skews each type's apparent share.
europmc-pmc3438173:
Duprez and the SMART study group asked in 2012 whether three blood markers forecast heart and vessel disease in people living with HIV. The parent trial compared taking antiretroviral therapy continuously versus in breaks. Blood samples from over five thousand participants let the team test inflammation and clotting markers against later cardiovascular events.

Over a median follow-up of about twenty-nine months, two hundred fifty-two participants had a cardiovascular event. Those in the top quarter for the inflammation marker IL-6 faced several times the risk of the bottom quarter, and two other markers roughly doubled it. The links held in both treatment strategies and after accounting for standard risk factors. Adding all three markers measurably sharpened risk prediction.

europmc-pmc6523673: Exosomes are nano-sized bubbles that cells release to trade proteins, RNA, and lipids with neighbors - a postal service between cells. frus-1861-d173:
Carl Schurz sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 August 1861. It is document 173 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By August, word of the Union defeat had reached Spain. Schurz had to face a court that now doubted Union strength. His report shows a young envoy learning to hold his ground with words when the news ran against him. A young envoy's growth, traced week by week, is one of this file's quiet pleasures. Growth of that kind, seen in real time, is a rare gift of a full record.
frus-1861-d273:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Mr. Brown, dated 17 July 1861. Congress received it as Document 273 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d73:
Frederick W. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 27 August 1861. The younger Seward served as Assistant Secretary of State under his father. The letter is document 73 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

When the Secretary was away or pressed, his son kept the London line open. The note shows the office working as a family shop in a crisis. It also spared Adams any gap in direction from Washington at a tense time. Frederick Seward later wrote the great memoir of his father's years in office. The son's hand kept the father's line unbroken through a crowded autumn.
frus-1862-d173:
On 17 October 1862 Charles Francis Adams sent a report from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 173 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams had held the London post since the spring of 1861.

The son and grandson of presidents, Adams kept a cool style in his official mail even when stakes were high. His reports mixed meeting notes with shrewd reads of British politics. A letter from this date belongs to the weeks when the British cabinet was quietly deciding against stepping into the war. That was the outcome Adams most wanted. The legation's clerks copied each dispatch into bound letter books before the mail sailed.
frus-1862-d273:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 5 May 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 273 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The same day, far away, Mexico's army won at Puebla.

The coincidence of dates is a reminder of how slowly news moved. Seward wrote in ignorance of the battle that would stall France in Mexico for a year. His letter belongs to the Washington-Paris routine of orders and arguments about the war. Read in sequence, such letters show policy being made on partial knowledge, then corrected by the next mail.
frus-1862-d373:
On 13 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to Viscount Treilhard, in a letter printed as Document 373 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The reply followed Treilhard's letter by a single day.

Prompt written answers were the State Department's way of keeping small matters small. In August 1862 that discipline mattered, because any dispute with a foreign representative could feed the larger debate over intervention. The Seward-Treilhard exchange, preserved in quick alternation, shows the method applied steadily through a tense month. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d473:
James E. Harvey, the American minister in Lisbon, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 July 1862. It is Document 473 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Portuguese file.

Portugal was a small power with Atlantic islands and ports that mattered to wartime shipping, and its neutrality had to be exact. Harvey, a Pennsylvania editor turned diplomat, held the Lisbon post through the war. Seward's orders to such outposts dealt in the practical law of neutrality: what belligerent ships could take on, and how long they could stay. The dispatch begins the Portuguese correspondence, a minor file with real stakes for the blockade at sea.
frus-1862-d573:
James Watson Webb in Brazil received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 December 1861. It is Document 573 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

December 1861 was the month of the Trent crisis. Seward's orders to distant posts had to assume their readers knew little of the latest turn. Brazil, an empire with Atlantic ports on the routes to the Pacific, had neutrality duties to define toward belligerent cruisers and prizes. Webb needed Washington's rules in writing. The instruction shows the Department reaching to the far end of its network. A letter there might take two months to arrive. It still had to govern conduct when it did.
frus-1862-d673:
Anson Burlingame wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 March 1862. He was the American minister to China, writing in the second year of the Civil War. The letter is document 673 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

By the spring of 1862 Burlingame had found his feet in the post. His mail reported on the treaty ports, the Qing court's straits, and the acts of the other foreign powers in China. Letters like this one were the State Department's eyes in East Asia. Kept in the printed volume, they still show how much of American policy rested on one envoy's word.
frus-1862-d73:
Washington's orders went out to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London in a dispatch dated 29 May 1862. Congress received it as Document 73 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d173:
On 25 April 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 173 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to Seward's first sheet of the day held the next point in line for the British brief. Pairs like this one let Adams take each matter to the foreign office in its own words and time. This letter closes the 25 April pair. It is a near-end piece of the run in this slice of the volume, which closes days later with an Adams report.
frus-1863p1-d273:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 27 August 1863. It is document 273 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d373:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 28 January 1863. It appears as document 373 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d473:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 22 April 1863 letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d573:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 18 June 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d673:
A dispatch dated 23 November 1863 went from Secretary William H. Seward to the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d73:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 73 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams wrote on the eve of a set piece in British public life: the opening of Parliament, set for the next day. His mail that week watched for what the Queen's speech and the houses would say of the war. Reports like this one told Washington how the land lay at the top of British power. It is a short step in the file from this letter to the famous one that follows it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d173: A draft message from the President to Secretary Hull, dated October 30, 1943, is preserved as Document 173 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Drafts earn their place in the official record because they show what was considered, and sometimes changed, before sending. Whether this one went as written, the record here does not say. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the Moscow closing papers, in the section the editors built for them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d273: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers two separate calls on President Roosevelt at Cairo during the forenoon of 26 November 1943. One call was by Admiral Mountbatten, and one by Madame Chiang Kai-shek. The calls are recorded in the President's Log, but no memoranda of either conversation appear to have been made. Elliott Roosevelt's account mentions both calls in passing. The editors presume the main subject of each was Chiang Kai-shek's attitude toward the proposed operations in the China-Burma-India theater.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d373:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the plenary session at Tehran on 30 November 1943 at four in the afternoon, the session at which the Overlord decision was announced to Stalin. Roosevelt opens by expressing his happiness at the decision reached that morning by the British and American staffs.

Brooke reports the agreement: Overlord will be launched during May 1944, with a supporting operation in southern France on as large a scale as landing craft allow. Stalin answers with the pledge he had already given the two leaders privately. Simultaneously with Overlord, the Red Army will launch large offensives at several points to pin German forces down and stop any transfer of troops westward. Roosevelt adds that the Overlord commander will be named within three or four days, and the Western staffs will return to Cairo the next day to work out the details.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d473:
Another message from President Roosevelt went to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 3, 1943, the day before the Second Cairo Conference opened. Roosevelt had finished at Tehran and was preparing to meet Churchill, and Turkey's President İnönü, at Cairo. The State Department kept the message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Two presidential cables to Hull in a single day suggest how much unfinished business followed Roosevelt out of Tehran. Hull, in Washington, was the fixed point of American diplomacy while the President traveled. For the reader, this second message underlines the working partnership between the two men at a peak moment of the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d573:
Patrick J. Hurley, now ambassador to China, wrote to Secretary of State James F. Byrnes on August 11, 1945. Hurley had gone from the President's personal representative in Iran to the hardest embassy in Asia. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

August 11 fell in the war's last days: atomic bombs had fallen, the Soviet Union had entered the Pacific war, and Japan's surrender was days away. Hurley's China was sliding toward civil war even as the world war ended. For readers, his report connects the volume's long China thread, opened at Cairo in 1943, to the moment everything changed in Asia.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d73: Hull wrote to Roosevelt on October 29, 1943, on the last day of the Moscow Conference. His letter is Document 73 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The secretary's Moscow reports were the high point of his long tenure, and this one belongs to the conference's close. The record supplies the date and the two men and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series for its own telling.
frus-1944-quebec-d173:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff opened their Quebec meetings at noon on September 12, 1944, with Sir Alan Brooke in the chair at Admiral Leahy's invitation. Early business was procedural: personnel shipping after Germany's defeat would be studied, and the conference program was approved. The chiefs then took up Eisenhower's appreciation, Scaf 78.

Brooke argued Eisenhower had understressed two points: opening Antwerp and Rotterdam, and a strong attack on the northern flank. He proposed an airborne operation to seize the Schelde islands guarding Antwerp. Marshall countered that German forces massed there, on coverless ground, made bombing more profitable than airborne troops. A draft reply approving Eisenhower's proposals, with the northern emphasis added, was presented for discussion.
frus-1944-quebec-d273:
Redeployment after the European war is the subject of C.C.S. 679, dated September 14, 1944. The United States Chiefs judged the whole problem, including repatriation, too large for the conference to settle. It needed combined study to assure the optimum use of personnel and cargo shipping, and to get forces against Japan to their theater at the earliest date.

They recommended the Combined Administrative Committee study and report on the problem, working with the transportation committee, the shipping authorities, and the staff planners. Questions needing earlier decision would go to the Combined Chiefs. The paper was approved the next day with Brooke's amendment adding the Combined Shipping Authorities to the list of collaborators.
frus-1944-quebec-d73:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on August 28, 1944. His letter sits among the papers gathered for the Quebec Conference. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. Hull led the department that handled the alliance's daily diplomacy.

Letters from Hull to Roosevelt carried the department's view to the top. Two weeks later, the President would meet Churchill in Quebec City. The conference faced Germany's coming defeat and the Pacific war. For readers, the letter shows the State Department stating its position in writing. It did so before the leaders settled questions in person.
frus-1945-50-intel-d173:
A memorandum dated 30 October 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy) and the Assistant Secretary of State for Administration (Russell). The reader was Secretary of State Byrnes. It is document 173 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d273:
On 11 May 1948, Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter sent a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). It stands as document 273 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d373:
The Director of the Executive Secretariat (Humelsine) addressed a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Webb) on 8 March 1949. Readers meet it as document 373 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d73:
The Department of State sent a telegram to the American embassy in London on 12 September 1945. Department telegrams speak in the secretary's name to posts abroad. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A telegram to London in September 1945 belongs to the weeks when embassies were being told how the wartime secret work would change. London was the greatest of the wartime intelligence stations, so word sent there mattered. Readers can place this telegram at the head of the volume's file on the State Department's own intelligence service. It shows the department addressing its posts as it prepared to take in the analysts the president's order was about to give it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d173:
One item survives in this excerpt from the Secretary of State's daily briefing for the President, dated 1 December 1944. The memorandum, “Special Information for the President,” gathers the notable foreign developments of the past few days. The excerpt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The item concerns Yugoslavia and the agreement lately drawn up between Marshal Tito and Premier Subasic, head of the exile government. Brigadier MacLean has told Ambassador Kirk the expected British course. Churchill will press King Peter to accept the agreement. Once it takes effect, Britain will send an ambassador to Belgrade. The short note marks how far Tito's partisans had come toward open allied backing.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d273:
George Kennan cabled from Moscow on 27 November 1944 about American and Soviet prisoners. His report, number 4526, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Note the year: the catalog's earlier summary misdated this cable to 1945. Kennan was chargé in Moscow in Harriman's absence.

At General Deane's request, Kennan had written to Molotov on 6 November about two-way arrangements for prisoners of war. Soviet armies had already overrun one camp known to have held Americans, and were closing on another near Budapest. Molotov's answer of 25 November is quoted in paraphrase. Moscow's first concern is help and homecoming for Soviet prisoners and for citizens deported by the Germans, now freed in the west. In principle, the Soviet government accepts Harriman's proposals of August.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d373:
Bohlen's minutes of February 7, 1945, list four subjects before the plenary: dismemberment, Poland, the world security body, and a French zone. Roosevelt began with Poland. He stressed that he cared less about tracing frontier lines than about the Polish government. He attached no importance, he said, to the continuity or legality of any Polish government.

In truth, he added, there had been no real Polish government for some years. Before going further, he called on Molotov to report the foreign ministers' meeting. The minutes show the President clearing the agenda with a blunt judgment that shocked some Poles for decades after.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d473:
Denmark opens this digest cable from Acting Secretary Grew to Stettinius, written February 2, 1945, while the Secretary was traveling. Washington's lukewarm stand on a three-power statement recognizing the Danes as allies, plus likely Soviet refusal, might send the matter to the Big Three. Meanwhile America was sending its own secret message to the Danish Freedom Council.

The message praised the Danish resistance movement's contributions to the common cause. Further items follow, including a report from Kennan in Moscow: the British chargé had expressed hope to Molotov about arrangements under study. Grew's daily excerpts kept the traveling Secretary briefed on a dozen fronts at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d73:
Six questions left unsettled at Dumbarton Oaks are listed for President Roosevelt in this 15 November 1944 paper. Acting Secretary Stettinius sent it ahead of a meeting at the White House. The memo is one of a set prepared that day and printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The six items start with voting in the Security Council and who the first members would be. They go on to the seat of the new body and to trusteeship plans. The court statute and the ending of the League of Nations complete the list. Advice is attached on the first four. On the court, legal experts would draft the statute before the founding talks opened.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d173:
The British Embassy passed on a Foreign Office proposal about population transfers in an extract dated June 28, 1945. The extract is document 173 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full message from London, dated June 22, appears later in the volume.

London thinks a full exchange of views with the Americans on transfers of ethnic minority groups in Europe would be valuable. Such talks might lead on to a three-power discussion at the coming Big Three meeting. The embassy is told to sound the State Department on the proposal and report its reaction. Behind the dry wording stood one of the era's harshest subjects: the planned uprooting of millions of ethnic Germans and others from their homes in Eastern Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d273:
A briefing paper argued that Austria should pay no reparations, in a paper dated July 4, 1945. The paper is document 273 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It proposes that the three powers agree on the question before the conference.

The United States opposes exacting reparations from Austria despite her part in the German war effort, the paper says. Such a demand would be economically unrealistic and politically dangerous in Central Europe. It would clash with the Moscow Declaration, which implied creating conditions favorable to Austrian independence. It might turn Austrians against the West and drive Austria back into Germany's arms. Austria's own capacity is doubted. Her World War I obligations were mostly cancelled by 1923. And the country, short of food, will need relief and aid. That aid would make America in effect pay Austria's reparations for her.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d373:
France's lesser request on reparations reached Harriman in a Washington cable of July 11, 1945. The French Embassy's aide-mémoire of June 25 accepted, for now, that France had no seat on the Reparations Commission in Moscow. It asked instead that the chief of the American delegation be told to keep the French ambassador in Moscow closely informed of the Commission's work.

Paris had sent like notes to the British and Soviet governments. Grew instructs Harriman to sound out the proper authorities informally and report their reaction. If asked, he may say Washington is most sympathetic to the French. The cable shows France settling, for the moment, for news instead of a vote.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d473:
Keeping American forces in Italy is urged in a briefing book memorandum for the President dated July 2, 1945. An attached telegram from Caserta indicates what Churchill will do. He will take up at the meeting, it says, the desirability of leaving substantial American forces in Italy. He will raise the same point for Europe as a whole, until major problems are settled. Military needs of redeployment must come first, the memo concedes.

Politically, though, it is most important to keep the Allied character of the forces remaining in Europe, through at least token American participation. Total withdrawal, it warns, would inevitably be read as a sign that the United States is relinquishing direct influence on future settlements. Even limited American numbers inspire confidence.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d573:
Ambassador Kirk reported a firm word from Field Marshal Alexander in an extract sent from Caserta late on June 26, 1945. It is document 573 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The subject was the Yugoslav reservation on article 3 of the Belgrade agreement.

Kirk says he asked Alexander for his view, and Alexander agreed the Allies must stand fast on that point. Alexander added a direct pledge in his own words. The Belgrade agreement, he said, gives him final say on civil rule in the Allied area. He would see to it that the reading of the deal matched the Allied view. The short extract is meant to calm fears in Washington that the commander might give ground.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d673:
Ambassador Winant passed on a British official's doubts about reopening the Tangier talks on July 11, 1945. His secret wire is document 673 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The official was Hoyer Millar of the Foreign Office.

Millar said he did not see how the talks could open unless the Russians were brought in. Yet bringing them in raised at once a harder question. How far would Russia share in any plan for the zone's future administration? That point had to be decided first, and it could not be decided on the minute. Millar's best course was to take the matter up at the Big Three meeting. No start on Tangier should be thought of until after that meeting ended.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d73:
Ambassador John Winant reported from London on June 16, 1945, on the fuss over Attlee's role at the coming conference. His telegram to the Acting Secretary of State is document 73 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. It lays out, step by step, how Churchill's invitation to the Labour leader drew a sharp public statement from party chairman Harold Laski.

Laski had insisted Attlee could attend only as an observer, since Labour could not be bound by deals it had not debated. Winant then quotes the letters Churchill and Attlee exchanged to settle the matter: the government would bear responsibility for decisions, but Attlee would come as a friend and adviser. The report shows election politics shaping Britain's team before Potsdam even opened.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1073: Soviet delegates presented this proposal on liberated Europe to the foreign ministers on July 20, 1945. Only a short extract is printed here. Its other portions appear as separate documents elsewhere in the volume, including the fuller Greece text printed just before this one. The extract charges that the present Greek government is breaking the peace with its neighbors. It threatens Albania and Bulgaria with military action, the paper says. All these circumstances, the Soviets conclude, create the need for urgent measures to end such a situation in Greece.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1173:
Generalissimo Stalin wrote to President Truman on 29 July 1945, nine days after Truman's note to him. The Soviet leader's reply kept the top-level exchange alive as the summit entered its last week. Direct word between these two men was rare and heavy.

Each side read such a message for tone as much as content. A phrase could signal room to deal or a line held firm. This note is Moscow's voice at the very top, set down while the final terms were still fluid. It belongs to the small set of leader-to-leader papers that framed everything the staffs did below.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1273:
The President wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 1 August 1945. The cable went out on the summit's last full day. Truman's word to his China envoy joined the German endgame to the Asian war in one channel.

Hurley's mission needed the president's backing at that hour. China's government was weakening, Japan's defeat was near, and the shape of Asia hung on choices being made in both capitals. A note from the top set the envoy's line for the weeks ahead. This message shows the president closing his Potsdam work with an eye already on the next crisis.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1373:
The United States delegation tabled a formal proposal at Potsdam on 25 July 1945. Unlike a working paper, a proposal was meant for the other delegations to read and answer. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

American proposals show what Washington chose to ask for in the open, in words the British and Soviets could accept or refuse. This one came late in the conference, when the end of the talks was in sight and each side pressed its last claims. Readers can weigh it against the final protocol to see the result of that press. The paper is a fixed point in the bargaining, useful for anyone mapping how the summit closed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-73:
A United States delegation memorandum sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 23, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Four heads of business are reported from the Monday morning session.

Reparations discussion was postponed so the economic subcommittee could study two new Soviet papers. On German economic principles, the Soviet side objected to paragraph 18 of the draft. Each zone, it argued, should as far as practicable draw supplies from the German areas it had drawn on before the war. That question went up to the heads of government. So did a new Soviet paragraph 19, on the priority between reparations and exports to pay for imports. On the Council of Foreign Ministers, by contrast, the revised text won final approval. Trusteeship business was settled by referral: the Italian colonies would be discussed by the new council.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d773:
Field Marshal Alexander, Supreme Allied Commander in the Mediterranean, wrote to the Combined Chiefs of Staff on July 18, 1945. Document 773 brings a theater commander's voice into the Potsdam record. Alexander's command covered Italy and the middle sea. His message reached the joint chiefs as the conference opened.

A theater commander's letter carries the weight of forces in place. Alexander spoke for armies and fleets still in the field. Readers see how field needs reached the summit's military advisers. The document links Potsdam to the war's remaining fronts. Decisions in Germany echoed in commands hundreds of miles away, and this letter is one echo in writing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d873: Soviet delegates offered this revised draft of Article 19 at Potsdam on July 23, 1945, apparently their second draft that day. It repeats that Germans must be left enough to subsist after reparations. It also provides means to pay for imports approved by the Control Council. The change is priority: exports sold to pay for those imports would rank ahead of reparations and home consumption.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d973:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov on August 1, 1945, about art objects held in the American zone. An identical letter went to Britain's Ernest Bevin the same day. Byrnes sorts the works into three classes, from loot seized from public and private owners to property that was truly German.

Orders have gone out, he reports, to return the first two classes to their countries of origin as fast as arrangements allow. For the second class, receipts will record what the Germans claim to have paid. The third class will be shipped to the United States for care and safekeeping. Its final fate awaits future decisions.
frus-1961-63v11-d173: A 1961-1963 FRUS editorial note from the Missile Crisis volume. The context. This note provides that background. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
gao-gaoreports-b-295973: AHNTECH took its May 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298573: Joint Systems took its October 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299873: General Dynamics cried foul over a 2007 tech award, and GAO's ruling is the final whistle. The defense-tech giant said the agency's pick was wrong; the call tests the protest against bid law. When industry titans clash over federal IT fortunes, this is the scorecard — public, reasoned, and binding.
gao-gaoreports-b-308773: The Capitol Police's operating rate got a fiscal ruling in this January 2007 GAO call, which sets the current rate under the continuing resolution. The decision reads the money law. The ruling keeps the guardians of the Capitol funded and legal. The watch had to be paid for.
gao-gaoreports-b-311273: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Professional Performance Development Group, Inc. Decided June 2, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-400173: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Colliers International. The July 3, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-273: The E-10A spy plane's buying plan needed a rethink in 2005, and GAO's report says strategy changes were required before development. The review pumps the brakes. The flying radar deserved the honest plan. The changes had to come first. The flying radar deserved the honest plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-373: Woody biomass promotion efforts got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says federal agencies were engaged, though more could be done. The findings take the measure. The report shows the wood fuel was studied. The efforts had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-673: Courthouse construction costs needed better oversight in 2005, and GAO's report says project cost and size information would help. The findings demand the data. The report warns that the justice palaces deserved honest budgets. The information had to help. The justice palaces deserved honest budgets.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-773: TRICARE's new contracts faced implementation issues in 2005, and GAO's report says the rollout and regional structure needed work. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the troops' health plans deserved smooth delivery. The issues had to be resolved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-873: Medicare contracting reform had gaps in 2005, and GAO's report says CMS's plan was incomplete and anticipated savings were uncertain. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the seniors' program deserved honest math. The gaps had to be closed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-273: The internet tax moratorium's revenue impacts varied in 2006, and GAO's report says the effects would differ by state. The findings do the math. The report warns that the online tax holiday had uneven costs. The impacts had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-473: Missile defense planning needed better cost visibility in 2006, and GAO's report says actions were required to improve operational planning and cost tracking. The findings demand the transparency. The report warns that the shield's billions deserved honest accounting. The costs had to be visible.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-73: D.C. charter school closures needed better handling in 2005, and GAO's report says strengthening monitoring and process could ease the transitions. The findings demand the care. The report warns that the students deserved orderly closures. The monitoring had to be stronger.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-973: FAA funding options got a GAO look in 2006, and the report offers observations on potential funding paths. The findings lay out the choices. The report asks who should pay for the skies of tomorrow. The options had to be weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-273: Open-ended Pentagon deals were bleeding in 2007 — GAO's report says time-and-materials contracts needed better insight and controls. The findings target the blank-check corner of defense buying. The report's fix: watch the clock, cap the meter, and stop paying by the shrug.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-373: Bad nursing homes needed better targeting in 2007 — GAO's report says federal helpers should aim aid where the care was worst. The findings demand smarter triage of the quality-improvement money. The report's cause: the frailest patients deserve the sharpest oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-573: Food stamp sign-ups were stuck in the paper age in 2007 — GAO's report says easier application methods could use a real boost. The findings press for modernization of the process. The report's logic is humane: hunger should not require a fax machine.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-673: Tax season 2007 was a stress test for the IRS — GAO's report gives the interim filing-season results and grades the 2008 budget ask. The findings link performance to funding in detail. The report's question: did the agency earn the dollars it wanted?
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-73: This 2007 GAO report presses the nuclear weapons labs to prove their safety push is real. The labs that build and tend the nation's bombs had launched fix-up drives for both bomb work and staff safety — but GAO found no hard proof the drives worked. The report demands facts, not pledges, from the most dangerous workshops in the land.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-773: The Government Accountability Office dug into human Capital: DOD Needs to Improve Implementation of and Address Employee Concerns about Its National Security Personnel System in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
On the morning of September 11, 1973, CIA officers briefed President Richard Nixon on the military coup then unfolding in Chile. That top secret President's Daily Brief stayed classified for fifty years. The National Security Archive posted it in August 2023, in a briefing book edited by Peter Kornbluh.

The brief told Nixon that Chilean officers were determined to restore political and economic order. It also warned that they might lack a coordinated plan to use the wide civilian opposition. Reading it shows exactly what the president was told, in the CIA's own words, on the day Salvador Allende fell.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_henry-ki: Kissinger Told Soviet Envoy during 1973 Arab-Israeli War: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
hodge-systematic-theology-vol3-1873:
Volume three of Hodge's Systematic Theology, in this 1874 edition, crowns the Princeton system with eschatology, the doctrine of the last things. Hodge had covered God, man, and Christ's work in the earlier volumes. The aged professor writes here with a lifetime of teaching behind him.

He treats death, the soul's state after death, the return of Christ, resurrection, and the final judgment in ordered sequence. His method stays the same: gather the Bible's statements, sort them, and answer rival views with calm reason. Princeton's students received the volume as the completion of the great Calvinist system in America.
human-science-or-phrenology-its-principl: Human Science, or Phrenology, 1873. The human science. This book preserves that work. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Kept for study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucas-louis-art:
Louis Arthur Lucas (1851–1876) was an African explorer born in London, profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind. After travel in the United States and Egypt, he organized an expedition to explore the Kongo. He reached Khartum in January 1876 and died at sea that November, aged twenty-five.

At the Albert Nyanza, Lucas navigated the lake’s northern part in the first steamboat ever launched on it, working alongside Colonel Gordon. He also compiled a vocabulary of Bisharin words, later published by the Anthropological Institute. Against Gordon’s advice he then tried to cross Africa, fell sick and paralyzed, and died on a steamboat between Suakim and Suez. He was buried at Jiddah. The entry tells a short, stark story of ambition, illness, and an early death in the age of exploration.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-lady-kat:
Lady Katie Magnus, an English author and communal worker, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Portsmouth on May 2, 1844, she was the daughter of E. Emanuel. She married Sir Philip Magnus. Her public life joined writing to service in London's Jewish community.

The article lists her books and her posts together. She served on committees of the Berkeley Street Synagogue and backed the Jews' Deaf and Dumb Home. As treasurer of the Jewish Girls' Club she worked for young women. Her writing began with Bible stories and holiday tales for children. Two sketches of Jewish history followed, one reaching three editions. Her Outlines of Jewish History was reprinted in America by the Jewish Publication Society. A second edition of her Jewish Portraits appeared in 1901. The entry shows a writer who taught her community its own past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manoah-b-jacob-:
Manoah ben Jacob, a French Talmudist of Lunel, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He lived in the second half of the thirteenth century. After a short stay at Narbonne, where he studied with Meir ben Simon and Reuben ben Hayyim, he returned to Lunel. He often cites rulings in his father's name.

The article centers on his one known work. Like several of his contemporaries, Manoah studied Maimonides closely. He wrote a commentary on the Yad ha-Hazakah, Maimonides' great code. Later writers quote it under the title Sefer ha-Manoah, or Sefer ha-Menuhah. It was printed at Constantinople in 1518, centuries after his death. The entry rests on the standard name-books of Azulai and Conforte and on Gross's Gallia Judaica. It preserves a Provençal scholar who helped France read Maimonides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matah-mehasya-m:
Matah Mehasya was a town in southern Babylonia. Solomon Schechter and Wilhelm Bacher untangle it from its neighbor Sura in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Sherira Gaon used the two names as if they were one place, since both named the seat of the great academy founded by Rab. The article argues from Talmudic passages, including one that contrasts the two towns' ways of speaking, that they were really separate towns. The school likely sat between them.

Most of the entry belongs to the age of Ashi, in the later fourth century. The academy then sat at Matah Mehasya, and Ashi himself lived there. He protected the town by forbidding houses taller than its synagogue. He also complained that its non-Jewish residents stayed hard-hearted. They saw the splendor of the Torah at the great Kallah gatherings twice a year, and still stayed unmoved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-isaac-:
Meir ben Isaac of Orleans, a French liturgical poet of the end of the eleventh century, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn. He and his son Eleazar are quoted in a commentary on Chronicles that was wrongly ascribed to Rashi, and the entry floats the possibility that Meir himself wrote biblical commentary. His certain work is poetry for the synagogue, signed in acrostics that spell the name Eleazar, apparently for his son.

Two poems are singled out. "Torah ha-Temimah" is a supplication woven with Aramaic and Talmudic phrases, expressing his horror of apostasy. "Almanot Hayyot" is a penitential prayer for the Day of Atonement, which Zunz translated into German. A third penitential poem, on a Crusader massacre of three thousand Jews, carries the same signature, but Zunz judged it a work of a century later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-nasi-fra:
Francisco Mendes-Nasi, head of a great Lisbon banking house and husband of the famous Gracia, is noticed in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling. One of the richest and most respected Portuguese Marranos, he died about 1536; his bank, with branches in Flanders and France, advanced money to Charles V and other rulers. His brother Diogo, who ran the Antwerp branch, succeeded him as the richest Portuguese Marrano, and with his sister-in-law spent great sums trying to keep the Inquisition out of Portugal.

The entry ends with a kinsman's repartee. Hector Mendes, a very rich man, was asked by the King of Portugal what he called his own, and answered: "The alms which I have given." The notice is short, but it sketches the banking dynasty into which Beatrice de Luna married and which she would soon lead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mezey-franz-107:
Franz Mezey, born at Acsad in Hungary on February 5, 1860, was a jurist who became the organizational backbone of Hungarian Jewry. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Destined by his parents for the rabbinate, he mastered Hebrew, then chose law and was admitted to the Budapest bar.

In 1883 Mezey was a mainstay of the defense in the Tisza-Eszlár blood accusation case, acting for Hungary's Jews. As secretary of the national Jewish chancery for twenty years, he drove progress in religious and school affairs. He co-founded the Hungarian Jewish Literary Society, edited journals with Bacher and Blau, and ran Budapest's burial society, grown to 10,000 members under him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mires-jules-isa:
