Muscles release these signals, called myokines, which help steer metabolism and growth. Their 2026 study compares forty-three children low in vitamin D with thirty-nine healthy matched children at one center, measuring three myokines plus bone-related blood markers.

Children low in vitamin D had far lower levels of all three myokines. Within the healthy group, higher vitamin D went with higher levels of two of them. Careful modeling kept vitamin D tied to all three signals after accounting for age, sex, and body size. The findings hint that vitamin D and muscle signaling rise and fall together in growing bodies.
plos-pone-0348973:
Julian Schach, Federica Valerio, and Anne Duplouy reconstructed the family tree of parasitic wasps that attack checkerspot butterflies, including two sets of species so similar they were long mistaken for one. Such cryptic species frustrate biodiversity research. Their 2026 study sequenced ten genes from wasps collected across Europe, Asia, and North America, covering twenty-two species in the genus.

The resulting tree was strongly supported and split into four major branches. Wasps attacking these butterflies appeared in three of the four, proving the group evolved the habit several times independently rather than inheriting it once. Each cryptic complex found its place in its own sub-branch, settling previously murky relationships. The authors offer the tree as a framework for studying how these wasps choose and switch hosts.
plos-pone-0349173:
RETRACTION NOTICE: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 notice withdrawing an earlier study claiming that leaf extracts from a tree killed brain tumor cells by harming their energy centers. Readers should not rely on the original findings. Questions after publication covered a figure, missing ethics details, and unavailable raw data.

Two panels in one figure partly overlapped, and the author said the figure had been put together wrongly and mislabeled. The team later produced an animal ethics approval and described how mice were monitored and euthanized. Even so, editors reviewing the underlying data found mismatches that deepened doubts about the results. The journal retracted the article because the evidence base could not be trusted.
plos-pone-0349373:
Mateo Vinueza Guarderas and colleagues mapped the genes of this white-spotted eagle ray from the Eastern Tropical Pacific, a species only recently recognized as distinct from its Atlantic relative. The split rested on unbalanced sampling, fifty Atlantic animals against five from the Pacific, so Pacific diversity was nearly unknown. Rays reproduce slowly and are caught in targeted and incidental fisheries, making them easy to overfish.

Mixing several genetic markers, the team assessed diversity, range, and how connected populations are across the region's varied coasts. Genetic structure decides whether the ray can be managed as one stock or must be protected region by region. Filling the Pacific gap also tests whether undescribed kinds still hide inside what looks like one species.
plos-pone-0349673:
Yun-Chen Tsai and co-authors reviewed a decade and a half of prostatic abscess cases at hospital in 2026, hunting for what predicts death. The uncommon infection, a pus pocket in the prostate, can kill when treatment lags.

Of more than eight hundred men with prostate infection, about one in eight had an abscess, and overall deaths ran near nine percent. Older age stood out as the steady death risk in adjusted analysis. Abscess size and other features instead predicted who received drainage or surgery. The split helps clinicians separate who is in danger from who needs a procedure.
plos-pone-0349773:
Learning to read starts with hearing sounds inside words. Maimoona Khalil and colleagues studied this skill in Urdu-speaking children. All the children had Down syndrome. They were aged four to twelve. The study ran at three centers in Lahore, Pakistan. It asked whether naming speed relates to sound awareness.

Children completed a timed naming task. They also picked out sounds at word starts and ends. A phone-based Urdu test delivered both tasks. Speed and accuracy showed no meaningful relationship. Starting sounds proved far easier than ending sounds. The two sound skills moved together moderately, though. The authors advise direct sound teaching. Faster naming practice alone will not lift accuracy.
plos-pone-0349873:
Milton Ali, Hervé Etienne, and co-authors screened one hundred sixty-five Ugandan robusta coffee genotypes for drought tolerance, hunting stock for a breeding program that lacks resistant varieties. Robusta supplies most of Uganda's coffee and supports millions of livelihoods, yet dry spells are worsening. Their 2026 screenhouse trial stressed wild, commercial, and breeder lines and measured water status, gas exchange, and leaf fluorescence before, during, and after drought.

Drought depressed every group, but twenty-four genotypes kept markedly better scores, holding their photosynthetic machinery steadier and their pre-dawn water status less negative under severe stress. Two fluorescence measures stood out as the most trustworthy tolerance markers. The authors offer both the winning genotypes and the quick leaf tests as a foundation for faster climate-ready coffee breeding in Uganda.
plos-pone-0350273:
Rebecca Murray, Cara E Staniforth, and Lucy H Eddy interviewed ten adults with developmental coordination disorder, a condition that makes movement and everyday tasks hard and affects roughly one in twenty people. Research on the condition focuses on children, leaving adult life largely undocumented. Their 2026 interviews covered health care, school memories, friendships, work, wellbeing, and relationships.

A single theme ran everywhere: other people simply do not know the condition exists. Participants described fighting for support in clinics, schools, and workplaces, and often feeling abandoned and unvalidated instead. Many said the condition reaches far beyond clumsiness into planning and organization. The authors call for far greater public awareness and for services that follow people across the whole lifespan, not just childhood.
plos-pone-0350573:
Kofi Effah and seven colleagues report Ghana's first nationally representative cervical screening drive. Their 2026 study covers the Rotary-backed 'Protect Your Pearl' initiative in early 2025. Fewer than one in twenty Ghanaian women had ever been screened, despite cervical cancer's heavy death toll. Trained graduates of a national training centre fanned out to twenty-nine facilities. All sixteen regions were reached. Each of over sixteen hundred women received two tests at once.

One test genotyped high-risk HPV from a swab. The other was a visual inspection of the cervix. About one woman in four carried high-risk HPV. Visual inspection flagged only four percent as positive. Unusual strains dominated: types 52, 58, and 51 led, while the famous 16 and 18 stayed rare. Eligible lesions were treated on the spot with heat ablation. HIV infection raised the odds of HPV sharply. The drive proves nationwide same-day screening and treatment is feasible.
plos-pone-0350673:
Fawaz Khaled Alarfaj tested machine and deep learning methods for sorting legal documents into case categories automatically. Courts and firms drown in complex legal text, and hand sorting is slow. Thousands of real legal files were turned into features ranging from word counts to modern sentence embeddings, then fed to many classifiers.

An ensemble of extremely randomised trees scored best at about eighty nine percent accuracy, beating deep models in this test. Pooling many varied trees curbed overfitting on tricky legal language. Reliable auto sorting can speed filing, search, and case triage, though high stakes legal calls still need human review of edge cases.
plos-pone-0351073:
Robin Dunbar revisits a famous claim about primate brain evolution in this 2026 paper. The brain lag idea says body size grew first, and brains caught up later using the energy saved. A well-known earlier analysis found no evidence for any lag. Dunbar re-runs the question with better statistics and updated data.

His reanalysis finds that the lag is real. But the story does not end as the original idea predicted. Brains did not settle back onto the expected body-size line. Instead, brain growth tracked larger social groups, used as a defence against predators. Real brain expansion also needed a fruit-rich diet to pay the energy bills. Dunbar argues that early humans followed this same path, starting from an ape-like baseline.
plos-pone-0351473:
M. Atif Qureshi and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One framework for judging whether explanations of medical machine learning models are actually any good. Clinicians increasingly receive reasons for a model's prediction, but studies measure explanation quality in inconsistent ways. The authors define six quality measures with explicit formulas and test five explanation methods on four public healthcare datasets.

One method reconstructed the model's scores exactly but produced complex explanations, while another gave simpler explanations that matched the model less faithfully and varied more between patients. Rule-based explanations were precise but covered few cases at strict settings. The authors release their code and a guide matching methods to measures, aiming to make explanation claims in high-stakes fields easier to check.
plos-pone-0351773:
Alexander Haake and colleagues compared two dog tumors at opposite ends of the danger scale. One is a benign gland tumor near the rear. The other is a highly malignant tumor of the anal sac gland. Both are common in pet dogs. The team read gene activity in real tumors from patients. They used the famous hallmarks of cancer as their checklist.

The two tumors differed hugely in gene activity overall. Through the hallmark lens, though, the gap shrank in odd ways. The invasion hallmark was not much stronger in the deadly tumor's RNA. The blood vessel hallmark was not either. Even benign tissue carried hallmark-like signals. The study questions the checklist itself. Tidy hallmark labels may blur at the RNA level, even when behavior could not differ more.
plos-pone-0351873:
M. Aiman Mohtar and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One lab study of a protein called AGR2. The protein helps breast cancer cells grow, move, and resist chemotherapy. The team used gene editing to delete AGR2 from breast cancer cells. They measured the fallout on cell behavior. They also tracked thousands of genes switched on or off.

Without AGR2, cells migrated less and invaded less. They were easier to kill with drugs. Gene profiling showed wide changes in signaling, stress response, and adhesion programs. Network analysis placed the estrogen receptor at the center of the disturbed web. That receptor is the classic driver of many breast cancers. Public chromosome data tied the receptor's activity to AGR2's own control region. The authors propose this axis as a future drug target.
plos-pone-0351973:
Yeong-Jang Lin and four colleagues ask whether curing hepatitis C also calms the immune system. Their 2026 cohort study uses a global health records network covering 2015 to 2024. Chronic hepatitis C stirs immune dysfunction and raises autoimmune disease risk. Modern direct-acting antivirals cure the infection at high rates. The long-term immune consequences were unclear. Treated and untreated patients were matched one-to-one on starting characteristics. Each group held over thirty-five thousand people.

Treatment came with measurably lower autoimmune risk. Rheumatoid arthritis risk fell by about a sixth. Autoimmune hepatitis risk fell by nearly half. A platelet-destroying immune condition also grew rarer. Control outcomes and sensitivity checks supported the pattern's robustness. Curing a virus is already its own reward. Evidence that cure also lowers later autoimmune disease strengthens the case for treating every hepatitis C patient early, not only those with advanced liver damage.
plos-pone-0352173:
Yan Xiao and three colleagues pool the results of randomised trials to ask whether exercise lifts mood and life quality in people with rheumatoid arthritis, in this 2026 PLOS ONE review. Fifteen trials covering more than sixteen hundred adults compared structured exercise with no exercise, tracking depression, anxiety, and quality of life, with the evidence graded for certainty.

Exercise probably reduced depressive symptoms by a moderate amount, on evidence the graders rated moderately certain. Anxiety likely fell too, and quality of life improved, though that evidence was weaker. Mind-body exercise and conventional exercise performed alike. The authors support exercise as an add-on to drug treatment, while asking for bigger, longer trials to show how durable the gains are.
plos-pone-0352273:
CORRECTION: The PLOS One Staff correct a table in a study of health insurance and mothers' care in Ghana. The study used the national health survey from twenty twenty-two. In its fourth table, two subheadings had shifted to the right. That shift left several columns with the wrong labels. This notice prints the table again in correct form. The publisher also apologizes for the error.

The corrected table links insurance cover to three parts of mothers' care. It covers how early antenatal visits start. It covers whether mothers complete the advised number of visits. It also covers whether a skilled attendant is present at birth. Anyone citing numbers from that table should use this fixed version.
plos-pone-0352673:
König and colleagues studied what shapes daily movement in Swedish adults living with heart and vessel disease in a 2026 study. Movement helps prevent further illness, yet many patients stay inactive. Participants in their fifties and early sixties wore motion sensors on the hip for seven days, giving a direct record rather than memory-based guesses.

The team grouped people by low, middle, and high levels of brisk activity. They then compared those groups across age, income, schooling, habits, and other illnesses drawn from surveys and health records. Sorting out which factors track with low movement helps clinics target support, such as coaching or follow-up, to patients least likely to stay active on their own.
plos-pone-0352873:
Mark Jaime and Elizabeth B daSilva ask whether people can read feeling from body movement alone, stripped of faces and labels. Actors moved to express anger, fear, or happiness, and their motion was reduced to moving dots that keep natural quirks of each performance. Viewers rated each display for pleasantness and energy without being told the aim, and their ratings were mapped against where each emotion should sit in feeling space.

Viewers with sharper social perception placed their ratings closer to the expected spots for the movements. The strength of that match varied by which emotion the actor had aimed at. Jaime and daSilva argue that raw motion carries usable feeling information, and that people differ reliably in how well they can read it.
plos-pone-0352973:
Cecilia Afua Lodonu-Senoo and three colleagues set out a protocol, published in PLOS ONE in 2026, for reviewing school-based HIV prevention aimed at teenage girls and young women living in sub-Saharan Africa. This group still carries a heavy share of new infections, and clinic-based services often miss them. Schools, by contrast, reach them reliably and at scale.

The planned review will collect trials and qualitative studies from 2015 to 2025. It will cover prevention medicines, condoms, and HIV testing delivered through schools. Two reviewers will screen and judge the studies. They will merge numbers where possible and themes where not. The goal is practical: show what school delivery can achieve and what blocks it.
plos-pone-0353073:
Tighe and colleagues surveyed young men in the United Kingdom about fertility knowledge in a 2026 study. Men are starting families later, yet age quietly lowers male fertility too. More than four hundred men answered questions on fertility facts, hopes for children, and money and life influences.

Over half of those who finished had no children yet, and most hoped for a first child in their early thirties. Answers revealed how much men know, and miss, about age and fertility. Gaps in knowledge matter because couples often learn about male age effects only when problems appear. Clearer public information could help men plan family timing with open eyes.
plos-pone-0353173:
Mohamud Abshir Musse and four colleagues compare the blood of adults with type 2 diabetes against healthy neighbours in Garowe, Somalia, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Diabetes quietly alters blood cells as well as sugar, yet no local data existed. One hundred and thirty-three patients and the same number of controls gave samples in late 2024 for cell counts, sugar measures, and haemoglobin checks.

Several measures — infection-fighting white cells, red cell size, platelet size and spread — differed significantly between the groups. Anaemia touched nearly a third of the diabetic patients and was tied to poor sugar control. The authors note anaemia also appeared in controls, hinting at wider nutritional causes in the population that deserve attention too.
plos-pone-0353273:
Son and colleagues studied swallowing problems after lung transplantation in a 2026 paper. Records covered more than one hundred adults transplanted at one center over fourteen years. Swallowing was scored by how much food patients could take by mouth at set days after surgery.

About one patient in three had serious swallowing trouble four weeks after surgery, though most recovered oral eating by discharge. Longer time on a heart-lung support machine before transplant, a breathing tube in the neck, and lung infection afterward each linked to the trouble. Patients with swallowing problems also survived less well over the next two years, marking it as a warning sign worth early attention.
plos-pone-0353473:
Onodera and colleagues measured the vagus nerve in older adults in a Japanese community study in a 2026 paper. The nerve helps control heart rhythm, and its size on neck ultrasound might reflect that control. Participants aged sixty-five and older had both heart tracings and neck scans in one survey round.

Heart tracing features were compared across small, medium, and large nerve size groups for each side of the neck. Any link would suggest nerve size tracks the heart's electrical behavior in daily life, not only in patients. Community data like these can reveal early signs of fading nerve control, which matters for fall and faint risk in older age.
plos-pone-0353573:
Million Mohammed Asfaw and Alemu Earsido Addila published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies how often type 2 diabetes is diagnosed late among adults in Central Ethiopia. The patients attended a comprehensive specialized hospital, and the study is facility-based and cross-sectional, examining attendees at one point in time.

Late diagnosis means years of high blood sugar quietly damaging eyes, kidneys, and nerves before treatment starts. Measuring how common delay is, and which factors travel with it, points to where screening should reach earlier. Ethiopian health planners and diabetes clinics are the readers who can act on this picture of missed years.
plos-pone-0353673:
Varesco and colleagues tested short thinking tests for young elite skiers training at altitude in a 2026 study. Thin air can dull the mind, but coaches need quick field tools to spot it. Mogul skiers took tablet tests after jump training and at rest, under normal air and under air thinned to mimic high mountains.

Low oxygen lowered thinking performance and seemed to raise mental fatigue. Jump performance also dipped late in the session under thin air. Brief tests combining mental and physical demand caught the changes best. Portable fifteen-minute checks could help teams adjust training loads on altitude camps before fatigue builds into injury risk.
plos-pone-0353773:
Bao and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a model that summarizes videos by picking their most important shots. A good summary lets a viewer grasp a long video in moments, which matters for surveillance review and short-video apps. Earlier graph-based methods struggled to blend close-up detail with the whole video's shape.

Their model turns each shot into a point in a graph, linked to shots with similar meaning. It then reads the graph at two scales: one attention method draws out local links between neighboring shots, and another network draws out global structure. The three views, original, local, and global, are fused to score each shot's importance. On two public benchmark sets, the method scored competitively against leading approaches. The authors offer it as a practical way to cut long footage down to its essentials.
plos-pone-0354073:
Lijuan Zhao and coauthors published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on automating the building of multibody dynamics models, the virtual machines engineers test before cutting metal. Hand-building such models in the RecurDyn software is slow and error-prone. Their method reads a design file's assembly features, identifies components with a wording-and-meaning system backed by a multilingual language model, then generates code that assembles the model automatically.

They tested the pipeline on the cutting unit of a drum shearer, a coal-mining machine, at three levels of structural complexity, then checked simulations against a test rig. Model building took less than one percent of the usual manual time. Simulated shaft speeds matched reality almost exactly, and drum vibration errors stayed within a few percent. The authors present the rule-driven approach as transferable to other complex machinery, turning weeks of modeling into an automatic step.
plos-pone-0354173:
Tanjina Rahman and six colleagues document how common malnutrition is among kidney dialysis patients in Bangladesh, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. One hundred and eighty-one patients on regular haemodialysis across four districts were assessed with two standard nutrition scoring systems. By the stricter criteria, over two fifths were malnourished, and about one in ten severely so; the other score flagged nearly three quarters.

One practice stood out sharply: patients who reused their dialysis filter more than twice had far higher odds of malnutrition. Age, body weight, and diabetes also played a part. In poor health systems, the authors argue, routine nutrition checks and safer equipment practices could save lives cheaply.
plos-pone-0354373:
Robi Cynthia Chacha and Ermias Mergia Terefe published this 2026 study of prescribing habits at Thika Level 5 Hospital in Kenya. With yardsticks from the World Health Organization, they reviewed six hundred prescriptions, a hundred patient visits, and the facility itself, comparing results with global benchmarks for sensible medicine use.

Prescriptions carried more drugs on average than recommended, few were written by generic name, and antibiotics appeared in well over half of visits, though most medicines came from the essential list. Chacha urges stronger antibiotic stewardship, generic prescribing, and better counseling for patients at the dispensing counter.
plos-pone-0354473:
Niazy and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, test an old cancer drug against a stubborn hospital germ. The germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, harms patients with weak defenses, and its swimming, crawling, and slime-building habits help it cause disease. Repurposing an approved drug is a fast route to new anti-germ tactics, so the team tried 5-fluorouracil at rising doses.

All three forms of movement shrank as dose rose, and genes for the germ's propellers and grappling hairs were turned down. So were genes for a tissue-chewing enzyme and for soap-like chemicals that help it spread. The picture for genetic material leaked from cells was mixed: it fell after one day, then rose at high doses after two days, alongside genes for DNA repair. The authors read the drug as a brake on this germ's attack tools, while noting the later DNA rise needs explaining.
plos-pone-0354673:
David J Lewkowicz and Julia McClellan published this 2026 eye-tracking study of the cocktail party problem: following just one talker among many when faces and voices arrive together. Adult volunteers watched competing talking faces on screens while the researchers varied lip-sound timing, face shape, and identity cues from face, voice, and word choice.

Timing synchrony separated talkers without needing a standard face layout. Word-choice identity helped on its own, and pupil size showed the mental effort each cue combination cost. Lewkowicz maps which clues adults actually use to untangle crowded conversation.
plos-pone-0354773: Akinyemi and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on loneliness and death risk in the United States. They examined whether people who report loneliness die sooner from any cause than those who do not. Loneliness is now common enough to count as a public health issue. If the link is strong, doctors may one day screen for loneliness like they screen for smoking.
plos-pone-0354973:
Carlos Abraham Herrera-Amante and co-authors checked how badly standard formulas estimate resting metabolism in professional footballers. Resting metabolic rate drives daily energy needs, yet measuring it directly needs costly gas analysis. Their 2026 study compared twelve common equations and a machine learning model against direct measurement in forty male professionals.

Every equation overshot the measured rate, by margins from small to more than a third. Agreement scores were poor across the board. The learning model, built from body measurements, made smaller errors than any formula. Even so, it explained only a limited share of the differences between players. The authors warn practitioners that off-the-shelf formulas can badly mislead diet planning for athletes.
plos-pone-0355173:
José García-Moreno and co-authors interview in 2026 patients waiting for spine surgery about what stops or helps them stay active before the operation. Activity before surgery may improve recovery from narrowed or slipped disc conditions in the lower back. Interviews used each person's own activity data as a prompt and were sorted through a behaviour framework, with a patient partner shaping the work.

Pain, low physical capacity, fear of harm, poor settings, and negative feelings blocked activity. Motivation, good settings, social support, positive feelings, workarounds, and daily habits helped. Tailored programmes before surgery should attack fear and pain while building on habits and support, the authors suggest.
plos-pone-0355373:
Bashige Chiribagula Valentin and co-authors recorded plants used to start or strengthen labour in Lubumbashi, in the Haut-Katanga region of Congo. Traditional birth practice there relies on plant knowledge passed down by healers and herbalists. For their 2026 study, the team interviewed more than two hundred local informants, including housewives, herbalists, and traditional healers.

Informants named close to a hundred plant species across many families, with the pea family most common. Leaves featured in most of the recorded labour remedies, often applied as a paste. Dozens of species had never before been reported for this use, and several were new medicinal records for the country. The inventory gives pharmacologists a starting list for safety and effect testing.
plos-pone-0355473:
Na Li and colleagues study a small helper protein in eye cells damaged by high sugar, a lab model of diabetic eye disease. Diabetes can harm the retina over time, and earlier work had linked this protein to several illnesses but not to this one. The team grew human retinal cells in very sweet conditions, then switched the protein down and read which genes changed activity or changed how their messages were cut and rejoined.

High sugar lowered both cell growth and the protein's level. Switching it down shifted hundreds of genes, mostly ones that run the cell division cycle, and altered the cutting of many more. Li and colleagues suggest the protein helps coordinate growth control in retinal cells, making it a candidate lead for protecting sight in diabetes.
plos-pone-0355673:
Matt Vogel and three colleagues question a growing habit in violence research in this 2026 paper. A federal index built to gauge how well communities withstand natural disasters, called the Social Vulnerability Index, is now often used to flag places at risk of gun violence. The authors ask whether a disaster tool really fits that job.

They compared the index head-to-head with a long-standing measure of concentrated disadvantage across census tracts in more than eighty American cities. The disaster index consistently explained firearm violence less well, and what power it had came almost entirely from its economic component. The authors argue that borrowing the index amounts to conceptual drift. It measures how a community absorbs outside shocks, not the local conditions that breed violence. Using it could steer prevention money to the wrong places.
plos-pone-0355873:
Anjali Saini and Shalini Rai present a plan to map laboratory evidence on traditional Indian mineral and herb mixtures used against cancer. The formulations come from the Ayurveda and Siddha systems of medicine. Their 2026 protocol asks what cell and animal studies actually show about these mixtures, since that evidence is scattered.

The paper reports a method, not finished findings. Two reviewers will search selected databases and sort studies using set eligibility rules. Results will be shown in tables and summary text, following standard reporting guidance for scoping reviews. Saini and Rai hope the map will help researchers pick the most promising formulations for closer study.
plos-pone-0355973:
Gabriel Haddad and three colleagues sort out which forms of an invasive malaria mosquito are living in Djibouti City, in this 2026 entomology study. Anopheles stephensi, an Asian species first found in Djibouti in 2012, has been linked to rising urban malaria across the Horn of Africa. It exists in three biological forms with different habitats and different abilities to transmit malaria, distinguishable by ridges on their eggs and, supposedly, by a scent-related gene.

Six hundred eggs collected at six city sites in April 2023 covered all three forms living side by side. Surprisingly, the form thought rural and a weak transmitter dominated even in high-malaria urban districts. The gene test did not match the egg-based identification, so the authors judge it unsuitable for telling the forms apart. They say the forms' actual roles in city transmission must be pinned down before control policy can be well aimed.
plos-pone-0356073:
Yang Wang, Asif Ali Safeer, and Yewang Zhou ask what makes travelers bond with artificial intelligence chatbots, in this 2026 survey study. Their respondents were Chinese tourists who use chatbots to plan and manage trips. Nearly seven hundred responses were analyzed with two statistical approaches, one tracing average pathways and one hunting for winning combinations of traits. The model connects chatbot features, through trust, to engagement and emotional connection, with the bot's social presence as a booster.

Personalization, interactivity, and ease of use each built trust, and trust in turn raised engagement and emotional connection; engagement itself deepened the emotional bond. A stronger sense of social presence further amplified engagement. The combination analysis singled out a personal touch, ease of use, and engagement as the key ingredients of emotional connection. The authors advise travel firms to design chatbots as relationship partners, not transaction machines.
plos-pone-0356173:
Chiel van der Laan and Alessandro Corbetta published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how pairs of pedestrians move through crowds. Most people in public spaces walk with a companion, side by side to talk, but crowds force pairs to adjust. The authors mined a huge dataset from Eindhoven Central Station, millions of walking pairs tracked over years, modeling how pair speed and formation respond to crowd density and flow.

Pairs slowed and reshaped themselves predictably as crowds thickened. Walking abreast favors conversation, while falling into single file favors pushing through, and pairs traded between the two as conditions changed. They built diagrams linking pair behavior to crowd state and introduced a number for how strongly a pair prefers side-by-side over in-file walking in a given situation. That measure breaks into two standard crowd diagrams, giving engineers a grounded way to include social groups in simulations.
plos-pone-0356373:
Petko Karagyozov, Inna Dobreva, and Ivelina Zhecheva report a Bulgarian tertiary center's experience with liver biopsy performed through an endoscope, in this 2026 study. Using ultrasound guidance from inside the stomach, doctors can sample the liver while watching in real time, avoiding some drawbacks of needle-through-skin and vein-based routes. The team reviewed three years of consecutive cases done with a fine 22-gauge Franseen-tip needle and a gentle slow-pull technique, for both widespread liver disease and focal lesions.

All seventy-two patients yielded tissue that pathologists judged adequate for diagnosis. About three quarters proved to have malignant disease and the rest benign conditions. No complications appeared in the first two days or over a month of follow-up. The authors present the technique as safe and effective, with shorter recovery than conventional biopsy routes, aided by live imaging that helps the needle steer clear of blood vessels.
plos-pone-0356473:
Lidong Hou and five colleagues explain why water quietly destroys mudstone from the inside, in this 2026 multi-scale study motivated by oil drilling. Mudstone formations that drink water make boreholes unstable, and the chief suspect is a swelling clay mineral, montmorillonite. The team combined mineral analysis, mechanical tests on soaked rock cores, and molecular dynamics simulations that watch individual water molecules at work.

Soaking cut the rock's compressive strength by more than half. The simulations show why: water slips between the clay's layers in stages, forming one, then two, then three molecular films, prising the layers apart unevenly while sodium ions shuffle among the water. That staged swelling explains why real cores first flake, then fragment, the longer they sit in water. The authors say blocking this interlayer hydration is the key to stable boreholes.
plos-pone-0356773:
Tae-Eun Kim and colleagues link an eye condition of early birth with later development using nationwide Korean health screening records. The eye condition scars the retina of premature babies. Records covered more than eight hundred thousand children screened near age five, including several thousand with a history of the condition, and tested six areas of development from language to movement.

Children with the eye history faced higher odds of delay in every area tested, with the largest gap in large-muscle skills. Risk ran higher still when eyesight at screening was also weak. Kim and colleagues propose the eye history as an easy flag in records, marking children who deserve close developmental watch and joined eye and development care.
plos-pone-0356873:
Nobuo Nagano and colleagues pool three Japanese clinical trials of tenapanor, a newer drug for the phosphate build-up that plagues dialysis patients. Failing kidneys cannot clear phosphate, which drives bone and heart harm; older binder pills work but pile up daily doses that patients skip. Tenapanor instead blocks phosphate absorption in the gut, and its dose is raised step by step until blood levels respond, though stomach side effects make some patients resist higher doses.

The pooled analysis asks which patient traits mark those who end up needing the high end of the dose range. Knowing the profile in advance could help doctors counsel patients and set expectations before titration begins. Nagano and colleagues draw on the three registered trials' combined records for this prescribing question.
plos-pone-0357173:
Abdul Mannan and co-authors model hepatitis C spread with a twist. Alcohol use deepens liver damage in infected people. Here it enters the transmission equations as its own factor. The virus drives much chronic liver disease worldwide. Their six-group model tracks people through stages of infection and drinking. Classic numerics can solve the stiff equations, but slowly. So the team also trained a deep learning solver. They compared its answers against trusted methods.

The learning solver matched the classic results with strong stability and convergence in their tests. Stability analysis located the thresholds where infection dies out or settles in, and sensitivity checks named the parameters that matter most. Mannan and colleagues present machine solving as a practical extra tool for epidemic forecasting.
plos-pone-0357273:
Hyeon Ah Kim and colleagues describe, organ by organ, what healthy tissue looks like under a microscope in baby common marmosets. Marmosets serve widely as lab primates, yet reference detail for the first weeks of life is thin. The team compared five major organs from infants in their first three weeks with the same organs from adults, using several standard stains and a marker of dividing cells.

Infant livers still made blood cells and held loosely layered tissue, while adult livers showed tidy plates. Infant kidneys were still building their filtering units, spleens held small pale zones, lungs had thick walls between air sacs, and hearts packed muscle loosely. Adult organs looked mature on every count. Kim and colleagues offer the atlas for judging normal growth against disease.
plos-pone-0357473:
Tancredo José Carlos and colleagues run field trials in Mozambique on feeding cowpea plants extra zinc and iron. Cowpea is a staple bean, and enriching it in the field could fight hidden hunger while raising yields. Their 2026 trial crossed three ways of applying the minerals, on soil, on leaves, or both, with several dose levels of each mineral in blocked field plots.

Combined soil and leaf feeding gave the best yields, and a growth curve pointed to one dose pair for the largest harvest. The profit peak, however, sat at lower doses, especially for iron, which could be cut nearly in half while keeping almost all of the yield gain. Risk checks stayed positive across treatments. The authors advise farmers to aim for the profit point, not the biggest harvest.
plos-pone-0357573:
Simon Alexander Berry and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for PAINLESS, a trial asking whether smoothing blood sugar can ease the burning pain of diabetic neuropathy. Painful neuropathy is common and hard to treat, and hints link flare-ups to glucose swings rather than average levels. Hybrid closed loop pumps, automating insulin delivery from continuous glucose readings, flatten those swings. The two-center crossover trial will recruit just under fifty adults with type 1 diabetes and painful neuropathy.

Each participant spends twelve weeks on the closed loop and twelve on standard care with glucose monitoring, in random order, keeping daily pain diaries. The main comparison is change in average daily pain. Secondary measures cover responder rates, quality of life, mood, and global change, while exploratory tests probe nerve function, sleep, and activity. If pumps relieve pain as a side benefit, the funding case widens beyond glucose numbers.
plos-pone-0357673:
Belal Elmarhoumy leads a lab study of the soft silicone used to rebuild faces after surgery or injury, asking how tiny added particles change its strength over time. Some samples sat outdoors in a hot, humid climate for two full years, while matching samples stayed indoors. The fillers were two common mineral powders mixed at low and higher shares into a medical silicone.

Fresh samples with a low share of silica powder tore and stretched far better than plain silicone. After two years outside, every mix lost stretch, but filled samples kept far more of theirs than the plain control, which lost about half. Elmarhoumy and colleagues conclude that a small silica dose helps prosthetic material survive harsh weather, a practical point for clinics in tropical regions.
plos-pone-0357773:
Yi Luo led a team of eight authors tracing air pollution damage in rats, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Breathing fine particles, PM2.5, harms the lungs first, but this team found effects far beyond them. Nasal exposure to the particles caused testicular injury and switched on a form of inflammatory cell death called pyroptosis.

Luo's group also tested inhibitors of that pathway and checked public gene data to support the chain. Their work suggests pollution's reach may extend to male fertility. If the damage route can be blocked, a future treatment path opens, though human evidence is still needed. The study adds weight to clean-air arguments by showing harm in organs people rarely connect with breathing.
plos-pone-0357973:
Rosella Muresu, Monica Rodriguez, and Andrea Squartini published a 2026 analysis in PLOS ONE questioning how well a standard bacterial barcode identifies Rhizobium, the root bacteria that help legume plants capture nitrogen. Identification usually rests on one gene, called 16S, assumed to match species, host plant, and origin. The team pulled thousands of Rhizobium sequences for that gene from the GenBank database and compared every pair that matched perfectly.

Among identical sequences with full records, about two-thirds disagreed on all three labels: species name, host plant, and country. Only a tiny share agreed on everything, and the single most common sequence appeared under dozens of host plants, many countries, and several species names. The gene, they argue, changes too slowly, while key traits move between bacteria on mobile DNA. Naming species needs genome, trait, and ecology data together.
plos-pone-0358073: Sowińska and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on bedsores as a safety problem in hospital care. Pressure injuries form when patients lie or sit too long without moving. The team reviewed cases at a specialist hospital from 2013 to 2020, treating each injury as an adverse event. Tracking these wounds over years shows whether prevention efforts are working.
plos-pone-0358773: Entwistle and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on why promising animal results often fail in people. They traced therapies for acute injury that began in small rodents. The trail runs from early promise through human testing to approval and safety results. As a systematic review, it gathers the full record. Seeing where the trail breaks can save money and spare patients false hope.
plos-pone-0358873:
Daniel Y Tsybulnik, Justin J Gillette, and Thomas F Heston ask whether language models agree with each other when grading clinical trial reports, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Journals expect trials to follow the CONSORT reporting checklist, and automated checking would help editors, if the checkers were consistent. The team had three leading models independently score twenty randomized trials from immunology journals against thirty-seven checklist points.

The models diverged sharply. One awarded an average compliance score of about eighty-one percent, a second about sixty-four, and the third about fifty-five. Against a strict ninety percent quality bar, the most generous model passed five papers while the other two passed none at all. Agreement between models was too weak for interchangeable use. The authors warn that swapping one model for another silently changes the verdict, so any editorial workflow needs a fixed, validated checker.
plos-pone-0358973: Hwang and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on drug-resistant gut germs in long-term care hospitals. Some patients carry carbapenem-resistant bacteria without being sick, yet can spread them. The team actively checked patients over time to measure how common carriage is and how people pick it up. They also hunted risk factors. Quiet carriers are a hidden route for outbreaks in care homes.
plos-pone-0359573:
Muna Elsadig, Shamsa Kanwal, Rab Nawaz, and Qazi Muhammad Zaigham Zia wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in applied mathematics. It studies beam-foundation systems, structures where a beam rests on a supporting base, with viscoelastic constraints, materials that behave partly like solids and partly like thick fluids. The authors model the system's computational dynamics.

Their focus includes damping-induced transitions, moments when energy loss shifts the system from one pattern of motion to another. Bridges, rails, and building foundations all involve beams on elastic supports, so these transitions matter for safety. Structural engineers and mathematicians share this ground where equations predict how real structures vibrate and settle.
plos-pone-0359773:
Orarat Karnjanawanichkul and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a prospective observational study of Thai adults under general anesthesia. The authors hunt for predictors of needing airway adjuncts, extra devices that keep the airway open, during mask ventilation.

Predicting who will be hard to ventilate lets anesthetists prepare equipment and help before trouble starts. Observing patients prospectively, as care unfolds, captures real practice rather than records alone. Anesthesia teams are the readers, since failed mask ventilation is one of the emergencies their specialty trains hardest to prevent.
pmc-13155173:
Milani and colleagues screened blood donations in Manaus, Brazil in 2026 for Oropouche virus during the 2023 to 2024 outbreak. A reshuffled virus lineage then caused tens of thousands of cases and was linked to brain complications and infections in pregnancy. No transfusion spread has been reported, but silent infection in donors could hide a route. The team tested pooled donations with a genetic assay, sequenced reactive samples, and tracked antibody levels in the population.

Among nearly twelve thousand donations, about six and a half percent of pools carried viral RNA, peaking in January 2024, and the donor viruses matched the outbreak lineage. Population antibody rates more than doubled across the outbreak, implying roughly 390,000 infections in the city, far above reported cases. The detectable window in blood was about five days. The authors say the findings raise real blood safety questions and demand continued donor and recipient watch.
pmc-13199673:
Jun P Hong and Michel C Nussenzweig present a 2026 protocol for a gene screen in mouse immune cells. Germinal center B cells mature antibodies inside lymph nodes, but no lab dish copies their biology well. Genetic screens must run in living mice, so the protocol adapts CRISPR tools, which cut or silence genes, for that setting.

Steps cover building a guide RNA library, delivering guides with a mouse-only retrovirus, and running the screen in an immunization model. Sequencing and analysis steps close the workflow. Tweaks include a refined guide scaffold and matched primers. Animal and biosafety approvals are stressed throughout. As a protocol, it reports no results; it gives labs a tested recipe for in vivo screens.
pmc-13200373:
Anett Mau-Moeller and colleagues compared inpatient versus outpatient rehabilitation after knee replacement in Germany in a 2026 trial. German care usually adds a three-week rehab stay after knee joint replacement surgery. Whether patients must stay in a facility or can attend daily was little tested, so the team ran a blinded comparison.

Patients chose their setting: twenty-six went inpatient and sixteen outpatient. Tests ran before rehab and three months after surgery. Outpatients logged far more daily steps in the first rehab week. At three months, outpatients also showed better joint position sense, the feel for where the knee sits. Other measures covered pain, swelling, motion, and timed walking tasks.
pmc-13200473:
Ayman Shaban and colleagues tested nano fertilizer sprays on olive trees in a 2026 field study. Olive trees often bear heavily one year and lightly the next, a pattern called alternate bearing. Spray feeding in the off-year might even out yields, so the team sprayed nano NPK and calcium-boron mixes on fifteen-year-old Picual trees.

Trials ran across the 2023 and 2024 seasons. The best blend raised flower counts, perfect flower share, and fruit set above controls. Off-year yield peaked under that blend, while fruit drop fell by about half versus controls. Leaf and fruit mineral levels rose. Oil kept its extra virgin grade with a richer share of oleic acid, its main healthy fat. Alternate bearing severity fell sharply.
pmc-13211873: A correction notice from Si-Ting Chen and co-authors, published in 2026, fixes figure errors in their 2023 eLife paper on embryo-derived TNF and uterine decidualization. Assembly mistakes had duplicated a loading-control band across two figures, copied immunoprecipitation bands into a later figure, and repeated one histogram in place of another. The authors replaced the affected panels, updated the source data, and apologized for the inadvertent errors. Only the correction notice itself survives here, so the study's data are not re-presented.
pmc-13220073:
Dmytro Kobzev and colleagues wrote this 2026 review of medicines that switch on only when triggered by a signal, such as light, heat, sound, or body chemistry. Such control could let a drug act at the right place and time instead of spreading through the whole body.

The authors mapped research from 2014 to 2024, covering over 90,000 papers and 1,000 clinical trials. Light was the most used outside trigger, while internal triggers like acidity and enzymes made up nearly half the work. They also list six barriers slowing use in patients, from complex designs to cost, and offer practical fixes for each.
pmc-13240873:
Chane's team at the University of Gondar gauged metabolic syndrome among long-shift health workers in Central Gondar Zone hospitals. Two hundred seventy-one professionals at three primary hospitals gave fasting blood samples in late 2023. Body measurements and questionnaires completed the picture. Syndrome status tracked the standard cholesterol-panel criteria.

About eleven percent met the syndrome definition. Over half carried at least one lipid abnormality, the commonest derangement, while high blood sugar was rarest. Being 35 or older, having a diabetic first-degree relative, and sleeping under six hours each carried several-fold higher odds. The authors urge routine screening and saner shift scheduling.
pmc-13242373:
Barros and colleagues in São Paulo pitted two hair-removal lights against each other, one per armpit. Forty-eight women with lighter skin types received four monthly sessions. Intense pulsed light treated one axilla; an 810-nanometre diode laser the other. Hair counts in a marked patch formed the primary outcome.

Both lights thinned and reduced hair significantly over time. At the primary endpoint, counts did not differ between sides. Seven months out, the laser side kept fewer, finer hairs. The laser hurt more and caused more follicle swelling, while pulsed light reddened skin oftener.
pmc-13244073:
Kiyotaka Yabe, Yuna Tosaka, and Kenji Matsuura built a deliberately low-tech tool for a common research chore: tracing animal movement from video. Their paper appeared in Ecology and Evolution in 2026. Automated trackers are powerful but demand tuned lighting, settings, and patience before they yield usable paths. For a handful of pilot videos, that setup cost can exceed the value of the data.

ManuTrace runs in a web page with no installation. The user plays and pauses the video, clicks the animal's position at chosen moments, and the tool fills the frames between clicks automatically. Finished paths download as spreadsheet-ready files. The team demonstrated it on termite group videos, where automated tools swung wildly in accuracy between natural and optimized footage. Manual tracing stayed dependable in both. The authors offer the tool for exploratory work where speed and simplicity beat throughput.
pmc-13246473:
This 2026 correction in Ecology and Evolution amends the acknowledgements of a study of the southern African tree genus Greyia, a group valued in traditional medicine. The original paper used a reduced-representation DNA method called 3RAD to discover single-letter genetic markers that tell Greyia species apart. The work was meant to support conservation of the trees and verification of medicinal plant material.

The authors found that several contributors had been left out of the acknowledgements by mistake. The corrected text now credits J. Pretorius and the Buffelskloof Nature Reserve, the South African National Biodiversity Institute's Kirstenbosch garden, the Wildlife and Environment Society of South Africa's Umgeni Valley reserve. The Ohrigstad Dam Nature Reserve, which provided sampling permits and field assistance. The authors apologize for the omission; the study's data and conclusions are unchanged.
pmc-13249073:
Romeo and an Italian team present a worked example of diagnosing one-sided eye socket disease, in a 2026 case series. Eighteen patients at a Milan referral hospital had biopsy-proven lesions in one orbit, reviewed with scans and tissue results side by side. The mix ranged from harmless cysts and blood vessel malformations to several kinds of cancer.

Imaging patterns and cell stains together sorted the lesions accurately, pointing each patient toward watching, targeted injections, full removal, or cancer therapy. No benign lesion returned during early follow-up. The authors offer their stepwise workflow as a reusable template for referral centers facing the same confusing presentations.
pmc-13250073:
Nouh and co-authors built a neutron star model with a layered recipe, in a 2026 Scientific Reports study. Real compact stars are not uniform, yet simple models use one stiffness rule throughout. Their composite model lets stiffness vary smoothly from core to envelope and solves Einstein's equations with a Monte Carlo method, which also maps how uncertain the answers are.

Sharper transitions between core and envelope produced more compact stars, and stronger relativistic effects shrank both size and mass. The stiffest layered recipe supported stars above three solar masses in the extreme case, while softer versions matched known pulsars of very different sizes. The authors offer the framework for narrowing down what dense matter inside neutron stars can be.
pmc-13250873:
Wang and colleagues hunt for signs that separate harmless lung spots from cancers in patients with bronchiectasis. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine study reviews patients at one Chinese hospital between 2019 and 2025 whose lung nodules had tissue results. Damaged, widened airways make such scan findings common and hard to judge.

Of one hundred forty-three patients, most nodules proved malignant, and those were usually invasive adenocarcinoma. Benign spots most often reflected simple inflammation. One imaging pattern, a pure ground-glass spot or ground-glass with a solid part, independently predicted cancer with strong odds. Upper-lobe location looked suspicious alone but faded after adjustment. The authors offer the ground-glass pattern as a practical flag for closer action.
pmc-13252773:
The editors of PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases issued this 2026 note on one of their past papers. The note updates an earlier statement of concern about a study that typed the bacteria behind relapsing fever in Africa. It reports what the journal found when it checked the study's ethics approvals.

The study used blood samples gathered in Ethiopia in 1994 and 2011, in Tanzania at an unknown time, and in Senegal in 2010. The paper named approval from a French committee. It named no local approvals and gave no reference number. In the inquiry, a co-author showed clearance papers from Tanzania. He also described approval in Ethiopia whose papers could not be found. A university ethics officer added that the samples were reused from older collections, and more papers were supplied.
pmc-13253973:
Mengjie Zhao and colleagues link insulin sensitivity to body aging in a 2026 study of United States adults. They analyzed 15,048 adults from national health surveys run from 2003 to 2018. A score called eGDR, built from waist size, blood pressure status, and blood sugar control, stood in for how well insulin works.

Each one-unit rise in the score tied to a 1.88-year lower biological age on one measure and 0.60 years lower on another. People in the top third of scores had 87 percent lower odds of sped-up aging on the first measure. The link held across subgroups, the authors report.
pmc-13256173:
Sabryn Hamila leads the authors of a 2026 journal article testing whether artificial intelligence can write good admissions interview stations. Multiple mini interviews, or MMIs, are short timed tasks used to judge medical school applicants on traits beyond grades. The study was done for domestic applicants to medicine programs at Monash Medical School in Australia, using its 2025 admissions cycle.

The team compared 56 stations in total: 17 written by AI and 39 written in the usual expert way. They were used with 824 applicants, giving 4,897 applicant-station interactions. AI stations scored a reliability of 0.82 against 0.81 for traditional ones, a gap that was not statistically meaningful. More AI stations were classed as optimal, so the authors say AI can match human work and may cut faculty workload.
pmc-13257973:
Ruinan Zhao, Zhifan Han, and Huiling Liu present a 2026 study building a knowledge graph of the South China Sea. A knowledge graph stores facts as linked subject, action, and object triples that computers can search. The region's records are split across many sources on history, law, and politics, in varied wording. The team used a large language model, an AI text system, to pull these sources into one structure.

Their three-stage process extracted facts, standardized names and terms, and then verified the results. The finished graph holds 59,836 entities and 652,018 triples. It supports answering questions with evidence drawn across centuries, finding hidden multi-step links between governments and local practices, and building quick profiles of single topics. The authors offer it as a model others can copy.
pmc-13259273:
Murat Konak and colleagues review how premature babies tolerated a thickened formula in intensive care. Locust bean gum formulas curb regurgitation, but their gut effects in preterm infants are murky. Their 2026 retrospective study follows twenty-six infants day by day after the switch.

Within a week, nearly all babies passed soft, normal stools and strained far less. Bloated bellies eased in almost every case, and gas passage settled for all. Oxygen levels improved too, with almost no infants still dipping by day seven. Growth stayed acceptable, though the authors want bigger prospective trials before firm claims.
pmc-13259573:
Sylvie Aucoin and colleagues ask whether an anesthesiologist's presence changes outcomes for cataract surgery in Ontario. Patients receive sedation under several care models, some with no physician anesthesiologist at all. Their 2026 population study mines linked health records for over a million operations across a decade.

About half the patients had fee-for-service anesthesiology care, a fifth had care-team coverage, and the rest had none. Adjusted odds of death, admission, or an emergency visit within a week were slightly lower with any physician involvement. Complications also dipped, though overall costs ran higher. The authors judge the gains small and urge rethinking routine coverage.
pmc-13259973:
Jessyca Janyny de Oliveira Saraiva-Maia leads a 2026 landscape study of forest fragility in the Lower São Francisco River Watershed in Brazil. The team measured how forest remains are arranged, using patch area, core area, and shape, and compared those measures with land use and land cover maps. Fragility levels were set by a ranked classification, and statistical tests linked fragility to how the surrounding land is used by people.

Farming and pasture covered 66.9 percent of the watershed, mostly pasture at 57.7 percent. The forest was split into 37,022 small, disconnected fragments, and 72.2 percent of them showed high configurational fragility. Savanna, the most common native vegetation, had 96.1 percent of its patches at intermediate to high fragility. The authors advise protecting strategic remains, intervening in middle zones, and restoring the most fragile areas first.
pmc-13260173:
Sarah Potiron leads a 2026 study of how spatially patterned radiation changes the cargo of extracellular vesicles, tiny sacs cells release to signal each other. The team compared minibeam radiation therapy, which delivers radiation in thin spaced beams, with conventional radiation in rat glioma, a brain tumor, and normal astrocyte cell lines. Vesicles were collected twenty-four hours after treatment and their small RNA cargo was sequenced.

Vesicle size, shape, and marker proteins stayed the same across conditions, so radiation changed cargo rather than the vesicles themselves. Glioma cells showed limited, cell-dependent changes, and one glioma line showed none. pmc-13261073:

pmc-13261373:

pmc-13261973:

pmc-13262073:

pmc-13262173:

pmc-13262473:

pmc-13262573:

pmc-13263173:

The authors weigh longer runs in the blood and kind treatment by the body against hurdles in making them the same way each time. pmc-13263373:

pmc-13263773:

pmc-13263873:

pmc-13264873:

pmc-13264973:

pmc-13267573:

pmc-13269573:

pmc-13270873:

pmc-13271273:

pmc-13271573:

pmc-13273873:

pmc-13274573:

pmc-13274873:

pmc-13275173:

pmc-13276273:

pmc-13276573:

pmc-13276673:

pmc-13277173:

pmc-13277773:

pmc-13282873:
