Survival calls were weaker by comparison in the test results. Clear uncertainty bounds may make AI forecasts safer for clinical use.
pmc-13284773:
David Baud and co-authors report a 2026 cohort study on sexual function twelve years after childbirth injury to the anal sphincter. Such tears can cause pelvic floor problems, and short-term work has found more pain and less pleasure after injury. Long-term evidence was scarce, so the team re-surveyed the same women with a standard sexual function questionnaire.

Replies came from 52 women with injury and 141 controls, a high return rate for this long follow-up. Total and domain scores were alike between groups overall. Still, women with injury more often reported poor lubrication and pain on penetration. A past gap in reaching orgasm had faded by year twelve. The authors show broad recovery with some lasting symptoms.
pmc-13284873:
James Muscat and co-authors give a 2026 case report and literature review on a rare open midfoot injury. A 30-year-old woman fell six meters and suffered an open fracture-dislocation of the medial cuneiform bone, plus tearing of the tibialis anterior tendon from its anchor. Such cuneiform injuries are uncommon and often hide within wider foot trauma.

Urgent care included washing and cleaning the wound, realigning and fixing the midfoot, and repairing the tendon through a bone tunnel with strong sutures. At six months, X-rays held the alignment with no hardware failure. Pain was minimal, no infection appeared, and she walked on her own. The authors call this the first report of this exact pairing.
pmc-13285173:
Rumaisa Riaz and co-authors give a 2026 overview of drug care for Alzheimer disease, centered on the newly approved antibody donanemab-azbt. Older drugs lift a brain chemical or calm a receptor, easing symptoms but with side effects such as nausea or dizziness. New antibodies aim at amyloid clumps, yet can cause imaging faults tied to swelling or bleeding.

Trial data show donanemab-azbt lowers amyloid load and slows thinking decline in early symptomatic disease, the authors report. That gain comes with a need for close clinical and scan monitoring during treatment. The overview weighs donanemab beside standard drugs and the earlier antibody aducanumab to guide early-stage care choices.
pmc-13285373:
Greener straw pulping with soda ash help is the advance in a 2026 study by Qixi Xu and co-authors. Normal oxygen-alkali pulping of wheat straw runs hot, chews up cellulose, and lets silicon foul the process. Their low-heat method adds sodium carbonate and recycles the alkali mix.

At set heat and alkali levels, pulp yields rose over the standard method, and the test paper grew stronger on both pull and crush measures in the trials reported here. Far less dissolved silicon stayed in the waste liquor than under the old method, easing a key snag. The authors say the route gives steady, high-grade straw pulp with less waste strain.
pmc-13285573:
A tail stretch of viral RNA steers how well Getah virus grows, sickens, and rides mosquitoes, Tongwei Ren and co-authors show in a 2026 study. This mosquito-borne virus threatens farm stock and people, with fresh outbreaks growing harsher. The team snipped parts of the tail stretch, called the 3 prime untranslated region, and watched each mutant.

The tail proved bendy: cutting up to three hundred ten letters still left live virus. Losing repeat bits slowed growth in some cells and blunted illness in mice. The biggest cut crippled spread to mosquitoes and caused only brief sickness, with no deaths. Joint gene reads tied the softening to immune path shifts. A weakened vaccine seed is the goal.
pmc-13286073:
Elizabeth R Boskey and co-authors run a 2026 randomized trial on whether readers notice gender-inclusive health writing. Handouts on sexual and reproductive health can use wording that fits all genders, yet critics claim general readers dislike the style. The trial handed adults paired versions of teen handouts, one inclusive and one gender-specific, in random order.

The study held 454 adults assigned female at birth, about a third of them LGBTQ+. Most readers never spotted a difference between the paired sheets, even in the first pair they saw. Many who said they favored gender-specific wording still picked the inclusive sheet as the one they liked better. Those who favored inclusive wording chose it far more often when they did notice. Quiet inclusion, the authors conclude, passes without friction across the political range.
pmc-13286573:
Megan S Laham and a large team refine a fingerprinting assay for liver X receptor drugs in a 2026 pharmacology study. These receptors command cholesterol handling genes tied to Alzheimer's risk, and their activators help in animal models of several diseases. The blocker has always been the liver: the same drugs switch on fat making there. Their assay reads, with glowing molecular tags, which partner proteins a drug recruits or dismisses at the receptor.

A combined version now watches a partner swap happen in real time. Strength at recruiting partners to one receptor form tracked how well drugs switched on a cholesterol export gene in brain tumor cells. Fat-gene activation followed murkier rules. Fingerprints ranged from full activation to outright blockade within single drug families, giving designers a precision screen for cholesterol-friendly candidates that spare the liver.
pmc-13286673:
Giuseppe Dell'Anna and colleagues describe fishing a stray gallbladder stent out through a second one in a 2026 case vignette. A 74-year-old woman with heavy comorbidity first received external gallbladder drainage elsewhere for moderate acute gallbladder inflammation, then arrived with leaking bile and lingering fever. The team converted her to internal drainage under ultrasound guidance, seating a 10 by 10 millimeter metal stent through the gut wall into the gallbladder.

A month later, checks showed the stent had slipped entirely inside the gallbladder. Rather than operate on a frail patient, the team placed a second stent beside it, widened the passage, and pulled the migrated stent out with grasping forceps through the new channel. A large gallstone followed with a basket tool in the same session. No complications ensued, and the authors commend the rescue route for expert centers.
pmc-13286873:
Chukwuka Elendu and co-authors recount a goat saved by timely surgery in a 2026 veterinary case report. A proven mother doe under smallholder care strained in active labor for about fourteen hours with nothing to show for it. Examination found an alert but exhausted animal, weak contractions, and a cervix that stayed firm and barely open, admitting at most two fingers despite the long labor.

Gentle manual stretching failed, and the team deliberately skipped drugs that would strengthen contractions against a closed cervix, fearing rupture. An emergency cesarean through the left flank under local anesthesia resolved the obstruction directly. The report's lesson targets field practice: when a rigid cervix ignores both time and manipulation, earlier surgery, not more tugging, protects both doe and kid.
pmc-13287973:
Sultan M Alsharif and co-authors sequenced bacteria in 2026 from soil hugging the roots of four date palm varieties grown near Madinah in Saudi Arabia. A marker gene survey named the resident groups, and a prediction tool inferred what growth-helping jobs those bacteria might carry.

One large bacterial phylum led in most samples, while a second led in one variety. Known helper genera appeared throughout, including Bacillus and Paenibacillus. Predicted genes for moving phosphate and sulfur, grabbing iron, and handling oxidation were plentiful. The authors present the root zone as a rich source of helper microbes that could support greener date farming after strain-level testing.
pmc-13288973:
Xinyan Chen and colleagues give a 2026 trial plan for pain drugs after heart surgery. The trial sits at one center in China. It deals with small-cut valve replacement. Pain care after such surgery is tricky. Strong pain drugs can cause side effects.

The trial will enroll 130 patients in all. Half will get oxycodone by a pain pump. Half will get sufentanil instead. Neither side will know their drug. The main test is pain on coughing at 24 hours. Staff will also track drug use and side effects. The goal is to match, not beat, the standard drug.
pmc-13289373:
Tracey Smythe and coauthors ran a 2026 pilot in Luuka district, Uganda, on group work to improve health care access for people with disabilities. Barriers to care are steep in low-resource areas, and few community fixes have been tested. The Participatory Learning and Action for Disability approach lets groups name local barriers and act on them together.

Five groups ran from May 2023 to March 2024, each with roughly 35 to 48 members, totaling 204 people meeting every two weeks. Trained facilitators led 11 sessions per group cycle. Interviews, group watching, activity logs, and surveys before and after checked appeal, demand, and early effects. Members found the groups relevant and wanted them to continue, though mentor support for facilitators lagged at times.
pmc-13289673:
Louisa Horvath and Silke Pawils explored a 2026 mixed-methods study on trauma-sensitive obstetrics from the provider side in Germany. Traumatic birth experiences draw growing concern, yet most research asks birthing people, not staff. An online survey ran from October 2024 to February 2025 with 102 providers, plus four expert interviews for depth on causes and fixes.

Most providers defined traumatic birth through loss of control and negative emotions for the patient. Poor communication and information topped causes at 97.1 percent, followed by lack of emotional support as reported. Emotional support also ranked as the top preventive step by mean score. Lack of time and staff shortages were the main barriers named.
pmc-13289773:
Shivangini Duggal headed a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on infection after cholangioscopy, a scope procedure that views bile ducts directly. The method helps with complex bile disease but seems to carry higher infection risk than standard duct procedures. Proof to guide preventive antibiotics for this specific scope was thin, so pooled rates were needed.

Five databases were searched through March 2025, yielding twelve studies with 4413 procedures for pooling. Blood infection pooled near 6.68 percent, with wide uncertainty and high variation across studies as reported. Duct inflammation and pancreas inflammation pooled lower. Technical success was very high and clinical success also high overall. Study design explained part of the variation.
pmc-13290573:
Testing whole blood, not just plasma, catches more infections in patients with blood disorders, a 2026 real-world cohort study from northern China by Cuicui Lyu and colleagues shows. Infection is a leading killer in this group, and standard blood culture misses most culprits.

The team reviewed 231 blood samples from patients with suspected infection who received metagenomic sequencing. Whole-blood sequencing, which reads plasma plus blood cells, detected pathogens far more often than culture and found 13 organisms that plasma-only testing missed among its 101 detections. Its agreement with final clinical diagnoses was also the highest of the methods compared. Treatment improved for most patients as a result, with needless antibiotics stopped and therapy better aimed. Lyu and colleagues back the combined sample for early infection care in these fragile patients.
pmc-13291073:
Yiwei Chen and colleagues report a 2026 case where gene sequencing of spinal fluid found the true cause of meningitis after standard treatment failed. Their patient was a 67-year-old man with chronic lung disease who arrived with four days of high fever and confusion, and first antibiotic cover with meropenem brought no gain.

Metagenomic sequencing named Listeria monocytogenes, a foodborne germ that strikes hardest at older and weakened patients, as the cause of meningitis alongside a flare of his lung disease. Care switched to ampicillin-based treatment plus gentamicin for set courses, and his symptoms and blood markers improved fast afterward. The case backs early use of broad sequencing when brain infections resist usual diagnosis.
pmc-13291473:
Remote rehab may beat home exercise for sore tendons. Shijie Fan leads a 2026 review of telerehabilitation trials. Tendon pain often gets exercise care without surgery. Remote coaching could add support that home plans lack.

Ten trials with 412 people were pooled. Remote care cut pain more than home exercise alone. Function also improved more with remote support. Against in-person therapy, remote care tied on both scores. No clear gap showed for pain or function. Study quality and bias were graded with care. Remote care thus looks like a fair swap for clinic visits. It may widen access for rural patients.
pmc-13291773:
Theodore Z Cook and co-authors present a 2026 data paper assembling the first specimen-backed occurrence dataset for stoneflies across West Virginia. Stoneflies signal clean water, and the state holds unusually rich diversity for the eastern United States. The team merged museum specimens, fresh statewide collecting, and trusted literature records, with funding from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and northeastern states.

The dataset holds more than 4,500 records from all 55 counties, spanning 134 years and drawn from 17 institutions and private collections. Checking specimens confirmed 150 species from all nine eastern North American families. Fourteen species reported earlier could not be found again, most likely because of naming changes. The records will anchor a planned distribution atlas and checklist.
pmc-13292573:
Lidan He and co-authors trace a 2026 protective circuit in the placenta that fails in preeclampsia, the dangerous pregnancy disorder. The deubiquitinase USP22 runs low in preeclamptic tissue while the necroptosis machinery, RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL, runs high. In oxygen-starved trophoblast cells, necroptosis proved the dominant death route among several tested with targeted blockers.

Removing USP22 worsened the necrotic signaling, while restoring it revived histone acetylation marks and calmed cell death. Gene scans after knockdown found 1,186 changed genes, including the silenced Wnt antagonist SFRP1. The mechanism: USP22 grips the acetyl writer KAT2A and shields it by snipping off K48-linked ubiquitin chains, keeping SFRP1's promoter acetylated and active. A rat model induced with L-NAME backed the pathway in living tissue.
pmc-13293373:
Benjamin N Rome and colleagues test, in a 2026 validation study, whether live prescription fill data can stand in for slow official insurance counts by state. Coverage data often lag, which delays judgment of new health policies.

Quarterly state coverage and fills by payer type were compared from 2013 to 2024 for Medicaid, private cover, and uninsured groups. Medicaid fills tracked Medicaid coverage closely, while cash-pay fills tracked uninsured rates fairly well, and both links were stronger for adults than children. Private cover links were weak. The authors suggest fill data could give fast early reads on policy effects, above all for Medicaid.
pmc-13293473:
Junghee Yoon and co-authors build, in a 2026 expert study, a first framework for virtual reality health literacy in clinical care. Headset-based virtual reality can teach and treat patients, yet the skills patients need to use it well had not been defined.

A three-phase Delphi process ran from January to April 2024, starting with a literature scan and a panel of 15 experts in health care, virtual reality, and health literacy. Two survey rounds rated draft parts, and 13 experts stayed for round two. The final framework holds 5 domains and 14 subdomains, covering expected benefit, effort, and other readiness traits. The work gives clinics a shared language.
pmc-13294273:
Jun-Chen Liu and coauthors pool early evidence on albumin-bound paclitaxel for advanced small cell lung cancer in a 2026 single-arm meta-analysis. Later-line options have improved survival, but the best regimen stays debated and trials of this drug were small and uncontrolled. Four databases yielded nine studies with 334 patients, covering response, survival, and side effects.

Pooled response rate was 25.0% and disease control rate was 62.5% in the reported figures. Median-style pooled survival values reached 3.16 months without progression and 7.23 months overall. Low white cell counts and anemia dominated side effects. Adding immunotherapy looked numerically better in subgroup checks, a lead for controlled trials.
pmc-13294373:
Ziqiang Ding and coauthors build a nanobody T cell engager that can reach targets inside cancer cells in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. Standard engagers only grip surface markers because inner proteins stay hidden, and bulky fragments clump easily. Their two-headed nanobody joins T cells via CD3 while the other head mimics a T cell receptor, reading peptide scraps displayed on HLA-A2 from WT1 or GPC3 proteins.

Lab tests showed strict target-only T cell firing and killing, sparing marker-free cells. In mouse grafts from cell lines and patients, tumors shrank, survival lengthened, and T cell entry rose, with no reported treatment harms. A modular route to inner targets opens many cancers.
pmc-13295873:
Julie Werenberg Dreier and colleagues measure lost working life among people with epilepsy in Denmark in a 2026 register study. They compare losses by the cause behind the seizures, from injury and stroke to unknown origin, against the wider population.

Following more than five million adults, the team find epilepsy after head injury cost the most working years, at just over ten on average. Tumour-related and stroke-related epilepsy also cut working life heavily, and even epilepsy of unknown cause cost over five years. Disability pensions and early death drove most losses, prompting a call for stronger job support.
pmc-13295973:
Mark Kalinich and colleagues propose, in 2026, using simulation to estimate how risky medical chatbots built on large language models really are. Device safety rules were made for predictable tools, yet these systems can give unsafe replies in ways that are hard to count directly.

Fourteen open models were tested on spotting suicidal thoughts and therapy-like requests using made-up datasets judged by psychiatrists. Failure rates fed into estimates of how often a hazard turns into harm, and those estimates spanned a wide range. The authors say simulation can stretch existing device frameworks to cover this new kind of risk.
pmc-13296273:
Junqi Guo, Jiamei Jiang and Hongbo Pan describe, in 2026, two new single-celled species from the mudflats of China's Yangtze Estuary. Using live watching, staining and gene sequencing, they place the ciliates in the little-studied genus Zosterodasys.

Both newcomers carry a distinctive S-shaped band circling the body and differ from relatives in size, shape and the pattern of their water-pumping sacs. Family trees built from gene data suggest the genus may not form one clean branch. The authors say the finds enrich records of estuary microbes and support future ecological monitoring there.
pmc-13296773:
Georgina Ortiz-Martínez and co-authors review, in 2026, melatonin as a many-sided protector after stroke from a blocked brain vessel. Beyond setting sleep, the hormone steadies mitochondria, calms inflammation and guards the blood-brain barrier, all relevant as injury unfolds in phases.

Animal studies consistently show smaller damaged areas and better recovery scores. Human trials remain few and small, hinting at safety and early benefit but unable to prove lasting gains. Dose and timing are still unsettled. The authors present melatonin as a promising add-on needing stronger, larger clinical testing in stroke patients.
pmc-13297273:
Federica Andreis and a large team review, in 2026, cancer-related thinking problems in breast cancer, often called chemobrain. Attention, memory and processing speed can suffer during and after treatment, denting work and daily life for many women.

Causes look many-sided: treatment itself, inflammation, hormone shifts, fatigue, poor sleep, distress and personal vulnerability. Brain scans and blood markers inform research but are not ready for routine diagnosis. Training, exercise, mindfulness and digital programmes help felt difficulties most reliably. The authors call for standard, long-running studies to personalise prevention, support and recovery for survivors.
pmc-13297373:
Two established medicines for alcohol dependence get a side-by-side appraisal in a 2026 review led by Maciej Rząca and colleagues. The authors weigh naltrexone and nalmefene, drugs that act on opioid receptors, and ask how each one performs against drinking outcomes that matter in practice.

Outcomes centered on total alcohol consumption and monthly heavy drinking days, alongside safety, side effects, dropout, and dosing convenience. Nalmefene, taken only when needed, cut both measures, with gains appearing within the first month and holding through follow-up. Naltrexone performed comparably in pooled analyses, and its long-acting injection eased dosing for some patients. Common side effects were mild, mainly nausea and dizziness.
pmc-13297673:
Tooth decay and gum breakdown are usually taught as separate problems, but Yasir Dilshad Siddiqui and co-authors argue in a 2026 narrative review that they form one connected path. Their framework follows disease across the tooth, pulp, and surrounding tissues as a single continuum.

Decay, driven by biofilm imbalance rather than single germs, lets bacterial products seep through dentin toward the pulp. Inflammation there can tip into pulp death, after which infection escapes through root openings and inflames tissues that resemble periodontal disease, blurring diagnosis. The authors propose a pathway-based way to tell these states apart and favor early, minimally invasive care that keeps the pulp alive and seals the tooth well.
pmc-13297873:
Garlic's prized compound allicin breaks down easily, so Hatice Kubra Sasmaz and co-authors tested a gentler purification route in a 2026 study. They paired supercritical carbon dioxide extraction with molecular distillation on garlic from Gaziantep, tuning pressure, co-solvent strength, and flow by response surface methods.

Distillation lifted allicin content from 45.77% after extraction to 67.10%. In digestion models the extracts strongly inhibited Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli during the oral phase, with zones of 36.33 mm and 26.50 mm in younger-adult simulations. Free allicin, however, vanished completely once intestinal conditions turned alkaline and enzymes attacked. The authors frame the process as a scalable, greener route to allicin-rich ingredients.
pmc-13299373:
A boy's stunted growth and developmental delay traced to a gene never before seen mutated in this way, report Niusha Mostafavi and colleagues in a 2026 case study. The six-year-old had early delays and mild scoliosis but none of the classic facial or body features of Wilson-Turner syndrome.

Exome sequencing found a new frameshift change in the LAS1L gene, inherited from his symptom-free mother and absent from population databases. Cell experiments suggested the variant weakens the protein, which helps build ribosomes. The authors argue LAS1L testing belongs in the workup of unexplained growth failure or delay even without the syndrome's textbook signs, and they review earlier reported cases.
pmc-13300473:
Closing a hole between the heart's upper chambers through a catheter is routine, until the anatomy turns awkward. Bushra Shahida Rana and two colleagues offer a 2026 expert review on advanced echocardiography for such challenging secundum atrial septal defects. Drawing on their own center's practice, they focus on transesophageal imaging during the procedure.

Problem anatomies include aneurysmal septa, several defects at once, missing rims, and misaligned septal tissue. Three-dimensional imaging, the authors explain, reveals defect shape and device fit in ways flat scans cannot, guiding size choice and placement in real time. Their practical walk-through aims to keep complication rates low even when the septum is far from textbook.
pmc-13301373:
Narrow blood-vessel grafts clog too easily, and fibrin, the body's own clot protein, might serve as a friendlier tube material. Clara Glomb and colleagues test that idea in a 2026 in vitro study, running human whole blood through fibrin grafts in a Chandler loop circuit. Heparin-coated synthetic ePTFE grafts, the current standard, provided the comparison.

Fibrin tubes, plain or heparin-coated, matched the synthetic grafts on blood-cell sticking, platelet activation, complement triggering, and clot-pathway activity over the short test window. Microscopy of the inner surfaces backed the blood counts. The authors read the parity as early support for fibrin scaffolds in small-diameter vessel engineering, pending longer and living tests.
pmc-13302473:
A blood-count index tracks how psoriasis treatment calms the whole body, Emanuele Trovato and colleagues find in a 2026 retrospective study. Two hundred ten adults received cyclosporine or one of three biologic classes for a year at a single center. The systemic immune-inflammation index, built from routine cell counts, was charted against skin severity scores at four visits.

The index moved with skin scores at baseline and at one year, though not at the middle checks. Its path split sharply by drug class: rising under cyclosporine and anti-TNF therapy, falling steeply and durably under IL-17 and IL-23 blockers. The authors propose the cheap index as a supporting gauge of body-wide inflammation.
pmc-13303473:
Ella P. Jackert heads a 2026 analysis of long-term survival gaps in head and neck cancer in the United States. Using the national SEER registry, the team examined tumor sites, treatment, and outcomes by race, ethnicity, and social factors.

The cohort held 117,893 adults with a primary head and neck cancer. Black patients received surgery less often even after tumor site and stage were taken into account. Five-year survival was lower in every minority group, and lowest for Black patients. Race and ethnicity, low income, and unmarried status each predicted higher death rates, underlining a need for policy and practice changes.
pmc-13304073:
Junyu Wei and co-authors track bacteria in coastal waters off the Leizhou Peninsula, China, through the seasons in a 2026 sequencing study. These microbes drive coastal nutrient cycles, but tropical water patterns over time were poorly known.

Samples gathered from August 2022 to June 2023 showed communities led by Proteobacteria and Cyanobacteria, with one cyanobacterial group peaking in warm months. Variety bottomed out in August and peaked in December, steered by water heat and phosphate. Salt levels shaped community makeup most strongly, and the balance between chance and filtering shifted by season.
pmc-13304173:
José Pereira, Reinaldo Souza, and Ana Moita review light-based electronic devices for renewable energy in a 2026 survey. Such devices harvest light, drive chemical change, and help manage power in cleaner energy systems.

Recent gains in perovskite and hybrid solar cells, light-driven chemistry cells, and nano-structured designs are covered in depth. Better light capture and fewer lost charges push performance upward, while making methods suit large-scale production. Weak points include long-term stability, weather endurance, and environmental safety. Computer-aided design, stacked cells, and joined energy systems are flagged as promising next steps.
pmc-13305273:
Zeenat Mesk leads a 2026 study testing mind mapping as a teaching tool for nursing students in anatomy and physiology. The subject is heavy going for many students, and diagram-based study may lift both scores and drive.

At Palestine Polytechnic University, 82 students split between mind mapping lessons and standard lectures. The mapping group scored higher on the end test with a medium effect size, and reported stronger motivation as well. Weekly study time did not rise in self reports, hinting that gains came from better organization of ideas rather than longer hours at the desk.
pmc-13306473:
Fan Wei studied how the toxic metal cadmium rewires chemical marks on DNA in a medicinal plant in a 2026 study. Sophora tonkinensis plants faced three cadmium levels while both gene activity and genome-wide methylation were measured.

Stress changed thousands of genes and methylation sites, with one sequence context holding most sites and another showing the deepest average marking in reported patterns. Changed regions clustered near gene promoters and edges. Hundreds of genes shifted in both marking and activity at once, many tied to photosynthesis, carbon handling, fat and sulfur pathways.
pmc-13307373:
Elaine Q Borazon and co-authors introduce in 2026 SHAPE Asia, a shared learning network that works to improve food settings in five countries. The network links Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines, and Sri Lanka, where cheap, energy dense, low nutrient foods are now easy to buy.

Members span policy makers, scholars, state agencies, global bodies, media, and civic groups. The network shares lessons across borders, builds skills for advocacy, and turns research into workable policy choices that can cut both undernutrition and obesity at once. It also joins peer coalitions in other world regions that pursue the same broad goal of healthier diets for all.
pmc-13309473:
Ana Maria Capela and colleagues ask in a 2026 review whether ball-like and organ-like cell clusters can stand in for animals in cancer research. The test case is long noncoding RNA, genetic material that does not build proteins but steers cell behavior. Such clusters sit between flat cell cultures and live animals in complexity.

Raising or silencing select RNAs in tumor clusters changed cluster size and growth in the same direction seen in mouse tumors. Clusters cost less and can carry a patient own tumor traits. Animal work still matters for spread and survival questions. The authors argue clusters can cover growth checks, letting animal use shrink to the questions clusters cannot answer.
pmc-13309573:
Iker Loidi and co-authors test number sense in giraffes in a 2026 animal cognition study. Many species can track amounts in the mind, a skill seen as a root of basic arithmetic. Hoofed animals had rarely been tested, and giraffes never had.

Four captive giraffes faced tasks where food amounts were covered after being shown, then joined, reduced, or moved between dishes. Giraffes beat chance when amounts were combined into one dish, but scored at chance when food was removed or shifted across. Two animals may have used simpler cues, such as picking the handled dish. The authors read the pattern as early quantity skill with clear limits.
pmc-13310073:
Fei-Fei Xu and co-authors track gene splicing changes during facial nerve pain in mice in a 2026 study. Trigeminal neuropathic pain is a long-lasting face pain with murky molecular roots. Splicing, the re-cutting of gene messages, can tune nerve cell excitability, yet its time course in the nerve hub was unmapped.

Gene sequencing of trigeminal ganglion tissue at day three and day ten after nerve injury covered onset and settled phases. Skipping of gene segments was the dominant splicing change at both times and grew markedly by day ten. Protein data and single-cell maps placed the changes in cell types. The authors chart splicing as a moving target for pain research.
pmc-13310773:
Maciej Blok reports a 2026 case of large central lung cancer treated with scan guided focused radiation. A woman aged 65 years had stage IV lung cancer that had spread to the brain, with a lung mass too big and too central for standard focused radiation. Immune drugs helped elsewhere, but the lung mass kept growing.

Brain lesions got focused radiation first, then immune care continued with one drug after lung harm. The lung mass then got three large doses spaced ten days apart, with plans redrawn as it shrank. Six month scans showed strong shrinkage and lower activity, with no noted harm. The case hints at a new option for hard cases.
pmc-13311273:
Tijana Tomic and co-authors in 2026 detail a study on how people in early psychosis expect faces to look. The work tests the idea that the brain's predictions about the social world grow less standard in psychosis.

Thirty-four people within five years of a first psychotic episode were compared with 34 controls on face expectation tasks. The psychosis group held less stereotyped expectations about facial expressions. A side analysis in healthy volunteers found a like pattern tied to schizotypy scores. The authors read this as support for psychosis lying on a spectrum, and as a lead for earlier detection.
pmc-13311973:
Shaun O'Hagan and colleagues analyze a 2026 survey study on mothers' views of the new maternal RSV vaccine in England and Scotland. The vaccine, Abrysvo, joined the national schedule in August 2024.

Free-text replies came from 388 eligible mothers of babies hospitalized with chest infections between September 2024 and March 2025 at 30 sites. Four themes emerged: trouble reaching vaccination, too little awareness and information about RSV, safety worries and hesitancy, and seeing the vaccine as a benefit. The results give antenatal services a clear fix list for raising uptake in the program's second season.
pmc-13312073:
Hassan Saleh and co-authors report a 2026 feeding trial testing whether bacteriophages or acidifiers in the diet can blunt a Salmonella Enteritidis challenge in broiler chickens. With antibiotic resistance rising in poultry production, such additives are candidates to protect flocks without routine antibiotics.

Seven hundred day-old Ross 308 chicks were split into five groups, including unchallenged and challenged controls and challenged groups given an antibiotic, bacteriophage, or acidifier. Infection cut feed intake, growth, and meat quality, but both additives eased those losses and raised antioxidant enzyme activity in the blood. The bacteriophage group also kept gut structure closer to normal and showed more helpful cecal bacteria and less Salmonella, results the authors say support phages in antibiotic-free production.
pmc-13312173:
Fan Jiang and co-authors comment, in a 2026 article, on new Australian survey evidence about dual sensory impairment, the combined loss of vision and hearing. Losing both senses is more disabling than either alone, since neither can cover for the other, and the Western Pacific is aging fast while hard data for the worst-affected groups stayed scarce.

The Australian Eye and Ear Health Survey found an age-standardized prevalence of 2.5 percent among adults aged 50 and over, climbing toward 10 percent past age 80. Rates were higher in Indigenous adults, at 5.2 percent against 2.8 percent for others, with the gap opening before age 70. Lacking private health insurance accounted for most of the Indigenous burden. The authors urge earlier, community-based, culturally safe services instead of screening that waits for people to come forward.
pmc-13312273:
Cornelia Carey and colleagues report a 2026 interview study on pre-birth mental health care planning in perinatal services in Dublin, Ireland. Advance planning can cut involuntary admissions and give service users more control, and pregnancy is a high-risk window for relapse, so two large urban maternity hospitals routinely hold planning meetings before birth.

The team interviewed 10 service users and 3 partners about the meetings and the written plans covering birth, the postpartum period, and crisis care. Five themes emerged: hoping for change, a wish to be heard, individualized care, the security of having a plan in place, and the role of the support network. Families valued the meetings, and the authors recommend offering them routinely while minding meeting size, timing, and who attends.
pmc-13312373:
Sanna Isosomppi and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 retrospective study of Finland's national HIV register, who gets diagnosed late and why. Late diagnosis delays treatment, raises illness and death, and costs more, so the team examined new registrations from 2008 to 2023 under an updated definition of lateness.

Of 2,683 people registered, half of the newly diagnosed, 50.3 percent, were diagnosed late. Older age stood out as the strongest independent risk factor, with odds rising steadily per decade of life. Among women, those born in Asia or Africa faced far higher odds of late diagnosis than Finnish-born women, while Finnish-born women had lower odds than men. The authors recommend stronger testing offers and risk awareness aimed at older adults and migrants from high-prevalence countries.
pmc-13313273:
Peter Suenaert and co-workers report a 2026 trial of a pasteurized gut bacterium as a treatment for metabolic syndrome. The strain, Akkermansia muciniphila MucT, had helped gut barrier health in lab work and in an early study of adults with obesity and prediabetes.

The double-blind trial ran in Ireland and Germany with 142 adults who had metabolic syndrome, with or without prediabetes. Each day for four months they took capsules with 30 billion cells of the pasteurized bacterium or a placebo. The main goal, whole-body insulin sensitivity by the Matsuda index, did not differ between groups. Later checks hinted at gains in liver insulin sensitivity after three months in some subgroups. Those gains showed in prediabetic people and in those aged 63 years or older, as reported by the authors. A rise in the hormone GLP-1 after a glucose test was also seen.
pmc-13314573:
Emma Schindler and co-workers report a 2026 case of a pregnancy growing in a cesarean scar that went unseen until surgery. This rare type of ectopic pregnancy follows past cesarean birth and can cause grave harm to the mother.

Their patient was a 31-year-old woman at 14 weeks of pregnancy who came for surgical abortion. The scar pregnancy was found only during the operation. An earlier visit elsewhere had read it as a normal womb pregnancy, and she had traveled out of state for legal care, as the report relates. The womb was emptied with success, but she then bled heavily and needed artery embolization and blood transfusion. The case urges high suspicion after cesarean birth and shows how limits on abortion access can compound risk.
pmc-13314773:
Jing He, Huijuan Wang, Wei Wang, and Na Dong compare two surgery styles for womb prolapse in work published in 2026. Repair with the patient own tissue and repair with a vaginal mesh are the two main routes, and past results clash on which wins on gains and safety.

The study drew 86 patients treated from January 2022 to December 2024, split into a native tissue group of 37 and a mesh group of 49, as counted in the report. The team compared surgery measures, symptom scores, quality of life scores, and patient-rated success. Complications and relapse within one year were also logged. Head-to-head data from one hospital can help women and surgeons weigh a mesh against its known late risks.
pmc-13315673:
V.S. Haetinger and O. Adeola studied in 2026 whether early phosphorus feeding changes how broilers later handle phosphorus in copra meal, a possible alternative feedstuff. Starter diets gave low or enough non-phytate phosphorus for the first 18 days, then grower diets used copra meal as the sole phosphorus source, with or without the enzyme phytase.

A phosphorus-free diet let the team measure basal losses from the body itself. The split-plot design tested whether starter nutrition reshapes later digestive capacity and standardized phosphorus digestibility. Knowing that carryover matters for fair feed values and for cutting phosphorus waste in poultry litter.
pmc-13315973:
Anouk van Hooij and colleagues profiled in 2026 the sugar coating on antibodies aimed at the leprosy germ, comparing patients with spread infection. Antibodies against phenolic glycolipid-I, a main wall part of Mycobacterium leprae, track with disseminated disease yet seem to protect poorly, and their exact role was unknown.

Using liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry in 160 Dutch and 55 Brazilian clinic patients, the team mapped antibody subclasses and Fc sugars. The main subclass, specific IgG1, carried more fucose with less sialic acid and galactose, a pattern usually linked to weaker effector action and poor immune activation.
pmc-13316073:
Jiaxuan Shi and colleagues surveyed in 2026 the health utility values of 827 Chinese patients across six common cancers, using the QLU-C10D questionnaire built for cost-utility work. Values were compared across social, behavioral, and clinical groups with rank tests and median regression models to find key drivers.

The highest median utility, at 0.802 in the reported values, belonged to gastric cancer patients, while breast cancer patients had the lowest, at 0.671 in those same values. Physical functioning and pain drove scores most, above all in gastric and lung cancer. Money pressure mattered most in esophageal cancer, and disease stage mattered most in breast cancer.
pmc-13316173:
Cam Anh Thi Pham, Nguyen Quynh Trang Le, and Dohyeong Kim used a choice experiment in 2026 to learn what draws family physicians to rural work in Vietnam. Commune health stations anchor primary care, yet doctors cluster away from rural areas, so 315 family physicians weighed job offers with varied pay, promotion, living conditions, and clinic support.

A 50 percent salary rise swayed choices most for doctors under 50, assistant doctors, and those with past rural exposure, though extra pay lost power past a point. Doctors who had moved up from commune stations valued promotion and private practice support over pay, showing mixed motives.
pmc-13316273:
J. Usset and colleagues built a statistical method in 2026 to find genomic signs that a cancer patient will not respond to a given therapy. Cancer drug costs keep rising, and targeted and immune therapies often help few patients, so spotting likely nonresponders could spare side effects and system strain.

Applied to whole-genome and transcriptome data from 2,594 patients with advanced disease, the frame recovered known signals and suggested new ones. Examples included immune evasion events in melanoma under checkpoint drugs and KRAS G12 changes in bowel cancer under chemotherapy. Power checks mapped where the approach can detect effects.
pmc-13316373:
Mike Rueb and fellow authors describe a 2026 study of film-based teaching in medicine, built around three medical students joining BaseCamp at the Locarno Film Festival. The young talents program mixes students from film, science, arts, and medicine to learn across fields.

The students screened festival entries, picked out seven films with medical themes, and ran a 75-minute workshop with peers from other fields. Feedback showed strong drive to keep working with film in teaching, and new ideas surfaced, such as video essays and making films jointly with art students. Learners also wanted links with similar projects worldwide. The authors propose a cross-field medical film festival and a symposium as next steps.
pmc-13317773:
Zhiheng Qian authored a 2026 narrative review on blood immune cells in sepsis, the runaway infection response that kills despite modern care. These circulating cells, monocytes and lymphocytes, offer a repeatable window on an immune system that swings between overdrive and shutdown.

Fresh single-cell and tissue mapping work shows monocytes changing state, losing a key display molecule, and lymphocytes dying off or tiring, alongside rewired energy use. Such shifts explain why some patients rebound while others slide into lasting immune paralysis and second infections. Cell-based markers could sharpen risk sorting and guide immune drugs, but mixed patient groups, age gaps, and unstandardized tests block routine use. The author calls for timed, age-aware trials.
pmc-13318573:
Zheng Wang and co-authors report a 2026 retrospective imaging study linking fat around the heart, measured in specific regions, to reduced blood flow in heart arteries as judged by CT-derived flow reserve. Participants were grouped by high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes status.

Scans from 576 people were analysed, with ischaemia defined as a flow value of 0.80 or lower in at least one major artery. Fat thickness was greater in ischaemic subgroups, most clearly beside the left atrioventricular groove, and that measure stayed linked to ischaemia after full adjustment. Adding it to clinical and calcium information improved detection, suggesting a handy extra marker for spotting patients at risk.
pmc-13318973:
Dmytro Kucherov, Serge Dolgikh, and Serhii Podelskyi offer a 2026 theoretical study of learning under tight resource limits. They compare biological learners with freely evolving, weakly bound AI systems. Limits on energy, memory, and computing shape how each explores its world. Models spell out those sampling choices.

For biological systems, steep differences in thinking cost push deep exploration of small regions. That focus yields sturdy, cheap learning. AI systems with ample resources face the opposite trap: no built-in priorities. Uniform or random sampling then wastes effort across the sensory field. No single search strategy wins on accuracy, sturdiness, and low cost together. The authors propose switching between strategies as conditions change. Their framework aims to guide future AI learner design.
pmc-13320173:
Siwei Ren and co-authors map links between brain aging and late onset mental illness in a 2026 computer based study. Older brains that age fast track with three major illnesses that can start late in life, covering wild mood swings, split thinking, and deep low mood. Shared roots, above all immune balance in the brain, may drive both paths.

Learning software first picked aging and illness traits and built an aging score for each person. Mapping models then joined that score to each illness, and network and gene set checks traced the key bridges. Shared traits centered on immune calm, cell upkeep, vessel health, and a heart brain link, while each illness kept its own marks. The work backs joint aging and immune views of late illness.
pmc-13323073:
K Julia Dierksheide and co-authors explain why many bacterial genes favour purine letters, in a 2026 study using a large reporter assay in Bacillus subtilis. In species where RNA polymerase outruns ribosomes, fresh RNA sits exposed to the ending factor Rho, which can stop transcription early.

Purine-rich coding strands dodge that risk because Rho targets differ in content from coding sequence, giving the polymerase room to finish. Species with this runaway transcription show strong purine bias unless they have lost Rho. The pressure also shapes codon choice, suppresses stray reverse transcripts and can block foreign constructs. Genome design, the authors argue, must respect this hidden constraint.
pmc-13324673:
Baoning Zheng and co-authors study how the build order of a three-part protein complex changes emulsion stability in a 2026 food science paper. The complex joins soy protein isolate, a tea polyphenol called EGCG, and polydextrose to carry beta-carotene.

Ternary complexes beat plain protein and two-part mixes on stability and antioxidant guarding. Order mattered most: protein, then polydextrose, then EGCG gave the best heat stability, holding 85 percent after heating. That mix also kept the smallest particles, near 517 nm, and the highest beta-carotene share after 21 days of storage. In lab digestion it released the least fat and carotene. The work shows build order as a design lever for nutrient delivery.
pmc-13325173:
Ufuk Atmaca, Songül Bayrak, and Cetin Bayrak synthesize 21 new propargyl sulfamate compounds as enzyme blockers in a 2026 chemistry study. The targets are human carbonic anhydrases, enzymes tied to glaucoma, altitude sickness, and tumor growth.

A practical route reacted propargyl alcohols with chlorosulfonyl isocyanate to build the set. All compounds blocked enzymes I and II at nanomolar levels, with IC50 values as low as 8.97 nM for the first enzyme. The star compound, labeled 2i, beat the standard drug acetazolamide by 7.72 fold on enzyme I and 15.35 fold on enzyme II. It also led against the tumor-linked enzymes IX and XII.
pmc-13327873:
Jing Zhou and co-authors study how social patterns shape thyroid risk in pregnancy in a 2026 Xinjiang survey. Iodine intake was adequate in the region, yet thyroid disease still varied, so the team looked past nutrition. They enrolled 1,166 pregnant women in 2021 and 2022, testing blood and urine and recording diet.

Grouping by region, income, schooling, job, and smoke exposure gave three patterns, from low-status housewife groups in the north and south to a highly educated professional group. The professional group showed lower TSH levels than the northern low-status group, and the southern group had lower odds of thyroid nodules, with an odds ratio of 0.32 in their model. Social setting thus carried risk apart from iodine.
pmc-13328273:
Alicia Montaner-Ramon, Fatima Camba-Longueira, and Josep Perapoch-Lopez review skin-to-skin care in newborn intensive care in a 2026 narrative review. Holding a fragile newborn against a parent's chest aids clinical and developmental outcomes, yet units apply it unevenly, often from safety worries. The authors map barriers and fixes at several levels.

Barriers span baby factors such as extreme prematurity and breathing support, unit factors such as missing protocols and thin staffing, and parent stress with patchy guidance. Evidence does not back withholding contact when monitoring, preparation, and positioning are sound. Training, simulation practice, checklists, and structured parent teaching raised contact rates in the studies surveyed, the review reports.
pmc-13328473:
Cui Zhao and co-authors engineer yeast to brew a eucalyptus compound from methanol in a 2026 study. Methanol, makable from carbon dioxide, is a tempting factory feedstock, and 1,8-cineole is a valued scent and medicine ingredient. The team rebuilt Pichia pastoris step by step to route methanol carbon into the terpene.

Adding a cineole synthase, strengthening the mevalonate pathway, and muting a rival route gave strong early output, and reshaping methanol assimilation lifted yield further. Boosting two genes, ADE3 and SHM2, curbed formaldehyde harm and raised yield by 82.2 percent in that step, ending at 386.3 mg/L in a 5 L bioreactor run. The platform suits green making of other terpenes too.
pmc-13329373:
Sambit Kumar Parida, Mohit Kotnala, and Suraj Mandal comment in 2026 on a review of stopping blood pressure drugs in older adults. The review pooled four trials with 2,173 patients and found no clear rise in deaths or falls. The comment argues that calling those results reassuring goes too far.

Wide ranges around the estimates leave room for real harm, the authors note, and certainty for many outcomes was rated very low. The four trials also enrolled very different groups, from fit community dwellers to frail nursing home residents with severe dementia. A plan that is safe for one group may not suit another. The comment urges care matched to each patient group.
pmc-13330673:
Saché M. Coury and a large team set out a follow-up study plan on schooling, sex, and later brain health in a 2026 protocol. Alzheimer disease hits women more than men, and early schooling and stress may shape that gap. The RISE-Up extension will re-study 300 people now aged 24 to 26 years from a natural schooling opportunity cohort.

Checks will span self-reports, thinking tests, body markers such as swelling and gut microbes, and brain measures. The aim is to see how teen mobility chances shape adult health and sex-specific paths toward later Alzheimer risk. Genes and early environment will be read together. Results could show where early support cuts later risk.
pmc-13331173:
Igor Baroni Cardoso and colleagues report surgery for rare spinal arachnoid bands in a 2026 case series. These dorsal bands squeeze the cord in the chest spine, disturb fluid flow, and can carve fluid cavities inside the cord. Six patients had microsurgical decompression at one centre between 2021 and 2025, with nerve monitoring during surgery.

The patients had a mean age of 49.3 years in the reported group, and four were women. The T6 level was hit most often. Surgery mostly used half-side bone removal to free six bands and four cavities. Five patients improved and one stayed the same after surgery. One chest infection was the sole adverse event. Scans showed full band and cavity clearing.
pmc-13331773:
Seraina L Meister and co-authors document a 2026 case series of a rodent lungworm, Angiostrongylus dujardini, killing cotton-top tamarins at a Swiss zoo. Seven monkeys died between 2005 and 2024, most found dead with no warning signs.

Post-mortem study showed darkened lungs, nodules, fluid in the chest, and worm eggs and larvae packed in lung tissue and blood vessels, wrapped in heavy inflammation. Rodents host this parasite normally, and monkeys were thought to be dead-end hosts that never pass it on. Finding first-stage larvae in the feces of the most recent case changed that picture, showing tamarins can complete the cycle and spread the parasite. The authors call for closer parasite checks in captive primate groups.
pmc-13333373:
Win Wah leads a large team reporting five-year survival after intensive care for sepsis in Australia and New Zealand, in a 2026 observational cohort study. Short-term sepsis outcomes have improved, but how long survivors carry extra risk, and whether the infection itself or prior ill health explains it, stayed unclear.

From a binational ICU database, the study followed 557,538 adults who left hospital alive after emergency ICU stays from 2018 to 2024. Of these patients, 7.3 percent had sepsis, 11.5 percent had septic shock, and the rest had other conditions. Raw five-year survival was lowest after septic shock at 68.0 percent, then sepsis at 74.2 percent, then other conditions at 78.2 percent. After adjusting for age, frailty, and illness, sepsis without shock carried no extra risk. Septic shock kept an excess through years three to five, with a hazard ratio of 1.09 at that point. Age, frailty, and organ support needs were the biggest death predictors.
pmc-13333473:
Katrin Schmietendorf asks in a 2026 philosophy essay whether talk of circular causality in network physiology describes causation or a fiction. The field pictures the body as a self-organizing network whose patterns, from sleep states to stress, shape the cells and neurons that create them.

Schmietendorf works through the framework of Synergetics, which supplies the field's vocabulary. It offers order parameters that summarize a system's state, plus an enslavement principle by which those parameters govern their parts. Circular causality binds the directions together. She sets this against the debate over downward causation: the idea that higher levels exert causal power over lower ones. Reductionists contest that idea and emergence theorists defend it. Using examples from brain rhythms to immune stress responses, the essay weighs whether macro-to-micro claims are ontologically tenable or explanatorily handy. She argues the distinction matters for how seriously the field's claims should be taken.
pmc-13333773:
Inseo Kim and co-authors profiled lactic acid bacteria as candidate probiotics in a 2026 study joining lab assays with genome analysis. Probiotic value varies sharply by strain, and the genetic reasons for those differences are only partly known.

The team collected 27 isolates from the human mouth and cheese, identifying five species by 16S rRNA sequencing, with Lactobacillus rhamnosus the most common. Isolates differed widely in acid and bile tolerance, sticking to intestinal cells, fighting pathogens, and antibiotic sensitivity. L. rhamnosus and L. reuteri tolerated acid best and showed strong antimicrobial action, while L. reuteri adhered most strongly. Seven representative strains went on to whole-genome sequencing so gene content could be matched against the measured traits.
pmc-13336473: A 2026 correction notice repairs a figure in the Advanced Science article by J Chen and co-authors, whose single-cell study found an anti-inflammatory macrophage type in crescentic glomerulonephritis. The notice reports no new findings. In Figure 5D, a spleen image from one control mouse landed in the wrong panel, which represented a different control group, during figure assembly. It has been replaced with the correct image from a separate experiment batch. The authors re-checked the source files for every figure against the raw data.
pmc-13337373:
Xili Fu and a large team propose a gut-based route for a diabetes drug class to ease drug-resistant epilepsy in a 2026 hypothesis review. About one-third of epilepsy patients resist current drugs, and their gut microbes are often out of balance. The authors connect three strands of evidence into one axis.

DPP-4 inhibitors, they argue, may reshape gut microbes toward short-chain fatty acid producers. Those acids can trigger GLP-1 release, which in turn calms brain inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death while strengthening inhibitory signaling. Each link has support from other disease settings, but the full chain is untested in epilepsy. The review maps experiments that could confirm or refute the idea.
pmc-13337473:
Dong Cao leads a large 2026 team building an explainable machine learning tool for early liver fibrosis detection. Scarring predicts poor liver outcomes, yet early stages hide well. Using NHANES 2017–2020 data, the team classified 6,164 participants by liver stiffness scans and benchmarked 29 learning models after automated feature selection.

A Gamboost model won, reaching an AUC of 0.824 in training and 0.872 in testing cohorts in the reported evaluation, and it held 0.848 on an external set of 684 samples during validation. Body mass index, the liver enzyme AST, and waist size led the predictors, with high AST plus large waist jointly raising risk in the explanation analyses. Routine clinic data could thus flag fibrosis early without a biopsy.
pmc-13337773:
Rosemary Montle and co-authors review Cannabis sativa chemicals for cancer care in a 2026 article. Compounds such as cannabinoids, flavonoids, and terpenes interact with growth pathways and the endocannabinoid system. Interest centers on whether they can slow tumors or improve treatment response.

THC, CBD, and cannabigerol are described as triggering cell death, tuning oxidative stress, and blocking new blood vessel growth. Flavonoids including cannflavin A showed selective harm to several cancer cell types while sparing normal tissue in cited work. Combinations did not always help: some paired effects added up or clashed. A clinical spray, Nabiximols, is noted as early human evidence of combined action.
pmc-13337873:
Qilong Wang and colleagues build clear machine learning tools to flag thinking problems in adults with poor sleep in a 2026 study. Middle-aged and older adults with mild or severe insomnia, judged by nightly sleep length, were the focus. Earlier models rarely separated those severity groups.

Survey data from CHARLS 2015 trained the models, with CHARLS 2011 and hospital data from Gansu used for later checks. Feature selection narrowed the inputs, and a LightGBM model was tuned and explained with SHAP values. Accuracy, calibration, and clinical value were all tested. The approach aims to help clinics spot cognitive risk earlier in patients whose sleep is short.
pmc-13338573:
Barker and colleagues convened a roundtable in 2026 on why preventing a second stroke remains so hard in Australia. About one in four stroke survivors will have another stroke, and drugs plus lifestyle change can cut that risk. Risk control after stroke is often poor and no national care model exists. Twenty-five people joined an online roundtable and small group talks in 2023, including survivors, clinicians, researchers, advocates, and a government representative.

Most priorities clustered around models of care: which programs, settings, and services should carry prevention work. Barriers and aids grouped under coordination between services, funding and staffing, and the slow path from research to practice. Priorities were wide and sometimes clashed, though some were shared across all groups. The authors call secondary prevention a complex system problem and urge a national model that works with that complexity and builds on the shared ground.
pmc-13340073:
Vasu Saini and a large team develop a urine test for high-risk HPV to predict cervical cell changes in a 2026 study. Urine collection is easier than cervical brushing for screening. The PCR workflow detects 14 high-risk types tied to precancer.

In 82 women with confirmed CIN2 or worse, urine sensitivity reached 92.7 percent for CIN2-plus and 93.9 percent for CIN3-plus as reported, beating brush results there. A second group of 983 women tuned the cutoff values by outcome. Balanced thresholds for the two lesion grades were proposed. A urine-first path could widen cervical screening reach.
pmc-13341473:
Computer-aided drug discovery gets a history, toolkit, and ethics check in a 2026 review by Rebekah Clarke and colleagues. Four decades of computational methods have helped deliver several approved medicines, and artificial intelligence tools now put stronger prediction within reach of non-specialists.

Alongside the history, the authors compile two practical resources: cloud platforms for virtual screening and a large suite of free ADMET prediction tools for medicinal chemists. They close with emerging concerns around biased data, transparency, computing costs, and the environmental footprint of big models. The aim is a working guide for everyday discovery teams, not just specialists.
pmc-13341873:
Fasting plus weights performs about the same as weights alone, in a 2026 multilevel meta-analysis by Mengyuan Zhang and colleagues. Eleven studies with 303 mostly young participants compared intermittent fasting combined with resistance training against training alone over 4 weeks to 12 months.

Pooled effects across strength, endurance, muscle size, and explosive performance came to g = 0.09, a trivial difference, with no clear gaps in any single outcome. Time-restricted eating was the commonest fasting style, and training programs were matched between arms. For lifters eyeing fasting for other reasons, the synthesis suggests their gym progress need not suffer.
pmc-13342273:
Xiao-hui Hu and co-authors compare two keyhole operations for stubborn heel pain in a 2026 retrospective study. Both procedures treat chronic plantar fasciitis that has resisted standard care: one cuts the fascia, the other detaches part of it, and the team tracked patients for a year after surgery.

Records covered 33 patients treated between 2021 and 2023, with 14 in the cut group and 19 in the detachment group. Pain, foot function, and general health scores improved well in both groups. Patients in the cut group, though, recovered sooner and scored better on function and health surveys at three and six months. Either operation can work, but the simpler cut healed faster here.
pmc-13342473:
Zifang Kong and co-authors introduce a 2026 statistical method for studying repeated health events alongside measurements taken over time. Biomarkers are often sparse and unevenly timed, and repeat events such as kidney stones or heart problems are linked across time, which strains older joint models.

Their FRAILTY method first pulls key time patterns from scattered measurements using functional principal component analysis, then feeds those scores into a frailty model with an autoregressive structure. Simulations showed lower error, better agreement, and stronger detection than rival methods. Tests on blood pressure trial data and a kidney stone cohort showed the method works on real data and can sharpen forecasts.
pmc-13343973:
Elizabeth A. Alexander and co-authors find that a host stress protein helps Salmonella feast in the gut in 2026. The bacterium blooms by breathing nitrate made during infection, and the team asked whether the cell stress factor CHOP, part of the unfolded protein response, feeds that supply.

Infected mice showed colon stress markers rising while CHOP itself oddly fell. Mice lacking CHOP suffered far less inflammation, colonization, and tissue damage, and their colons held less nitrate because immune cells made less nitric oxide synthase. Starved of nitrate, wild-type Salmonella lost its growth edge over a mutant unable to use it. Host stress signaling, it turns out, provisions the invader.
pmc-13347673:
Hellen Myezwa, Tania R. van der Merwe, and Tonderai W. Shumba introduce a special edition that rethinks clinical training, in an editorial from 2026. Writing from a Global South setting where most people rely on stretched public care, the editors argue that skill drills alone cannot prepare health workers for fair, tech-rich, complex practice.

Three linked strands run through the collected pieces, covering learning design with simulation and digital tools, growth of professional identity and reflective judgement beyond task skill, and system accountability for curricula. Frameworks such as the global functioning classification are woven into teaching, aiming for practitioners who think sharply, act fairly, and adapt with care.
pmc-13347773:
Deepak Bangera, Shrikanth Muralidharan, and Raghavendra M. Rao review massage effects on the circulation, in a literature review from 2026. Clinical trials, prior reviews, and mechanism studies were gathered to judge how hands-on soft tissue work shifts blood pressure, heart rate, limb flow. Vessel function in varied patient groups.

Helpful effects were supported overall, yet results swung with massage style, session length, and who was treated, which left the picture uneven across studies in the synthesis. People with high blood pressure or weak limb flow are named as groups who might gain most as an add-on therapy. But standard trial designs are urged before firm dosing advice can be given.
pmc-13347873:
Norma Houlihan and colleagues map what helps or blocks migrants with prior mental illness from reaching primary care, in a scoping review from 2026. Five databases were searched for work from 2014 to 2024 under a standard scoping method. Thirteen studies passed the entry rules for combined telling of access factors in this group.

Barriers far outweighed helpers, and linked barriers pointed to care that fails to fit varied language, culture, and combined body-mind needs of migrant patients in the synthesis. Services built around the majority culture leave this group underserved at the first door of care, so the review charts where redesign and future study should focus first.
pmc-13347973:
Anna Greti Everding and colleagues report four cases of stress heart syndrome during cosmetic surgery, in a case series issued in 2026. Four healthy young women aged 27 to 34 years became unstable during varied plastic procedures. Heart ultrasound through the food pipe showed the ballooned, weak left ventricle that marks Takotsubo syndrome, followed by severe shock in each case.

Heart support machines were started for all four, heart motion later returned fully to normal, and survival reached 100 percent in the small series. Added adrenaline drugs, stacked procedures, and long operating times may worsen such cases, so the authors urge risk screening, fast ultrasound, and early support to cut deaths.
pmc-13349773:
Andrio Palayukan and Ummi Maimunah report a hidden spleen abscess twice mistaken for chest fluid, in a case report from 2026. A 52-year-old man with healthy immunity came in with fever and left belly pain after earlier hospital care for pneumonia and pleural fluid gave only brief relief. Two weeks later scans finally showed a spleen abscess behind the returning symptoms.

Blood tests showed high white cells and inflammatory marks, broad antibiotics plus surgery followed, and pus growth came back empty in the reported course. Recovery was full, and the authors argue that empty cultures in such hidden cases should speed, not stall, the call for surgery.
pmc-13349873:
Chen Liang and co-authors studied a liver-protecting drug, magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate, in patients with blood cancers receiving newer antitumor therapies in a 2026 multicentre analysis. Records came from 13 Chinese centres, and matched groups compared 324 treated patients with 182 controls.

Rates of liver injury were similar between groups at 21, 30, and 60 days, and overall side effect rates matched after baseline. Controls, however, showed larger rises in several liver enzymes, and treated patients had fewer overall liver-related side effects, driven by fewer mild enzyme changes. Severe events stayed similar. The drug may soften mild liver strain during treatment without adding clear risk.
pmc-13350173:
Qilong Wang and colleagues compared eight large language model chatbots in 2026 on public mental health information. With mental illness burdens rising and professional help scarce, people increasingly ask chatbots, whose quality, clarity, and warmth in this sensitive area needed testing.

A bank of 48 questions from literature, search trends, and clinic consultations was put to each model. Scores covered information quality, source openness, reading level, and empathy as judged by psychiatrists and from a user's view. Two models led on quality, but none wrote at the recommended easy reading level, and models rarely volunteered their sources. The results urge caution and better design before chatbots advise on mental health.
pmc-13350573:
Ana González-Cordón and a Barcelona team reported real-world results in 2026 for long-acting injectable HIV treatment, cabotegravir plus rilpivirine given every two months. The prospective study followed people switching to the injections at one hospital from February 2023 to February 2025 and gathered their own ratings of the experience.

Women made up only 8 percent of switchers, 57 of 741, against 14 percent among those staying on other therapy, a gap the authors highlight. Virus control was checked several ways, split by sex. Replacing daily pills with six injection visits a year suits many, but who gets offered the switch matters.
pmc-13351673:
Ya Dai leads a 2026 narrative review of behaviour-based vision training for childhood amblyopia, often called lazy eye. Standard care with patching or drug blurring often suffers from poor adherence and weak gains in two-eye vision. Training built on brain plasticity offers another route, and the review covers its basis, main forms, and results.

PubMed and Web of Science were searched for work from January 2015 to December 2025, and 100 studies were included. Forms covered include perceptual learning, two-eye training, digital treatments, and virtual reality. The review compares training with standard therapy, looks at combined plans and adherence, and notes wide differences in study designs that block pooled analysis.
pmc-13352473:
Yiran Deng and co-authors sort mixed anxiety and depression patterns in older Chinese adults and link them to thinking scores in 2026. Anxiety and depression often occur together in later life, but their combined forms vary. A survey covered 5,116 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older, using standard anxiety and depression scales plus a brief dementia screen.

Latent class analysis found four groups: high mixed symptoms at 7.41 percent, moderate mixed at 8.64 percent, high depression at 13.94 percent, and low symptoms at 70.01 percent. Mixed and depression-led groups scored lower on thinking tests, with all P values below 0.001. Adults with both anxiety and depression showed the steepest thinking disadvantage.
pmc-13353073:
Praveen Baskaran, Abigail S Bower, and Ashley I Simpson review early care for lower brachial plexus injury after shoulder trauma in 2026. Unlike earlier optimal-contribution software, OptOrch exposes its objective function and constraints so breeders can adjust orchard-specific rules, including diversity thresholds, contribution limits, graft availability, relatedness restrictions, and outside pollen flow. The authors demonstrate the toolkit with simulated scenarios that vary diversity thresholds and pollen contamination. The simulations quantify the trade-off between genetic gain and diversity and compare feasible deployment strategies under realistic conditions.
