pmc-2836773:
Webb, Joseph, Yardley, and co-authors review internet programmes that aim to change health behaviour. The internet is used ever more to deliver such interventions, from quitting smoking to eating better. Earlier reviews had not sorted out, in a systematic way, which features make online programmes work.

The team pooled results across studies and linked effectiveness to three things: the theory behind a programme, the behaviour change techniques it uses, and how it is delivered. Their findings give designers evidence for building online health tools that do more than inform; they actually shift habits.
pmc-3163573:
Alikhan, Petty, Ben Zakour, and co-authors present BRIG, the BLAST Ring Image Generator, for comparing microbe genomes. Seeing genome matches as pictures is of great use for spotting genetic differences between closely related microbes. Fresh ways to draw genomes were needed to check, read, and share sequencing results well.

BRIG draws genomes as ring-shaped bands, aligning shared and missing regions at a glance. Differences that signal new traits, such as resistance or virulence, become easy to point to. The simple format made genome comparison accessible to labs without specialist graphics skills.  Doctors use such matches when a familiar microbe behaves in a new way in patients.
pmc-3599573:
Akbarzadeh, Rezaei-Sadabady, Davaran, and co-authors review liposomes: their kinds, how they are made, and their uses. Liposomes are sphere-shaped vesicles made of one or more fat-like layers, much like cell membranes. First described in the mid-1960s, they have become useful models, reagents, and tools in many sciences.

The review covers fields from physics and chemistry to medicine, where liposomes carry drugs inside their shells. Sorting types and making methods helps researchers choose the right carrier. Liposome delivery now supports approved medicines and vaccine tools used worldwide.  Cosmetics and food science also use liposomes, a breadth the review covers.
pmc-3933873:
Zhang, Kobert, Flouri, and co-authors present PEAR, a fast and accurate tool for merging Illumina paired-end reads. Illumina paired-end technology reads DNA fragments from both ends at once. When fragments are short enough, the two reads overlap and can be merged into one longer read.

Tools for merging already existed for some cases, but accuracy and speed varied. PEAR was built to merge reads reliably at scale. Longer, cleaner merged reads improve assembly and variant detection in sequencing projects of every kind.  Amplicon studies merge reads first, so merger quality shapes all downstream ecological conclusions.
pmc-4081273:
Van der Walt, Schönberger, Nunez-Iglesias, and their team presented scikit-image in 2014. Scikit-image is a library for image processing in the Python language. It supplies algorithms and helper tools for work in research, teaching, and industry.

The library is released under a liberal open source license, so anyone may use and adapt it. Its interface is well documented, which lowers the bar for new users. Tasks range from cleaning and filtering images to finding edges and shapes. As part of the wider Python science stack, it helps labs build image workflows that others can run and check.
pmc-4261873:
Bardou, Mariette, Escudié, and their colleagues built jvenn in 2014, an interactive viewer for Venn diagrams. Venn diagrams are a common way to compare lists, showing what is shared and what is unique. Biologists use them often to compare gene lists from different analyses.

Unlike a static picture, jvenn lets users click and explore the overlaps directly in a web browser. Lists from different conditions or species can be swapped in and compared at once. The shared part often holds the genes most worth studying further. A clear, hands-on view saves time and helps teams agree on what a list comparison really shows.
pmc-4839673:
Talevich, Shain, Botton, and their colleagues built CNVkit in 2016. Copy number variants, where a DNA stretch is deleted or repeated, matter in inherited syndromes and in cancer. Targeted DNA sequencing is increasingly used to infer such changes from read depth.

CNVkit detects genome-wide copy number changes and draws them for inspection. It works with the targeted panels that clinics use for cancer and genetic testing. Clear plots help analysts judge whether a change is real and where its edges fall. Reliable copy number calls from standard sequencing panels widen access to this layer of diagnosis.
pmc-5014473:
Martin, Murrell, Golden, and their co-authors released RDP4 in 2015. RDP4 is the latest version of a recombination detection program for sequence alignments. Recombination, where viruses swap genome pieces, can distort evolutionary trees if it goes unseen.

The Windows program runs a wide array of methods to detect and visualize recombination in virus genomes. It can also strip the evidence of recombination from an alignment so other analyses run cleanly. Viruses such as HIV recombine often, which affects vaccine and drug work. RDP4 helps researchers spot those events and judge how virus families truly evolved.
pmc-5267473:
Sekhon, Cartwright, and Francis studied the acceptability of healthcare interventions in 2017. Acceptability, whether patients and staff find an intervention suitable, is increasingly seen as something to consider when designing, evaluating, and putting care into practice. The literature gave almost no guidance on defining the term or measuring it.

The authors reviewed existing reviews on the topic and built a theoretical framework for acceptability. A clear framework gives trial teams questions to ask before and during a study. Interventions that patients dislike fail in real life, however well they work in theory. The framework helps designers catch that problem early and improve uptake.
pmc-7296073:
Bianca Parker and co-authors surveyed in 2020 a genus of gut bacteria called Alistipes, a group scientists are only beginning to understand. Members of this genus were first isolated mostly from medical samples, and they belong to the Bacteroidetes, a large bacterial phylum with a strong role in gut imbalance and disease. Interest grew as studies began linking these bacteria to conditions well beyond the gut.

The review gathers evidence tying Alistipes to inflammation, to cancer, and to mental health, and weighs where the links look protective and where they look harmful. The authors are candid that findings conflict and that context seems to matter a great deal. Their summary gives researchers a clear starting map of a microbe whose story is still being written.
pmc-7319273:
Xiandong Chi and colleagues reported in 2020 that they had found a human antibody able to block SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19. Their target was the viral spike protein, the three part structure the virus uses to latch onto cells and fuse with them. Most antibody work at the time aimed at the spike's receptor binding region, the part that grips the cell.

This antibody instead attaches to a different stretch of the spike, its N-terminal domain, and still stops the virus from infecting cells. That result mattered because it showed the spike has more than one vulnerable spot. Drugs and vaccines that press on several spots at once are harder for a changing virus to escape.
racine-athaliah-donkersley-1873:
Athaliah, Racine's last tragedy, stages a child king hidden in the Temple of Jerusalem. J. Donkersley's 1873 English blank verse renders the biblical drama of Joash and the high priest Jehoiada. Queen Athaliah, who seized the throne by blood, dreams of a child she cannot name.

The priest guards the boy until the hour comes to crown him before the people. Racine drew the tale from scripture and gave it the tight, singing form of French classical tragedy. In English dress the play completes a shelf of Racine's tragedies, and many judge it his most sacred work.
ralston-russian-fairy-tales-1873:
W. R. S. Ralston, a Scots scholar at the British Museum, made this first great English set of Russian tales in 1873. He read Russian well and drew from the best stores of tales in that tongue. No such set had been made for English readers before his work.

The tales hold the rusalka, the water maid of Slav lore, in her gay and grim forms. House spirits, wood demons, and bold young heroes fill the rest of the rich store. Ralston's set gave the English world its first true sight of the fairy lore of Russia.
riemann-hypotheses-geometry-clifford-187:
Bernhard Riemann gave his famous lecture on the foundations of geometry in 1854, though it was printed only after his early death. William Clifford's 1873 English version brought it to a wider world. Riemann asks what we truly know about space itself.

He argues that space need not be flat, and that its shape is a fact to be measured, not assumed. Curved spaces of many kinds become open to math for the first time. Einstein later took Riemann's tools to build general relativity. Few short lectures have changed physics and math so deeply. Clifford, himself a fine geometer, kept the translation close and clear.
stowe-palmetto-leaves-1873:
Palmetto-Leaves, printed at Boston in 1873 with pictures, gathers Stowe's sketches of Florida. She wintered at Mandarin on the St. Johns River and wrote as a delighted newcomer. The contents open with Nobody's Dog and A Flowery January in Florida.

Orange groves, alligators, and steamboat trips fill the bright early pages. She also describes freed Black families building new lives after the end of slavery. Part travel book and part gentle sales pitch, the sketches urge Northern settlers south. Historians credit the book with helping to spark Florida's first great land boom in the years that followed its release.
the-alchemy-of-happiness-1873: The Alchemy of Happiness, 1873. Another edition. This book preserves that work. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
the-alchemy-of-happiness-tr-from-the-tur: The Alchemy of Happiness, tr. from the Turk, abridgement by H, a, homes, 1873, the turkish abridgement. This book preserves that translation. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
the-great-riots-of-new-york-1712-to-1873: Joel Tyler Headley chronicles New York's long history of mob violence — from colonial slave revolts to the terrible Draft Riots of 1863. Each uprising is told with a journalist's eye for drama and detail. A gripping, sobering tour through the city's turbulent past.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume twenty-three of Casanova's memoirs: the tale winds toward evening. The adventurer's road grows longer. Twilight approaches. Twenty-third volume: evening approaches, the long road lengthens, the long road lengthens toward evening, the long road lengthens toward evening.
tob-10173:
Hosea is the twenty-eighth book in this King James ordering, named for the prophet at its center. Unusually, Hosea lived out his message. According to the text, God told him to marry an unfaithful wife, so his broken home became a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to God.

Through grief, accusation, and forgiveness, the short book pleads for the nation to return. Judgment speeches give way in the closing chapters to promises of mercy reaching beyond punishment. Readers feel the argument in domestic terms: betrayal, anger, and a love that refuses to end the story at divorce. That personal frame sets Hosea apart among prophetic books.
tob-10273:
Enoch, the patriarch who walked with God, became the hero of writings that the Hebrew Bible left out. R. H. Charles translated the Book of Enoch, or 1 Enoch, the version kept as Scripture by the church in Ethiopia. Its visions shaped ideas found later in the New Testament.

Enoch tours heaven and watches the fall of the Watchers, angels who came down to earth and sinned. He sees stores of wind and fire, thrones of judgment, and the fate of the wicked and the just. Charles's careful work made the strange, vivid book readable again for modern students.
tob-10473:
Psalms through Malachi complete the Douay-Rheims Old Testament in Part Two, in the revision associated with Bishop Richard Challoner. The translation began at the English College in Douai in 1609, made for Catholics living under a Protestant crown. Its language is solemn and formal, close to the Latin Vulgate behind it.

The Psalms in this rendering carry a distinctive music long used in Catholic prayer, and the prophets speak with grave weight. Wisdom books and the later histories fill out the volume. As a monument of recusant scholarship, the Douay-Rheims remained the Catholic Bible in English for generations and is still prayed by traditional Catholics.
tob-10573:
A letter known as First Clement went from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth near the end of the first century. Tradition credits Clement, an early leader at Rome, as its author. It ranks among the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

Corinth had thrown out its elders, and the letter urges the church to restore them and live in order and humility. It cites the Old Testament, the words of Jesus, and examples of envy and its harms. Early churches read it aloud beside scripture, and it shows how Christian leaders taught within living memory of the apostles.
tob-4073:
One architectural treatise survives from ancient Rome: the Ten Books of Vitruvius, written under Augustus. Joseph Gwilt's translation of 1826 carried it to English builders. Temples, theaters, houses, waterworks, and war machines all fall within the Roman architect's brief.

Vitruvius demands that building unite firmness, usefulness, and beauty, a trio still quoted in schools of architecture. He treats proportion, site, climate, and materials with a practitioner's care. Renaissance masters from Alberti to Palladio rebuilt the classical world from his pages. Checked from the 1919 printing, Gwilt's version remains readable, direct, and full of working detail.
tob-4273:
Lewis Spence surveyed The Myths of Mexico and Peru in 1913, introducing English readers to the gods of the Aztecs, Maya neighbors, and Incas in one illustrated, wide-ranging volume. Quetzalcoatl the feathered serpent, Huitzilopochtli the war god of Tenochtitlan, and Viracocha the creator in the Andes receive full treatment, along with creation stories and flood tales.

Behind the myths stands the calendar-stone cosmos: ages of suns, each ending in destruction, and rituals meant to keep the current world alive. Spence also records what the Spanish conquest did to these traditions and their texts. Readers get the pre-conquest religions of two civilizations as a popular scholar of his era understood them.
un-ga-res-a-69-73:
Central Africa's states built a standing team on safety in 1992, and Resolution A/69/73, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, backs its work. The United Nations Standing Advisory Committee on Security Questions in Central Africa was set up by the Secretary-General. Its task is to spur arms limits, disarmament, and calm in the sub-region, and to rebuild trust among its member states.

The text recalls the guides for full disarmament from the first special session of 1978. It notes the shared stand the team's states took at Sao Tome in 2011, on the world arms trade pact then in the making. Trust steps and arms limits, worked out by the region for the region, are the core of the call.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/73, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, reviews regional confidence-building measures through the United Nations Standing Advisory Committee on Security Questions in Central Africa. It notes the Kinshasa Convention on small arms control. It notes a road map against terrorism and proliferation. It notes concern over the Central African Republic crisis and the creation of the MINUSCA mission in April 2014. It notes shared action against threats such as Boko Haram and the Lord's Resistance Army.
un-sc-res-1073:
Clashes over a tunnel exit at Jerusalem's holy places drew the Council on 28 September 1996. Saudi Arabia's letter of 26 September, for the Arab League states, told of Israel opening an entrance to a tunnel near the Al Aqsa Mosque. Days of fighting followed in Jerusalem, Nablus, Ramallah, Bethlehem, and Gaza. Many Palestinian civilians died, and Israeli soldiers and Palestinian police also clashed. Foreign ministers joined the Council's debate on 27 September.

The Council called for the instant halt and reversal of every act that had worsened the state of affairs. The safety and protection of Palestinian civilians had to be secured. Talks inside the Middle East peace process had to resume at once on their agreed basis. The agreements already reached were to be applied on time. The Council decided to follow the situation closely and stay seized of the matter.
un-sc-res-1373: One of the Council's formal texts, Resolution 1373 is carried in this catalog under 2001. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1473: Resolution 1473 is a voted act of the fifteen-member Security Council, preserved from the official UN record through English Wikisource. Such texts matter because their wording can bind every UN member state. The entry gives the full decision, from its opening clauses recalling earlier steps to the closing paragraphs that set the action in motion.
un-sc-res-1573:
Timor-Leste's United Nations support mission received its final extension on 16 November 2004. The Council praised the Timorese people and government for their peace, stability, and institution building. The mission, UNMISET, was in its consolidation phase under resolution 1543 (2004). Yet the country had not reached self-sufficiency in public administration, law enforcement, or security.

The Council extended UNMISET for a final six months, to 20 May 2005, keeping its tasks, shape, and size unchanged. The mission was told to focus on its exit strategy and on Timorese ownership of the work. Donors were urged to keep giving, and United Nations agencies were told to plan a smooth shift to a development framework. The Council noted the Serious Crimes Unit's push to finish its probes by November 2004. It also conceded the unit might not fully answer the call for justice over the 1999 violence.
un-sc-res-1673: Kept under number 1673, a Security Council resolution survives as a record transcription from English Wikisource. The Council's authority on peace and security comes from the UN Charter, and resolutions are its exercise in writing. This entry preserves one exercise entire: the findings the members adopted and the steps those findings set in motion.
un-sc-res-173:
Security Council Resolution 173, adopted on July 26, 1962, recommended Burundi for membership in the United Nations. The small central African kingdom had gained independence from Belgium on July 1 of that year, ending decades of rule first by Germany and then by Belgium under League and UN mandates. Its leaders at once sought a seat in the world body.

The council found Burundi fit under the Charter and sent the bid to the General Assembly, which seated the new state that September. Burundi joined in the great wave of African nations entering the UN as empires wound down. The brief text is one tile in that larger picture of decolonization.
un-sc-res-1773: Kept as Resolution 1773, this Security Council text comes from the official record through a transcription by English Wikisource. The format will be familiar to any reader of UN documents: concern weighed in the preamble, action ordered in the clauses. Preserving the format along with the words keeps the entry faithful to the original act.
un-sc-res-1873: Adopted in 2009, Resolution 1873 is a Security Council act preserved through a Wikisource transcription of the record. Its paragraphs are numbered for a reason: each can be lifted out and cited on its own in later disputes. The entry keeps all of them together and in order, which is how the Council issued them.
un-sc-res-273: Holding number 273 in the Council series, this resolution carries a 1963 date in the library catalog. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-573:
Israel's bombing of the PLO headquarters in Tunis was condemned in October 1985. Tunisia's complaint letter of 1 October told of an air raid on Hamman-Plage, in the southern suburbs of Tunis. Israel claimed responsibility at once. The raid caused heavy loss of life and wide material damage. Tunisia's foreign minister addressed the Council.

The Council condemned vigorously the act of armed aggression against Tunisian territory. It was a flagrant breach of the Charter and of international law, the text said. Israel was told to refrain from such attacks and from threatening them. Member states were urged to take measures to dissuade Israel from striking at the sovereignty of any state. Tunisia was declared entitled to reparations for the loss of life and the damage done, for which Israel had claimed responsibility. The Secretary-General was asked to report on the text's working by 30 November 1985.
un-sc-res-673: In the sequence of Security Council decisions, Resolution 673 is the entry catalogued for 1990 in this library. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations.
un-sc-res-73:
Armistice agreements between Israel and its Arab neighbors changed the Palestine question in 1949. The agreements had been reached through talks led by the United Nations mediator. They grew out of Resolution 62 of 1948, which had called for an armistice. Resolution 73 was adopted on 11 August 1949. Later texts cite that date, although the file's own header gives 21 August.

The Council noted the agreements with satisfaction. It called them a major step toward lasting peace in Palestine. The armistice replaced the truce ordered in 1948, but one part of that order stayed in force. The call for an unconditional cease-fire, from Resolution 54, held until a final peaceful settlement was reached. The acting mediator, his work complete, was released from any further duties under the Council's earlier resolutions. The mixed armistice commissions would now watch over the agreements, with help from the truce observers on the ground.
un-sc-res-973:
Western Sahara's promised referendum still had no date in January 1995. On 13 January 1995 the Security Council restated its pledge to hold the vote without further delay. The vote would let the territory's people choose their future. The Settlement Plan accepted by both parties set the rules. Voter identification had begun, though it moved slowly. The Council praised MINURSO for the progress made so far.

Both parties had to work fully with the Secretary-General and the mission. The planned timetable in his December report set the pace. The Council stayed committed to a just and lasting solution. It asked him to keep it informed of every step. Identification of voters later bogged down in appeals, and the vote never came.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1073, adopted on 28 September 1996 by fourteen votes to none with the United States abstaining, answers a week of deadly clashes in Jerusalem and the West Bank. Israel had opened an entrance to an archaeological tunnel near the Al Aqsa Mosque. Fighting spread through Jerusalem, Nablus, Ramallah, Bethlehem, and Gaza, killing many Palestinian civilians and also costing lives in clashes between Israeli soldiers and Palestinian police.

The Council called for an instant halt to, and undoing of, every act that had sparked the crisis, including the tunnel opening. It urged both parties to honor their existing agreements and get the peace process moving again. Foreign ministers of several countries had joined the Council's debate, underlining the alarm.

Binding world rules against terrorism are laid down here on 28 September 2001, weeks after the September attacks. Passed under Chapter VII, the text orders every state to act, not just those directly attacked. Its target is the money and support networks that let terrorist groups operate.

States must block terrorist funding, freeze the assets of people involved in terrorism, and ban help or safe haven for them. They must also share intelligence, tighten border and document controls, and bring terrorists to justice. A new Counter-Terrorism Committee, made up of all Council members, would track how each country carried out these duties, with reports due within 90 days.

East Timor's support mission, UNMISET, has its drawdown adjusted on 4 April 2003. Timor-Leste had made real progress since independence with the mission's help. Yet security problems remained, and building a capable national police force was the top priority identified.

The cuts are slowed and reshaped. The police component gains an international formed unit for one year and more training capacity in key areas. On the military side, two battalions stay near the border line through December 2003, with supporting units, rather than leaving on the old schedule. Total military peacekeepers are to fall more gradually, reaching 1,750 later than first planned.

Timor-Leste's UN mission gets a final stretch in Resolution 1573, adopted unanimously on 16 November 2004. The Council praised Timorese leaders and citizens for the peace and stability they had built since independence, and credited UNMISET, the support mission, for progress during its consolidation phase. Partners helping with institutions and development were thanked as well.

Even so, the text is candid that Timor-Leste had not reached self-sufficiency, above all in public administration, law enforcement, and security. The Council extended UNMISET into May 2005 so its remaining tasks could be finished in an orderly wind-down. It also noted improving ties with neighbors and work toward settling border questions, and it commended the Serious Crimes Unit's efforts.

The committee that watches over resolution 1540, the text barring weapons of mass destruction from reaching non-state actors, is extended on 27 April 2006. The committee had reviewed the first round of national reports on how states were applying the rules. Not every state had yet reported.

The 1540 Committee's mandate is extended for two years, and it is told to step up its work promoting full implementation. States that had not filed a first report are called on to do so without delay. The committee is to keep helping states that ask for assistance with their laws and controls, and to report back on progress before its renewed mandate ends.

A Belgian-run trust land in central Africa became a kingdom in 1962. Burundi won its freedom on 1 July that year. King Mwambutsa IV took the throne of the new state. Its bid for a UN seat came weeks later. Resolution 173 passed with no dissent on 26 July 1962.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit the Kingdom of Burundi. The Assembly agreed that fall. Burundi came in beside its twin, Rwanda, freed the same day from the same trust. The two states shared much: hills, tongues, and a tense mix of Hutu and Tutsi. Their paths since have been marked by bloodshed. This calm one-line text holds none of that dread. It is a plain legal birth note.

Lebanon's force, UNIFIL, is extended until 31 August 2008 on 24 August 2007. The force had been greatly expanded after the 2006 war. Commitment to Lebanon's sovereignty and to full respect for the cessation of hostilities and the Blue Line is restated.

All parties are called on to respect the halt in fighting and cooperate fully with the United Nations and UNIFIL. Work on the causes of the conflict is pressed for, with a note that the abducted Israeli soldiers still had not been released. The Secretary-General is to keep reporting on the carrying out of the 2006 settlement, including progress toward a permanent ceasefire and a long-term settlement between Lebanon and Israel.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended on 29 May 2009. Full settlement talks between the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders had been running since 2008, and the progress made and the leaders' joint statements are warmly welcomed. Finding a solution, it is echoed, rests first with the Cypriots themselves.

UNFICYP's mandate is extended for a further period, and the leaders are strongly urged to use the rare opening: faster talks, more trust, and a constructive spirit. More confidence-building steps are sought, including opening further crossing points. Both sides are also told to settle the demarcation of the buffer zone with the force. That is a matter of urgency, so the mission's work is not hampered by disputes over its lines.

UN Security Council Resolution 1973 — the historic 2011 resolution authorizing the no-fly zone over Libya. It permitted all necessary measures to protect civilians from Gaddafi’s forces. The 2011 Libya no-fly is the historic authorization: the Libyan civilians’ protection formally permitted.

Senegal complained to the Council about shelling from a Portuguese base in late 1969. Shells fired from Portuguese Guinea had hit the village of Samine in southern Senegal. One person was killed and eight were badly wounded on 25 November. More shelling followed on 7 December. Resolution 273 was adopted on 9 December 1969.

The Council strongly condemned the Portuguese authorities for the shelling. Houses were destroyed in the attacks, and a gendarmerie building was struck. Portugal was again called on to stop violating Senegal's sovereignty and territory at once. The Council warned that it would meet to consider other measures if Portugal failed to comply. It also kept the question on its agenda, so the matter stayed open for further action.

Sao Tome and Principe is recommended for United Nations membership in Resolution 373, adopted unanimously on 18 August 1975. The Council weighed the bid of Sao Tome and Principe, a two-island country in the Gulf of Guinea. It had gained independence from Portugal a month earlier, in July 1975.

The Assembly was asked to admit the new state, and it did so that September. Admission texts rarely run longer than this one; the real work is done by the recommendation itself, which the Charter makes a condition for membership. For one of Africa's smallest countries, the resolution marks the formal start of its presence in international politics.

Israel's bombing of Tunis is condemned in Resolution 573, adopted in October 1985 by fourteen votes to none with the United States abstaining. On 1 October, Israeli jets had struck a target in the southern suburb of Hammam-Plage, and Tunisia complained to the Council the same day. Its foreign minister told the Council the raid caused heavy loss of life and extensive material damage, and Israel claimed responsibility openly.

The Council condemned vigorously what it called armed aggression against Tunisia's soil, a flagrant breach of the Charter. It demanded that Israel refrain from such attacks and from threatening them. It also held that Tunisia was entitled to appropriate reparations for the lives lost and damage done.

Israel refused to receive a fact-finding mission to the occupied territories in October 1990, and the Council answered on 24 October. Resolution 672, passed on 12 October after deadly violence in Jerusalem, had ordered the mission. The Secretary-General briefed the Council on the refusal on 19 October. Resolution 673 is the reply.

The Council deplored Israel's refusal to receive the mission. The Israeli government was urged to reconsider its decision. The Council insisted that Israel comply fully with Resolution 672, so the mission could go ahead as planned. The Secretary-General was asked to send in the report that the earlier resolution required. The Council said it would give that report full and speedy consideration. The dispute over access became part of the wider record on the occupied territories.

Armistice deals between Israel and its neighbors drew the Council's blessing in 1949. On 11 August, it adopted Resolution 73. Nine members voted yes and none voted no. The Ukrainian and Soviet republics held back. The deals had grown out of talks held under the Council's 1948 truce calls.

The text hails the deals as a big step toward lasting peace. It declares that they replace the earlier truce. It restates the order for a full, lasting ceasefire. Mixed armistice panels, chaired by the UN truce chief, would watch the lines. The Council also frees the Acting Mediator from his duties. The lines blessed here shaped the region's map for eighteen years.

Resolution 973 was adopted unanimously by the UN Security Council on 13 January 1995, and it deals with Western Sahara. The Council was trying to move a long-delayed settlement plan toward a referendum that would let the people of the territory decide their own future. Progress on identifying who could vote had begun, but it was going slowly.

Acting on a December 1994 report from the Secretary-General, the Council approved a larger deployment for MINURSO, the UN mission running the referendum process. It repeated its pledge to hold a free and fair vote without further delay and pressed both parties to cooperate fully with the mission. The Secretary-General had to report back by the end of March 1995 on staffing, supplies, and final plans.
wheatley-poems-1773:
Phillis Wheatley published Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral in London in 1773. The title page names her as servant to Mr. John Wheatley of Boston in New England. Brought from Africa as a child and held in slavery, she had won rare fame as a young poet by then.

The contents list verses on virtue, on the works of God, and on the death of preacher George Whitefield. Elegies, hymns to morning and evening, and a poem on Goliath of Gath fill out the book. Her clear and poised verse forced a doubting world to face Black genius, and it fed early calls to end slavery.
zola-fat-and-thin-1873:
Vizetelly's English version calls Zola's 1873 novel The Fat and the Thin, or Le Ventre de Paris. A Shakespeare motto up front gives Cassius a lean and hungry look. Vizetelly's opening essay centers on the vast central markets of Paris, the Halles.

The markets form a world of their own, teeming with life at set hours. Zola loved subjects where vast crowds could be shown in motion, Vizetelly notes. Into that plenty steps Florent, an escaped political prisoner, thin and haunted among the fat and thriving. The clash of hunger and plenty becomes a strong parable of appetite in all its forms.
